sources.title: Casey Adams: discipline, curiosity and gratitude, and how a podcast built a company
sources.originalTitle: Ep. 027 - Unleashing the Power of Discipline and Gratitude: Interview with Casey Adams
sources.summary: Casey Adams explains how a career-ending sports injury pushed him into entrepreneurship, how he used a podcast to build relationships, and how that network funded and launched Media Kits. He lays out his core values and the discipline habits (75 Hard, cold plunges) behind them.

principles.text: Do hard things on purpose; the discipline you build carries into every area of life.
principles.quote: just doing things that are hard you learn so much about yourself

principles.text: Say yes to uncomfortable opportunities; you can't predict which one pays off.
principles.quote: you can't predict those correct occurrences in life and I think that's the beauty of just you know saying yes to things

principles.text: Use a podcast as a vehicle to meet people, learn, and create business opportunity.
principles.quote: the podcast was just a vehicle that I wanted to start to meet people to learn something and to create business opportunity from

principles.text: Set an aggressive volume goal and cold-DM your way there to build confidence and rapport.
principles.quote: I set a goal I wanted to do 60 interviews in the first 90 days of hosting the show and that was my mission of just cold DM Outreach

principles.text: Build real relationships first; don't ask for favors, and opportunities follow.
principles.quote: I truly believe in just letting things happen and not being like can you do this favor and get this person on my show

principles.text: Stay narrowly focused: be the best at one thing rather than doing everything.
principles.quote: we just wanted to go what we said inch wide mile deep

sources.title: How Casey Adams turned a bedroom podcast into relationships, investors and Media Kits
sources.originalTitle: CASEY ADAMS: Running An Empire In Your 20s & Interviewing @LarryKing  | BEEHIVE PODCAST
sources.summary: Casey Adams recounts starting his podcast at 17, landing Larry King through a chain of networking luck, and building the Media Kits startup from a manual pain point. His core themes are starting without overthinking, seizing opportunities, putting relationships first and improving daily.

principles.text: Don't overthink starting; just begin and iterate from there.
principles.quote: أعتقد أن الكثير من الناس يبالغون في التفكير بشأن مجرد البدء في حين أنه من المهم فقط أن تبدأ الأمور وتنطلق من هناك.

principles.text: Create opportunities by putting yourself around great people, then keep showing up.
principles.quote: يجب عليك فقط وضع نفسك في موقف يجعلك تختلط بأشخاص عظماء، سواء كان ذلك في عشاء، أو في فعالية تواصل، أو من خلال تقديم بودكاست.

principles.text: Grab opportunities in the moment; ask "if not now, when?" and don't bet they'll return.
principles.quote: الفرص تأتي وتذهب، والأمر يعود إليك لتغتنمها في لحظتها، ولا تراهن على ظهورها مجدداً.

principles.text: A podcast builds lasting relationships that can become investors and partners.
principles.quote: كانت نسبة كبيرة من المستثمرين في Media Kits نتيجة مباشرة للعلاقات التي بنيتها على مر السنين عبر البودكاست.

principles.text: Build products from a repeated manual pain you personally lived (stale, unverified creator stats).
principles.quote: لماذا لا توجد طريقة لصُنّاع المحتوى لإنشاء مجموعة إعلامية لا تصبح أرقامها قديمة بمرور الوقت؟

principles.text: Use social media as a producer, not a consumer: reply, message and create.
principles.quote: أحاول دائماً قضاء وقتي في جانب الإنتاج

sources.title: Casey Adams on happiness, relationships, listening and how he landed the Larry King interview
sources.originalTitle: Finding Happiness, Favorite Podcast Guests and Larry King | Casey Adams & Jacqlyn Burnett DSH #282
sources.outlet: Digital Social Hour Podcast by Sean Kelly
sources.summary: Casey Adams and fiancée Jacqlyn Burnett discuss happiness, gratitude, vetting relationships and mentorship. Casey shares how he got to interview Larry King through organic relationship-building, plus the importance of listening and commitment in business and love. Light on tactical growth content.

principles.text: Don't judge people before you know them; time and quality interactions are how you vet relationships.
principles.quote: don't judge someone if you don't know someone

principles.text: Lead relationships with value: ask how you can bring value to the person rather than being transactional.
principles.quote: the first question I always asked myself when getting to meet someone is just how can I bring value to this person's life

principles.text: Great opportunities come from genuine, organic relationships, not from asking. Get to know people first and the timing follows.
principles.quote: I'm not one that would ever say like ask hey can I have your dad on my show but just the timing and the natural organic relationship that we had

principles.text: Listening beats talking. Prioritize being a listener in both business and relationships.
principles.quote: you'll never learn anything when you're talking therefore Embrace being a listener

principles.text: In a world of endless options, commitment wins in both business and relationships; you can't do everything.
principles.quote: in business you need to commit to something you can't be the person just trying to do everything cuz you're going to go nowhere

principles.text: Treat a business plan and a relationship alike: regularly sit down, assess, and adjust rather than set it and forget it.
principles.quote: you sit down you assess you maybe pivot the business plan a little bit maybe you add some things in there right same thing with a relationship

sources.title: Casey Adams on podcasting as a network-building engine and pivoting from sports to entrepreneurship
sources.originalTitle: Episode 01 - Casey Adams
sources.summary: Casey Adams recounts how a neck injury ended his football path and pushed him into entrepreneurship, then shares how he started his podcast to build relationships and why he now prioritizes quality and just starting. He also touches on handling hate with understanding, surrounding yourself with good people, and NFTs as proof of ownership for artists.

principles.text: Use a podcast as a relationship and deal-flow engine, not just a content format.
principles.quote: he talked about building relationships making creating deal flow from it and really making it a platform to have conversations with people that you want to talk with

principles.text: Set an aggressive volume goal early and move fast; scrappy execution teaches you the craft.
principles.quote: I really set a goal out I said hey I want to interview 60 people in the next 90 days right so I just set out on this mission to move quick

principles.text: As a space gets crowded, quality and distribution matter more than output volume.
principles.quote: it's now all about quality and distribution

principles.text: Don't overthink starting: pick a concept and title, begin, and figure it out as you go.
principles.quote: don't overthink it have a show idea come up with a great title and concept and start and figure it out

principles.text: Respond to haters from a place of understanding; most people flip when they see your intentions.
principles.quote: I would say like 90 of people flip okay and they see my point and apologize sometimes

principles.text: Be careful whose advice you take and surround yourself with great people.
principles.quote: you have to surround yourself with great people and you have to be very careful with the advice you take

sources.title: How Casey Adams turned a podcast into investors, deals and a business: relationships, cold DMs, long-term commitment
sources.originalTitle: Podcasting and Entrepreneurship with Casey Adams: Insights from Creator Economy & SaaS Innovations
sources.summary: Casey Adams explains how six-plus years of hosting a podcast produced relationships that later became investors, advisors and clients. He covers a simple cold-DM blueprint for landing big guests, why podcasts should be monetized through brand and vertically integrated deals rather than CPMs alone, and why long-term commitment beats short-term hacks.

principles.text: Build relationships by giving value first and listening deeply; business opportunities follow later without being forced.
principles.quote: I've never learned anything while I was listening and to Simply Be a listener

principles.text: Make it easy for a guest to say yes: research them, reference someone they like, state a clear ask, and keep the time ask short.
principles.quote: I was like hey it would be an absolute pleasure to have you on my show you know my podcast uh I recently had Robert Green on the show

principles.text: Cold DMs are still the main way to land guests; keep shooting your shot and persist.
principles.quote: you don't you miss 100% of the shots you don't take

principles.text: Focus on getting your reps in early rather than chasing the biggest names; skill compounds and momentum follows.
principles.quote: getting your reps in is the most important part

principles.text: Relationships built through content become a natural gateway to validation, warm intros and fundraising.
principles.quote: we raised a round of funding from 37 Angel Investors and about 80 to 90% of those investors were past guests on my podcast

principles.text: Don't sell podcasts on download numbers alone; treat the show as part of your personal brand and package vertically integrated deals.
principles.quote: you could look at three different media kits in this example where they could have the same exact data

sources.title: How Casey Adams built a fulfillment company: calculated bets, copying the best, customer transparency
sources.originalTitle: THE CALCULATED SUCCESS OF CASEY ADAMS
sources.summary: Casey Adams recounts going from a casino family and mediocre student to lawyer, operator and investor who helped scale a fulfillment business to a Maersk sale. Key themes: treat investing as risk/reward math, copy experts and improve slightly, fix weaknesses by going straight to the activity, and win customers through transparency and acquisitions worth more to you than to the seller.

principles.text: Treat investing as calculated risk and reward, not a system you can beat or fall in love with.
principles.quote: it's just a question of risk and reward

principles.text: Don't invent; copy the best and add one small improvement.
principles.quote: I'm trying to take 99% copy and do one little thing a little bit better

principles.text: Interview the top performers, compare to your own approach, then build your own process.
principles.quote: I figured out who all the best students were and I went and asked them what they did and compared it to what I did and I built my own process

principles.text: Be honest about your weaknesses first; ego blocks learning.
principles.quote: it's being internally honest about weakness yeah and admitting hey I should be good at this and I'm not

principles.text: Make a hidden service transparent to customers; itemized value also uncovers unbilled revenue.
principles.quote: I wanted them to understand what we were doing why we were doing it I wanted them to feel like our warehouse was theirs

principles.text: Buy what is worth more to you than to the seller, and sell when it is worth more to others.
principles.quote: something was more valuable to us than to someone else we should buy it yeah and if something was more valuable to them than to us we should sell it

sources.title: Curiosity Compounds: Casey Adams on podcasting as a life and business engine
sources.originalTitle: Curiosity Compounds: Lessons from 500+ Interviews
sources.outlet: Inside The Inspired with Jonathan Z. Cohen
sources.summary: Casey Adams reflects on eight years and 400+ episodes of hosting, and how his podcast became the foundation for his companies, his angel round, and his network. He covers where podcasting is going, how he preps interviews, why curiosity and showing up beat strategy, and the thinking behind his new company Listener.com.

principles.text: Use a podcast as a vehicle for business, not just content: it opens doors to capital, partners and relationships.
principles.quote: during my first uh tech startup we raised round of funding from 37 angel investors and pretty much 90% of the investors were past guests on my podcast

principles.text: Podcasting is still early, and competition is high but there is room to find a unique voice.
principles.quote: there's more competition than ever, but there's still so much room to find your unique voice if you are someone that's looking to step into this world.

principles.text: Prepare for interviews lightly so the process stays exciting and sustainable over years.
principles.quote: what's allowed me to be so like have longevity and have so much excitement about every single interview I still do is because I don't make the preparation for each show like so daunting

principles.text: Attach stories, rules and quotes to lessons so they stick and shape daily behavior.
principles.quote: having rules and laws and stories to reference in your life of why you do things I think is super empowering

principles.text: Cultivate relationships with peers and people around you now, since they become tomorrow's movers and shakers.
principles.quote: the people that are right around you today are the people like the movers and shakers of tomorrow.

principles.text: There is no strategy for spotting rising talent; curiosity about everyone, and saying yes to rooms and opportunities, is the edge.
principles.quote: I don't think there's a strategy to it. I think it's just a a curiosity, right?

sources.title: Casey Adams on bouncing back from injury, momentum, and 'keep going, never quit'
sources.originalTitle: I Interviewed 400 Successful People (Here's What They Told Me About Failure) | Casey Adams
sources.summary: Casey Adams explains how a near-paralyzing football injury at 16 reshaped his identity and drive, and how he started a podcast at 17 with no plan, just momentum. He argues for focusing on the next single step, building relationships through content, and letting adversity become part of your story.

principles.text: Make adversity part of your story instead of letting it define you as a victim; ask who you are now that it happened.
principles.quote: I think the people that are able to take those situations and grow from them and make it a part of their story is whether that's a comeback story or just something that was a a pivot

principles.text: Attach meaning to positive milestones the way we do to negative ones; that builds identity and compounding momentum.
principles.quote: put it in reverse of the day you did something significant and like attach meaning and purpose to it because that is what not only cements who you are your identity

principles.text: Start before you're ready; the first version doesn't need perfect gear or strategy, just ship it and build momentum.
principles.quote: it wasn't this grand plan and strategy and launch strategy and let me get the perfect title and audio equipment

principles.text: A podcast compounds into relationships, learning, and later business opportunities, including funding from past guests.
principles.quote: about 80 to 90 percent of the funds raised were J like from past guests on the show

principles.text: Don't let comparison paralyze you; ask what the one simple step is today that moves you forward.
principles.quote: what is one simple thing you can do can you share a thought on a tweet can you make a 15 second video on Tick Tock

principles.text: Focus on the next step in front of you; big goals become doable when reduced to today's action.
principles.quote: focus on the next step in front of you and ask yourself will this next step kill me and if the answer is no you can keep moving forward

sources.title: How Casey Adams built credibility, pivoted, and launched MediaKits from a neck injury
sources.originalTitle: How Casey Adams Built MediaKits in his 20s
sources.summary: Casey Adams recounts how a sports injury pushed him into entrepreneurship, personal branding and podcasting, and how that network led to MediaKits. He shares principles on building credibility by showing up, documenting stories, pivoting deliberately, and spotting product ideas from repeated client requests.

principles.text: Build credibility by genuinely associating with credible people, starting small and scaling up.
principles.quote: it was build credibility by associating with credible people and and to do that very genuinely and for me it was through the podcast

principles.text: Show up physically and digitally: DMs, events, in-person meetings. Showing up opens doors a young founder otherwise can't reach.
principles.quote: you have to show up whether that's digitally in the dms or you know posting content or physically and showing up to events and just being in the right rooms

principles.text: Document your experiences and tell stories; authentic stories are what stack credibility over time.
principles.quote: it's just documenting those experiences right it's talking about them right like this is a clear example talking about this on a podcast

principles.text: Set an ambitious, hyper-focused volume goal to build skill and open doors fast.
principles.quote: i want to do 60 interviews in 90 days and i ended up knocking that out of the park

principles.text: Pivot deliberately and go all in: focus, build, and if it doesn't work, pivot again. Stay comfortable being uncomfortable.
principles.quote: when you pivot you like focus on it and build it and figure out if it works stick to it if it doesn't pivot again

principles.text: Spot product ideas from repeated customer requests: manually building and updating media kits revealed the need for an always-current, shareable one.
principles.quote: why isn't there a way for creators to easily build up media kit that never gets out data that you can easily share through a link

sources.title: Casey Adams on raising VC from podcast guests, landing big guests, and building a network from nothing
sources.originalTitle: E #37: How to attract High Quality Guests Ft. Casey Adams
sources.summary: Casey Adams explains how he raised $1.5M pre-seed for Media Kits largely from podcast-guest relationships, and how he built a network from a small Virginia town. He shares how to land high-profile podcast guests, prepare for interviews, build lasting relationships, and why to just get started.

principles.text: Your network is your net worth: fundraising came from relationships built long before you need the money.
principles.quote: your network is your net worth and you know it's a very cliche thing to hear and say but the only reason that I was able and we as care to myself my business partner and our team were able to raise Capital uh was from our pre-existing relationships

principles.text: Raising capital: nail your story, pitch people who give real feedback and want you to win, and stay consistent.
principles.quote: number one really nail down your story of what you're doing right like every product every company you're selling a story right you're selling why you why now and just why in the market

principles.text: Fundraising is a game of consistency; there is never a perfect time, so get after it.
principles.quote: it was a game of pure consistency getting Nose getting rejections but just truthfully powering through

principles.text: Start an interview podcast as a growth hack for networking, learning, and building a personal brand.
principles.quote: starting a podcast specifically an interview show is such a growth hack to building a network

principles.text: Land big guests by starting with people you know, then ask and follow up persistently via social DMs.
principles.quote: never be afraid to not only reach out but follow up to um to go out there and ask right you never you're never going to get anything unless you ask for it in a polite way in a unique way

principles.text: Build relationships through consistent small acts of showing up, responding, and caring over time.
principles.quote: building relationships means showing up to an event that they invite you to building relationships means getting back to someone's text message or picking up their phone call whenever they call you

sources.title: How Casey Adams built a podcast into a fundraising and relationship engine from age 17
sources.originalTitle: Decades of Knowledge at 23… Casey Adams Blows My Mind🤯
sources.summary: Casey Adams explains how starting a podcast with no plan at 17 compounded into 450+ interviews, a funded startup and an exit. He covers shipping fast, consistency, intentional relationships, building products from real pain points, and listening as a learning edge.

principles.text: Start immediately; overthinking a launch costs months and a quick first step beats a perfect plan.
principles.quote: there was no you know overthinking there was no like true strategy or plan and I think that was one of the uh the biggest blessings at the time

principles.text: Set an aggressive volume goal with a deadline and execute against it to create momentum and access.
principles.quote: I set a goal I wanted to do 60 interviews in 90 days which is a lot and I just started being diligent about reaching out to people that I wanted to have on the show

principles.text: Cold outreach to bigger names works if you shoot your shot; a small ask can open the door.
principles.quote: I ended up getting a meeting with Gary ve when I was 17 like a five minute thing in New York City just from a cold DM on Instagram

principles.text: Long-form content compounds into intentional relationships and trust, which turn into real business opportunities like fundraising.
principles.quote: about 90% of those investors were previous guests on the podcast right so when I think about the uh the long tale of not only creating content but the compound effect of relationships but intentional relationships

principles.text: Build products from pain points you or people close to you actually experience, starting with the first small step.
principles.quote: it was just a problem that again we were dealing with that we saw through a friend and we just started with the first step

principles.text: Stay consistent by tying the medium to a bigger purpose; it is the backbone creating opportunities, not the only business.
principles.quote: it's not that the podcast is something that oh like it's my only business and the only way I make money it's it's the backbone of everything that creates so many opportunities

sources.title: How podcast advertising really works in 2026: trust, beyond-the-download analytics, and ecosystem sponsorships
sources.originalTitle: How Podcast Advertising Actually Works in 2026, with Casey Adams & Jonathan Baer
sources.summary: Casey Adams (Listener) argues that podcast value now lives beyond the monthly download. Publishers should represent their whole ecosystem (long form, clips, newsletters) to sponsors, and small shows should win creative long-term deals with brands already in their orbit.

principles.text: Podcast trust compounds from long time in the listener's ears, which expedites relationships and makes ads more valuable.
principles.quote: you can expedite relationships from you and a guest to you and a listener when you're sitting with someone in their ears for an hour or two hours.

principles.text: Monthly downloads are a weak metric: a download is a device fetching a file, not proof anyone listened.
principles.quote: If I subscribe to your show, it's your device downloading it. I might download 12 episodes from a podcast this month and not listen to one of them.

principles.text: Show sponsors the impressions they missed by buying only the long-form episode; use that as a sales tool.
principles.quote: we think our tool can help say, "Hey, you only sponsored X, but you missed out on 8 million impressions the last 90 days."

principles.text: Advertisers should vet a show on culture and brand signals across platforms before looking at download reports.
principles.quote: is there an emerging listener base? Can you find a culture on social and comments and shares?

principles.text: Emerging shows should build long-term partnerships with brands that believe in them, not cold pitch big budgets.
principles.quote: brands that you believe in that believe in you and that you can actually build partnerships with long term.

principles.text: Do the reps early without worrying about listeners; volume of episodes teaches you what works and opens doors.
principles.quote: But by doing the reps, it opened up so many doors

sources.title: How Casey Adams turned a teen podcast into a funded startup and Listener, an AI podcast analytics platform
sources.originalTitle: From Podcaster to Platform: Casey Adams on Listener, Data, and AI
sources.summary: Casey Adams explains how a podcast started at 17 became the foundation of his career, funded his last startup from past guests, and led to Listener. He covers data fragmentation beyond downloads, AI features for podcast networks, how brands should use podcasting, and his delusional-optimist view of AI.

principles.text: A podcast builds a network that later becomes capital and opportunity: his guests became his angel investors.
principles.quote: we ended up raising just over a million dollars for the business and we had 37 different angel investors and pretty much all of those investors ers were past guests on my podcast.

principles.text: Treat a podcast as a multimedia business, not just audio: video, clips, events, communities and merch all matter.
principles.quote: the modern podcast is, you know, yes, has great audio and they're on all the platforms, but video, the live events, the private communities, the merchandise

principles.text: Use AI to remove manual workflow, e.g. auto-associating social clips to episodes with human approve/deny.
principles.quote: we think about it like getting to inbox zero for your podcast of like hey we we know that you know here's 15 to 20 clips that the AI believes is associated with this episode

principles.text: Brands should engage podcasting three ways: start a show, sponsor shows, and get executives booked as guests.
principles.quote: getting booked on F podcast as a brand from like an executive level is critically important of like going direct to source

principles.text: Stay lean and fast with AI; slow six-month builds get outdated, so ship and get feedback quickly.
principles.quote: if you're a team and you spend 6 months building something, the reality is in 6 months things will be a lot better, be a lot different.

principles.text: The biggest AI risk is being unaware of its capability, so be a lifelong learner and optimistic about the upside.
principles.quote: the biggest risk I don't think is um you know, how we implement it or what it's used, but it's being unaware of the true capability and the impact of what is happening right now.

sources.title: Casey Adams (Degreed): Culture, Saying No, and Why Trust Is a Leader's Core Job
sources.originalTitle: How Having Great Leaders Is The Key To Building A Successful Company | Casey Adams, Degreed
sources.summary: Casey Adams, who leads global business solutions at Degreed, explains how a market-defined category can trap an innovator, why he says no to distracting customer demands, and how hiring and hard-problem handling shape culture. He closes with a view that breaking an employee's vulnerability-based trust is the worst leadership betrayal.

principles.text: Culture is set by how you handle hard problems and treat people in them, not by perks.
principles.quote: when you get into the hard things, I think the way that you respond to problems and challenges and treat people with dignity and respect, I think that helps set your culture more than anything.

principles.text: Every hire or exit shifts culture, so hire the best people around a core set of values and fit them to the team.
principles.quote: every single person that you add or remove from your team has a little impact on the way your culture works.

principles.text: Refuse customer demands that pull you off your product DNA, even when they would pay for them.
principles.quote: there's definitely customers who have said I need you to also have this LMS component. We said we're not going to do that. It's not the DNA of what we want to build.

principles.text: Don't let a market-assigned category box you in; complacency there makes an innovator irrelevant.
principles.quote: it's really easy to get complacent and stay in that box. And to do that in an innovative tech space is a surefire way to become irrelevant.

principles.text: Once everyone adopts your buzzword, re-educate the market on how to make it drive business impact.
principles.quote: the word skills is almost meaningless anymore.

principles.text: A leader's biggest betrayal is building trust and then using people's vulnerability against them.
principles.quote: I think the biggest betrayal you can do is to break is to create that environment and then take that trust and then put it somewhere else.

sources.title: Casey Adams on personal branding, podcasting as deal flow, and building Media Kits
sources.originalTitle: Casey Adams Talks About Podcasting, Entrepreneurship and Building Your Personal Brand (2021)
sources.summary: Casey explains how he used a podcast and in-person networking to build a personal brand that opened doors to investors, mentors and his startup, Media Kits. He covers focusing on one platform, earning confidence through track record, and treating time quality as more important than hours.

principles.text: Personal brand is built on accomplishments and association credibility, which is how people remember you.
principles.quote: your personal brand is built on your accomplishments built on what you're doing and that's how people are going to remember you

principles.text: A podcast works as a vehicle for authority, deal flow and networking by collaborating with people who have credibility.
principles.quote: the podcast for me has always been deal flow networking opportunities has connected me with so many great people that have that has led to business opportunity

principles.text: A strong personal brand makes you attractive to partners and investors who bet on you, not just the business.
principles.quote: they know I have great relationships through my podcast and through meeting all these people but my personal brand is something that they want on their cap table

principles.text: Meeting people in person has outsized upside over Zoom; showing up builds lasting relationships.
principles.quote: there's so much upside in that because a you're more easily remembered b you have that connection of actually shaking someone's hand

principles.text: Confidence comes from a track record you can point to, built through consistency before pitching big names.
principles.quote: the confidence comes from track record and actually knowing what you're talking about

principles.text: Focus on quality of time and tangible goals rather than hours worked.
principles.quote: it's not necessarily about the time you spend working is about the quality of time you spend

sources.title: Casey Adams on why podcasting is now a multi-platform media business, not just downloads
sources.originalTitle: Podcasting vs. Modern Media: What You're Getting Wrong
sources.summary: Casey Adams, founder of Listener.com, argues that podcasting has outgrown RSS and download counts. Shows are now ecosystems spanning long-form video, short clips and newsletters, and publishers should treat them as media companies. He covers per-platform measurement, brand trust over CPMs, and why execution matters more than ideas in the AI era.

principles.text: Follow the audience: formats keep shifting, and clinging to the past costs you opportunities.
principles.quote: هو: أين الجمهور؟ وأين يتجه الاهتمام؟ وإدراك أن الصيغ لا تتغير الآن فحسب، بل ستستمر في التغير، وإذا حاولت البقاء في الماضي، فلن أقول إنك ستتخلف عن الركب، لكن لن تحظى بنفس الفرص

principles.text: Run a show as an ecosystem: long-form, short-form and a newsletter are different ways to reach people.
principles.quote: وأعتقد أن على كل بودكاست وشبكة التفكير في عرضهم كنظام بيئي يضم المحتوى الطويل، والمحتوى القصير، والنشرة الإخبارية المرتبطة بالعرض.

principles.text: Treat your show and network as a media company, with serious commitment and production investment.
principles.quote: عليك أن تعامل برنامجك وشبكتك كشركة إعلامية ، لأن الأمر ببساطة هكذا.

principles.text: AI can give ideas, analysis and strategy, but execution is what separates winners.
principles.quote: ولكن مثل أي شيء في الحياة، التنفيذ هو كل ما يهم، أليس كذلك؟

principles.text: Keep reinventing: your show today shouldn't look like your show a year from now.
principles.quote: أنت بحاجة إلى الاستمرار في التغيير وإعادة الابتكار؛ فبرنامجك اليوم لا ينبغي أن يشبه برنامجك بعد عام.

principles.text: Brands buy trust and association, not just impressions; sell the long-term brand connection.
principles.quote: لكن الأمر يتعلق أكثر بالارتباط بالعلامة التجارية. وأعتقد أن هذا هو موطن الثقة في البودكاست التي تريد العلامات التجارية حقاً الاستفادة منها.

sources.title: How Casey Adams went from a neck injury to founding MediaKits: momentum, commitment, and timing
sources.originalTitle: Casey Adams - CEO and co-founder of MediaKits and Host of The Casey Adams Show
sources.summary: Casey Adams traces his path from a high school sports injury to podcasting, a book, and co-founding MediaKits, a creator analytics tool. He stresses stacking small wins, going all in on a venture, spotting problems firsthand, and building confidence through uncomfortable repetition.

principles.text: Stack small early wins; they build momentum that keeps you committed longer.
principles.quote: just micro wins do build momentum and i believe momentum helps you stick with something longer and have more fulfillment in the process

principles.text: Once you have something worth pursuing, go all in; part-time founding invites hurdles.
principles.quote: there's no part-time founder and if you are a part-time founder it's i'm sure you're gonna have a lot of hurdles

principles.text: Don't wait for perfect timing; the right moment never just arrives.
principles.quote: if you have a great idea and you know you don't think the time is right like the truth is the time will never just be right

principles.text: Turn a non-technical weakness into a strength by making team-building your core focus.
principles.quote: we're non-technical co-founders right which could be looked at as a disadvantage but for us we use it to our advantage to build an incredible team and to make that our core focus

principles.text: Build products from problems you see firsthand, like repeatedly hand-editing a friend's outdated media kit.
principles.quote: why isn't there a way for creators to easily share their data and analytics that never get outdated that you can simply share through a link

principles.text: Build confidence by putting yourself out there and introducing yourself to people.
principles.quote: to build confidence number one is like put yourself out there and just introduce yourself to people and start learning more about them

sources.title: Casey Adams on podcasting: brand value, imperfect launch, and Spotify tag sharing
sources.originalTitle: Casey Adams & Chase Chewning: How to Be a Full Time Creator & Podcaster | Ever Forward Radio
sources.summary: Casey hosts Chase Chewning and mostly asks questions; his own contributions are brief. He frames podcasting as a brand and networking tool, shares that he launched imperfectly on AirPods and a $100 mic, and notes that frequent episodes and Spotify tagging drove download spikes.

principles.text: Start a podcast for brand and networking value; it pays back many times over.
principles.quote: starting a podcast is very beneficial to your brand and networking and that's the main reason i do it and there's there's you know it comes back tenfold

principles.text: Ship imperfect and build momentum; quality can improve later.
principles.quote: i not didn't care about the quality but i was just so obsessed with putting it out there getting something going and going with that momentum right like the quality can always become better

principles.text: Don't wait for perfect; take imperfect action.
principles.quote: you can't you know just wait for it to be perfect exactly and then go gotta take imperfect action

principles.text: Frequent episodes drove a spike in downloads.
principles.quote: i saw a huge spike in downloads because i was putting out so many frequent episodes and it was easy to do interviews

principles.text: Share podcast links in a way that lets tagged people reshare in one tap; a big account's reshare spiked downloads.
principles.quote: if i tag you and i'm sharing your our spotify podcast link and it's on my instagram story and i tag you if you share that post you automatically share the spotify podcast

sources.title: Casey Adams on podcasting: how a 17-year-old turned a bedroom show into a career and a company
sources.originalTitle: Episode 2 with Casey Adams
sources.summary: Casey Adams recounts starting his podcast at 16-17 after a football injury, how it led to fundraising from past guests and building listener.com, and his tactics for landing big guests. He stresses starting now, staying flexible, offering value to guests, and doing hard things.

principles.text: Pitch guests on what's in it for them: do deep research and reference what they care about right now.
principles.quote: don't make it about you, don't make it about your show, your audience. ... recognize what's important to them during that time.

principles.text: Use your past guests as social proof to speed up trust in cold outreach.
principles.quote: you can kind of stand on the shoulders of your guests

principles.text: Be persistent and show up everywhere: consistency, follow-up and serendipity landed the biggest guests.
principles.quote: you kind of have to be everywhere. You want to cold email, you want to cold DM, and most of the time you're probably never going to hear a response.

principles.text: A personal video DM is hard to ignore and cuts through busy people's attention.
principles.quote: If you get a someone that, you know, you follow or maybe you've interacted with and they send you a video on Instagram, like you're going to watch the video.

principles.text: Stay flexible and rebrand your show as you evolve; don't get attached to one format or name.
principles.quote: if it doesn't excite you and you don't feel proud to step like to stand on it, to share it, to kind of promote it, I hey, you should probably think about how do you reinvent it

principles.text: Podcast guests become investors and relationships; the medium builds trust fast and amplifies business.
principles.quote: pretty much all of the investors were past guests on my podcast.

sources.title: How Casey Adams turned a teen podcast into a network that funded a startup and launched Listener
sources.originalTitle: He Built a $1M Network at 17. Here’s How
sources.summary: Casey Adams explains how he started a podcast at 17 to meet great people, learn, and create business opportunity, and how that network later funded Media Kits and led to Listener. He shares his cold-outreach framework for landing big guests and why founder-led media is a distribution channel.

principles.text: Judge the podcast by a simple checklist, not revenue: meet great people, learn from them, create business opportunity.
principles.quote: meet great people, learn from them, and create business opportunities.

principles.text: A show's network compounds into capital: most of his angel investors were past guests.
principles.quote: we had 37 angel investors and pretty much 90% of those investors were past guests from my podcast.

principles.text: Make cold outreach short, tied to what the person cares about right now, and respectful of their time.
principles.quote: figuring out what they care about, you know, he loves Robert Green, he's a friend of his, and you kind of the barrier kind of goes down

principles.text: Use mutual connections as social proof in the ask: name someone they know and like who has been on your show.
principles.quote: hey Rick Ross, I recently had your friend Robert Green on my podcast. It would be such an honor to have you on my show for 15 minutes to talk about your new book.

principles.text: Time pitches to why now: guests are most receptive when promoting a book, film, or cause.
principles.quote: you'll see a lot of these bigger creators or celebrities go on these podcast tours because they're talking about something specific that they care about at that time

principles.text: Don't fear rejection: send the ask anyway and expect far more no's than yeses.
principles.quote: I've probably had more nos or me messages that didn't respond than I've ever had received or the big guests that you've heard of

sources.title: How Casey Adams turned a podcast into a network, a $1.5M raise and an exit
sources.originalTitle: Casey Adams on Lessons from Larry King & Elon Musk’s Mom | Podcast 7
sources.summary: Casey Adams explains how a high-school podcast became a business development engine: guest outreach by DM, a network that funded his startup, and bundled sponsor deals. He also covers how Media Kits got its first 10k users organically and the long-game mindset behind it.

principles.text: Treat a show as a long-term network and deal-flow engine, not a one-off ad channel.
principles.quote: I think about my podcast as in like the next 10 20 years like how can I bring the most incredible Minds in the world into my world to then create this network where I can help other people you know connect the dots

principles.text: Volume of outreach wins: set an aggressive output goal and DM relentlessly.
principles.quote: the first 90 days of Hosting my show I had a goal to interview 60 different people so like very ambitious

principles.text: Cold outreach works when you give a reference point, a short time frame, and ask for nothing else.
principles.quote: you're only one dm away or you're only one message away from opening up a conversation

principles.text: Sell the whole personal-brand stack to sponsors, not just a podcast ad slot.
principles.quote: it's not the one-off podcast it's the entire vertical integrated brand stack

principles.text: Early users came from organic, scrappy tactics: creator content on TikTok and deep community giveaways on Twitch.
principles.quote: from September to the new year we got over 10 000 users like organic no paid media all Grassroots stuff

principles.text: Build products for problems you personally have; founder-market fit builds conviction.
principles.quote: if you are solving a key problem that you're having I believe you can be so much more convinced and bought in on it

sources.title: How Casey Adams went from a neck brace to a MediaKits exit at 26 and built Listener
sources.originalTitle: Casey Adams: From Neck Brace to MediaKits Exit at 26
sources.summary: Casey Adams explains how podcasting from age 17 became the foundation for his network, his first raise ($1.5M from 37 angels, mostly past guests) and his MediaKits exit to Viral Nation. He then shares lessons from that exit and how he keeps his second company, Listener, lean while preserving optionality.

principles.text: Be crystal clear on why you do a hard medium like podcasting; clarity makes it stop feeling like a heavy lift.
principles.quote: know why you're doing it. It's a hard medium. There's a lot of in, you know, long format. It's hard to get attention. It's hard to build that like true listener base. But if you're clear with why you're doing it, it should never feel like that heavy lift.

principles.text: Use a podcast as a network engine: guests can become your investors, introducers and strategic partners.
principles.quote: we ended up raising, you know, $1.5 million from 37 angel investors. And you'll love this and then I'll I'll pause for a moment. Pretty much all of those 37 angel investors were past guests on my podcast.

principles.text: Do the reps before the opportunity: volume of interviews prepared him for the Larry King chance.
principles.quote: the butterfly effect of like those 60 or 100 interviews that I did beforehand is what gave me that opportunity to be prepared for that opportunity.

principles.text: Stay narrow: be an inch wide and a mile deep, doing one thing great rather than many things okay.
principles.quote: We were an inch wide and a mile deep. Like our name was media kits.com. The easiest way to build a media kit.

principles.text: Take an early exit when the future is uncertain; a win on the board proves you can run the full lifecycle and is reusable.
principles.quote: for us it was like getting a great win on the board and being able to utilize that into future ventures.

principles.text: Stay lean and keep optionality: don't over-raise before you've figured out the product, so you can raise, grow sustainably, or be acquired.
principles.quote: give yourself the ability to have optionality like we have great investors and the option to if we wanted to go raise a like prop around.

sources.title: Casey Adams on building a personal brand: authenticity, three pillars, collaborations
sources.originalTitle: #33 Build Your Personal Branding with Casey Adams
sources.summary: Casey Adams (then 18, CEO of Build Your Empire) explains how a neck injury, a DM to Ty Lopez and relentless outreach led him to interview 80+ entrepreneurs. He lays out a simple personal-branding playbook: commit fully, define three pillars, collaborate constantly, and climb the interview ladder through associates.

principles.text: When starting out, be authentic and document your real journey instead of putting on a persona or big labels.
principles.quote: tell people that be authentic as possible because that's what people want that's what they respect and overall that's how you're going to win

principles.text: Personal branding demands full commitment; part-time effort and mostly consuming means you lose.
principles.quote: if you're 50% committed to building a brand and you only think about it maybe two days a week and rest of the days you're just on Instagram scrolling and consuming you're not producing you're going to lose end of the story

principles.text: Define three brand pillars and make them obvious in the first line of your bio.
principles.quote: it's really understanding why you want to Brand yourself how you want to Brand yourself and overall what that looks like

principles.text: Consistency, collaborations and tolerance for rejection separate you from everyone else; it's a numbers game.
principles.quote: the thing that separates someone that's for example myself from another 18-year-old is the consistency of collaborations and the willingness to get rejected

principles.text: Build up in steps: start with people in your network and climb toward big names as your reputation grows.
principles.quote: you want to start with zero to one Z one to two two to three three to four and start building those Stepping Stones before you completely interview all these big people

principles.text: Reach big names through their circle: interview their associates first so your pitch carries association.
principles.quote: you don't want to go direct to Source you want to in you want to interview their friends or people that they know

sources.title: How Casey Adams built a 400+ interview podcast and Media Kits from a bedroom at 17
sources.originalTitle: Casey Adams: Interviewing Larry King, Grant Cardone, & Rick Ross | The Danny Miranda Podcast 247
sources.summary: Casey Adams explains how he landed Grant Cardone, Larry King and Rick Ross interviews by getting creative, showing up, and valuing people's time. He covers relationship building through presence and context, staying consistent with a long-term project, and the origin of his creator-economy startup Media Kits.

principles.text: Put yourself in positions to win; never expect opportunity to come to you, just show up.
principles.quote: never have an expectation of opportunities coming up just get out there and put yourself in a position to win

principles.text: Get creative with outreach and commit to a plan before you know how you'll execute it.
principles.quote: figuring out how to put yourself in positions to win and to create opportunity starts by getting creative with how you think about things

principles.text: Pitch busy people by referencing someone they respect, naming a clear reason, and asking for a small time commitment.
principles.quote: I brought up someone that he respected Robert Greene... and I only needed 10-15 minutes of his time to do the show

principles.text: Find connection points before reaching out to someone, because context breaks through the surface-level DM.
principles.quote: if you find a way to break through that uh that glass of you know just another DM but someone that cares and you know draws some connections to you I think it's a good thing

principles.text: Build relationships by caring, being fully present, and following up with quality touchpoints like thoughtful story replies.
principles.quote: building relationships comes down to one thing is that's just caring about someone like caring about the time you spend with them are you actually paying attention

principles.text: Use social media as a producer, not a consumer: spend most time in DMs and commenting to create touchpoints.
principles.quote: every time I go on there I try to be a not a consumer but a producer

sources.title: How Casey Adams built a network and personal brand through podcasting at 19
sources.originalTitle: #1 ELEVATE HER PODCAST- How Casey Adams became a world-class entrepreneur at 19!
sources.summary: Casey Adams explains how, after a football injury at 15, he went all-in on social media and podcasting, interviewing Gary Vaynerchuk, Grant Cardone, Jordan Belfort and Larry King. He covers value-first outreach via Instagram DMs, association marketing, personal branding pillars, building skills, and communication as the core skill.

principles.text: Offer a platform as your value: a podcast gives successful people a reason to say yes.
principles.quote: anyone that's looking to be a value to someone how can you be a value provide them a platform to talk about themselves and their product service or business that's what a podcast is

principles.text: Keep outreach simple (an Instagram DM), but have a brand, content and consistency behind it.
principles.quote: you have to have a brand you have to have content you have to have consistency to get responses like that

principles.text: Association marketing: build your brand on top of quality people; past guests unlock bigger ones.
principles.quote: I like to call it Association marketing and building a brand on top of qualified people instead of saying hey listen to me look at me this is why just associate with quality people and the rest will fall in the place

principles.text: Look for strategic ways to provide value; every relationship must be a two-way street.
principles.quote: you always want to look for the strategic ways to provide value

principles.text: Build a brand through extreme collaboration, and document your current reality so your audience grows with you.
principles.quote: build a brand through collaboration that's what would buy B is the number one like secret of branding is just extreme collaboration

principles.text: Communication is the most important skill because every business is run by and sold to people.
principles.quote: I look at communication that's like the most important skill set

sources.title: How Casey Adams used a podcast to build a network, raise capital and exit Media Kits
sources.originalTitle: Casey Adams | Entrepreneur + Podcast Host | Creating Your Life Story
sources.summary: Casey Adams explains how a cold-outreach podcast started at 17 became the foundation for relationships, a ~$1.3-1.5M raise from past guests, and the acquisition of his Media Kits startup. He also covers building a personal brand by producing consistently, pitching brands proactively, and acting despite fear of failure.

principles.text: Use a podcast as a relationship engine: meet quality people, learn from them, and let opportunities follow.
principles.quote: business is a people game right like even in today's world with Ai and all these incredible tools that I love so much

principles.text: Set an aggressive volume goal and cold-reach out to hit it; reps compound into momentum.
principles.quote: I set out a goal the initial in 90 days to do 60 interviews in 90 days

principles.text: Relationships built through intentional conversations become your funding base when you launch a venture.
principles.quote: about 90 95 of the people that invested in the media kits which was about 37 people I believe came from or were previous guests from the podcast

principles.text: Build products from repeated, observed pain, and revisit shelved ideas when timing improves.
principles.quote: why isn't there a way for creators to create a Media Kit that never gets outdated that you never have to go back and update

principles.text: Grow a personal brand by producing, not consuming: pick a medium, model top creators, and be consistent.
principles.quote: the ability to focus on output instead of input instead of scrolling all day and consuming how can you be a producer on social media

principles.text: Never wait for brands or guests to come to you; proactive outreach is the non-starter fix.
principles.quote: never expect a brand to ever reach out for you even if you're gaining momentum you're putting out content the whole thing you need to be proactive and reach out to them

sources.title: Podcast monetization beyond the midroll: multiplatform campaigns, brand guests and reporting
sources.originalTitle: Podcast Monetization: More Than the Midrol
sources.summary: Casey Adams moderates a Podcast Movement panel with brand buyers from Timeline and Caraway on moving past midroll ads into multiplatform partnerships. His own contributions are framing points: brand experts as guests, using missed-impression reporting to upsell multiplatform, and reporting that earns renewals. Most of the substantive insight comes from the panelists, not Casey.

principles.text: Brands putting their own experts (CEO, head scientist) on a show is an under-discussed monetization format beyond the ad read.
principles.quote: I love when I've worked with brands in the past for my show and they say, "Hey, you should have our CEO on the show or a head scientist."

principles.text: Show brands the impressions they missed on other formats to move audio-only deals into multiplatform campaigns.
principles.quote: They might just be doing audio, but then they'll show them, hey, you missed out on 20 million impressions of the short form that for the next one, let's do that instead.

principles.text: For complex products, team experts as guests deliver customer education a short ad read cannot.
principles.quote: there's like multiple people on the team that will bring that customer education, which is so vital on the shows themselves as guests.

principles.text: Publishers should understand what brands care about and report campaigns accordingly, with renewals as the goal.
principles.quote: they are hearing things from the brands understanding what they care about understanding the things that you've the dos and the don'ts and then kind of their best representing the campaign to them for the goal of getting renewals

sources.title: How Casey Adams built MediaKits to an acquisition and launched Listener.fm
sources.originalTitle: Casey Adams: Co-Founder of MediaKits and Listener.fm (Kara Goldin transcript)
sources.summary: Casey Adams recounts going from a teenage podcaster to co-founding MediaKits (raised $1.5M, acquired about a year after launch) and then Listener.fm. He stresses unscalable hands-on user contact, using a podcast as a relationship and fundraising engine, and telling the founder story relentlessly.

principles.text: In the earliest days, do unscalable things: talk to users directly in DMs and be hands-on with feedback.
principles.quote: just in the earliest days, it's so important to just do things that are, as I said, on not scalable, the communication with people on social media and the DMS, like be so hands on

principles.text: Use a podcast to build a trusted network that later becomes your angel investors and collaborators.
principles.quote: probably about 90% of them, but as I like to say, we're from my podcasts or previous guests on my show that I've nurtured these relationships with.

principles.text: Be your product's biggest evangelist; tell the story through organic content and your own circle.
principles.quote: you need to be the biggest evangelists for what you're building so that people are even aware of it, whether that's organic content on social or telling your friends and families.

principles.text: Find early users on Twitter by searching the niche and reaching out with genuine, crafted messages to get feedback.
principles.quote: like reaching out to podcasters in a genuine way, whether that's with an audio message, or just a, you know, a truly crafted message to their show

principles.text: Build for a problem you personally live with; that gives you a clear sense of what the product must solve.
principles.quote: I just wanted to solve a problem for what I've dealt with

principles.text: Validate by bootstrapping with your own resources and serving real users before raising capital.
principles.quote: bootstrapping it initially just with our own resources and trying to get a sense of what it could look like

sources.title: Casey Adams on leading small businesses: listen more, stay agile, and focus on customers
sources.originalTitle: Casey Adams on navigating the future of work (Slack Q&A)
sources.summary: In this Slack Q&A, Casey Adams recounts starting a podcast at 16, co-founding MediaKits (acquired by Viral Nation), and what he took from 300+ interviews. He shares leadership and small-business advice on listening, adaptability, competitive pricing and customer relationships, plus how he uses Slack to run his team.

principles.text: Listen more than you talk; spending more time listening to your team makes you a better decision-maker and leader.
principles.quote: I have found that spending more time listening to my employees and team members has been incredibly beneficial for my leadership.

principles.text: Actively listening surfaces insights and perspectives you would otherwise miss, which leads to better decisions.
principles.quote: By actively listening and paying attention to what they have to say, I have been able to gain valuable insights and perspectives that I may not have considered otherwise.

principles.text: In uncertain markets, stay agile: keep up with trends, be open to new ideas and tech, and be willing to pivot.
principles.quote: First and foremost, it’s important to stay agile and adaptable. The business landscape is constantly changing, and being able to pivot and adjust to new challenges is crucial.

principles.text: Stay competitive through quality plus competitive pricing, which may mean streamlining operations and cutting costs.
principles.quote: This may require finding ways to streamline operations and reduce costs, as well as being mindful about pricing and promotions.

principles.text: In a crowded market, a loyal customer base built on service, responsiveness and consistent trust is a major advantage.
principles.quote: In a crowded market, having a loyal customer base can be a major advantage.

principles.text: Build human connection with a remote team by sharing personal updates, which strengthens professional relationships.
principles.quote: This has helped to create a more human connection with my team, which has in turn strengthened our professional relationships.

sources.title: How Casey Adams used premium domains to build MediaKits and the Listener podcast network
sources.originalTitle: Listener.com: Casey Adams' growing podcast network
sources.summary: Casey Adams explains how owning MediaKits.com gave him conviction and trust that fueled 25,000 creator signups in 6 months, and why he pursued Listener.com for six-plus months of slow broker conversation before buying. He argues founders should secure social handles and premium domains early as brand and IP assets.

principles.text: A premium domain gives conviction and an edge in first impressions, brand awareness, and early trust.
principles.quote: Having that domain was such an edge to first impressions, brand building awareness, and that initial growth and trust.

principles.text: Own the category-defining name so you can credibly position as the industry leader.
principles.quote: There’s no other place to go besides MediaKits.com, right? We wanted to be the industry leader.

principles.text: Start a slow, low-pressure conversation with a domain broker long before you urgently need the domain.
principles.quote: I just kept the conversation going slowly but surely.

principles.text: Before launching, check social handles on all platforms and whether the preferred domain is for sale.
principles.quote: Before you start a business, go and see if you can get the social handles on all platforms. Go and see if the preferred domain is even available for sale.

principles.text: Treat brand and domain as intellectual property that will be valued later in an acquisition or IPO.
principles.quote: If you don't value the intellectual property of whatever you’re building today, you're going to have to value it later if you're ever going to have to go through an acquisition or take a company public.

principles.text: Owning the word your industry revolves around pays long-tail brand-building dividends.
principles.quote: I know it's going to pay dividends when it comes to the long tail effect of brand building. Owning that part of the industry is huge.

sources.title: How Casey Adams went from a neck injury to a top-200 business podcast and an events company
sources.originalTitle: Meet Casey Adams of Build Your Empire & Rise of The Young
sources.summary: A 2019 local profile of Casey Adams, who built a personal brand, the Rise of The Young podcast and the Build Your Empire events company as a teenager. He shares what he learned about time, saying no, relationships and bringing people together.

principles.text: Learn when to say NO to opportunities; entrepreneurs get flooded with them.
principles.quote: As an entrepreneur, you’re introduced to so many opportunities and learning to say NO has truly impacted my life.

principles.text: Know when to distance yourself from people and move on from a situation.
principles.quote: You must know when to let go, and when to move on from a situation or an individual.

principles.text: Bringing people together through events is powerful leverage.
principles.quote: After throwing dozens of business events all across the world, one of the biggest things I’ve learned is that there is power in bringing people together.

principles.text: Interviewing influential people teaches listening, which underpins real relationships.
principles.quote: Being able to interview such impactful people at 18 years old has truly given me insight into the power of listening.

principles.text: How you position yourself online is a source of power; build a personal brand.
principles.quote: After traveling all of the world speaking on stages about personal branding, I’ve realized that we have so much power by the way we position ourselves online.

principles.text: A support system of people who care is the most important asset.
principles.quote: Having a support system of people who truly care about you is the most important asset I have, and I attribute that to luck.

sources.title: Podcast reporting is underselling shows: lead with omni-channel reach, not downloads
sources.originalTitle: The podcast industry is underselling itself
sources.summary: Casey Adams argues that podcast campaign reporting undervalues what shows deliver because it centers on downloads, while modern shows span audio, YouTube and social. He positions Listener.com around omni-channel campaign reporting and outlines a four-step workflow for networks and brand partners.

principles.text: A modern podcast show is audio plus YouTube plus social; report and sell all of it.
principles.quote: A show today consists of audio, YouTube, and social content. Innovative brands are paying for all of it, and that's where modern campaigns are succeeding.

principles.text: Leading reports with downloads undersells value, since downloads are only one piece of what a show delivers.
principles.quote: But most campaign reports still lead with downloads, which is only one piece of what a show or network delivers.

principles.text: Sharpen your product around one clear job: omni-channel campaign reporting.
principles.quote: we've sharpened Listener.com around one thing: omni-channel campaign reporting for the modern podcast industry.

principles.text: Build trust by letting brand partners verify results themselves.
principles.quote: Report results your brand partners can see for themselves.

principles.text: Make the sales motion simple: pitch with one link, prove reach, run campaigns with live pacing.
principles.quote: Pitch your network with one link. Prove your true reach across episodes. Run campaigns and watch pacing live.

principles.text: Put every podcast, video and clip in one report so sponsors see the full campaign.

principles.text: Reporting is a sales tool: give your team what it needs to sell, report and renew with confidence.

principles.text: Use a partner's own words as proof; a named VP describing the unlock does the selling.
principles.quote: A huge unlock for our partners.

principles.text: Make the call to action small: a 15-minute booking for teams running multi-channel sponsor campaigns.
principles.quote: Running sponsor campaigns across audio, YouTube and social? Book 15 minutes with us.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Casey Adams explains how a career-ending sports injury pushed him into entrepreneurship, how he used a podcast to build relationships, and how that network funded and launched Media Kits. He lays out his core values and the discipline habits (75 Hard, cold plunges) behind them.

chunks.heading: Background and origin story
chunks.text:
- Casey Adams grew up in Chesterfield County, Virginia, 30 minutes south of Richmond, in a non-entrepreneurial family. His mom was a special ed teacher and babysitter, and his dad worked at Philip Morris for about 30 years.
- As a kid he always looked for ways to make money: knocking on doors, shoveling snow, selling bracelets, charging his brothers $5 to cut the grass.
- He was a lifelong athlete (hockey from age 3, then lacrosse, then football). At 15 he landed on his head in the first hitting practice and was diagnosed with spinal ligament damage. He could never play football again and wore a neck brace for six months.
- He spent the first two to three months depressed and angry, having lost his identity as an athlete. In the back half he immersed himself in personal development and entrepreneurship content (Gary Vaynerchuk, David Meltzer).
- That led him to start a business doing Facebook advertising and social media for local businesses. He calls the injury "the one moment in particular that completely changed the course and direction of my future."
- He didn't go to college. He moved to Arizona a month after high school and sees himself as a lifelong learner.

chunks.heading: Why he started a podcast and how he launched it
chunks.text:
- He launched The Casey Adams Show on December 21, 2017, at 17, recording the first episode on wired Apple headphones while walking around his room.
- The stated purpose has not changed in five years: meet people, learn something, and create business opportunity.
- His first 10 to 15 guests were friends and young entrepreneurs he'd met on social media.
- He set a goal of 60 interviews in the first 90 days, using cold DM outreach and publishing three to four a week, sometimes two a day. It built confidence in reaching out and taking a "no" or a "yes."
- The podcast also grew his personal brand, through clips and guests sharing their episodes.
- By his account he has interviewed about 400 founders, entrepreneurs, musicians and athletes.

chunks.heading: Podcasting as a relationship-building and fundraising engine
chunks.text:
- He argues a one-on-one recorded conversation builds a much deeper relationship than meeting at an event or over a drink, and it expedites the early stages of a relationship.
- It also forces both people to prepare, which makes it a better medium than a loud networking event.
- He deliberately used the podcast to build rapport with people he might one day ask for tactical advice, such as on fundraising.
- It paid off with Media Kits: he says 90 to 95% of the investors in the round were past podcast guests.

chunks.heading: How he landed the Larry King interview (and what it taught him)
chunks.text:
- The chain: a friend introduced him to restaurateur Tilman Fertitta, who was promoting his book "Shut Up and Listen." Casey interviewed him, which led to an invite to a dinner in Beverly Hills.
- At the dinner he sat across from Larry King's son, Chance. They were about the same age and became friends without Casey asking for anything.
- He says his approach is not to meet someone and ask for an intro. He believes in "letting things happen" and building real relationships, and he texts people on holidays to put good energy out there.
- Months later he asked what it would take to have Chance's dad on the show. The first answer was "not the best time" (Larry was coming off a stroke). Around Thanksgiving, Chance came back with a yes.
- The interview happened on December 10, 2019. Larry was 87 and Casey was 19, a 76-year age gap.
- His takeaway on opportunity: say yes to things even when you don't know what they'll bring. Opportunities arrive disguised as events you don't feel like attending, and most won't be a "grand slam," but some become real friendships.
- The lesson from Larry: "I've never learned anything while I was talking." Casey admits that in his first 10 to 20 episodes he was anxious about the next question, and he now treats being present and listening as the core skill.

chunks.heading: The origin and build of Media Kits
chunks.text:
- **The idea (2018-2019):** a YouTuber friend (JR Garage, 1M+ subscribers) asked Casey and his partner Kieran to make him a media kit. They built it in Canva/Photoshop in about an hour and he got the deal. Weeks later Ferrari asked for his kit, and they had to manually update numbers after he gained 55,000 subscribers.
- **The insight:** why can't a creator have a media kit that never goes out of date, and why can't brands see verified, trustworthy data directly from the creator?
- **Timing:** they shelved it in 2018-2019. In mid-2020, with TikTok exploding and "creators being minted overnight," they came back to it. They bootstrapped designs for about four months and validated the idea with creator friends.
- **Funding:** they raised just under $1.5M in a pre-seed, with a rolling close over about six months. It was Casey's first raise.
- **Product:** a platform where creators, podcasters, musicians and others get a digital resume with real-time data via the APIs of Instagram, Facebook, Twitter, Twitch, YouTube and more.
- **Timeline:** users could sign up on August 11, 2021, and the company was sold to Viral Nation in late August the following year, about 12 months after launch.
- **Team and focus:** a small team of 8 to 10 the whole time. They wanted to be the best at one thing, the go-to source for real-time data in a shareable link, and used the phrase "inch wide, mile deep." The domain was mediakits.com.
- **Launch:** a big launch party in Los Angeles with Dan, Wiz Khalifa performing and about 700 creators and friends, to make a branding splash.
- **Early struggle:** in the first 45 days they didn't get more than 1,000 users on a free tool with a paid upgrade, which forced them to dig into why people weren't signing up or using it.

chunks.heading: Non-negotiables and operating principles
chunks.text:
- He says "how you do anything is how you do everything" and ties business and life together.
- Three core values:
  - **Stay curious:** about the world, about your own ability, about how you can help people and about new technology. He notes small-town people often cap themselves by assuming some opportunities are "not for me."
  - **Never stop learning:** he treats learning as lifelong and as continuing well after school.
  - **Extreme gratitude:** he looks for moments daily to be grateful, and he cites Robert Greene's chapter on confronting your mortality as a reminder that life is fragile.
- He also draws inspiration from guests who have overcome adversity, such as Nick Santonastaso, and says they help him look at his own life.

chunks.heading: Discipline and doing hard things
chunks.text:
- He is on day 58 of his second 75 Hard (the first was in 2020, which he failed once before completing). The daily rules are:
  - Two 45-minute workouts, one outdoors.
  - A gallon of water.
  - 10 pages of reading.
  - A progress picture.
  - No alcohol or cheat meals.
  - Following a diet.
- He calls it a mental toughness challenge, not a fitness one. He says there's never a perfect time to start, and the discipline transfers to every area of life.
- He says his first marathon in December 2023 came when he was not "naturally a runner" and had never run more than about two miles.
- He does a cold plunge five days a week and deliberately puts something daunting on the calendar.
- His belief is that doing hard things prepares you for life, and that staying "emotionally at Center through the ups through the downs" is what allows you to be great.
- He says the initial excitement for any commitment (75 Hard, a business, a podcast) fades fast and "the only answer is truly discipline."

chunks.heading: Current direction: Listener.fm
chunks.text:
- After leaving Viral Nation he is building in the podcasting tech space, focused on AI automating post-production.
- His tool Listener.fm takes an audio file and outputs titles, descriptions, show notes and similar assets. He says it's being tested with many podcasts and podcast networks.
- His stated aim is to take what he learned from Media Kits and apply it to a new venture, while keeping the podcast at the core.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Casey Adams recounts starting his podcast at 17, landing Larry King through a chain of networking luck, and building the Media Kits startup from a manual pain point. His core themes are starting without overthinking, seizing opportunities, putting relationships first and improving daily.

chunks.heading: Starting the podcast: low-friction launch and relationships as the payoff
chunks.text:
- Casey started his podcast in 2017, at 17, from his bedroom in a small Virginia town. He had no entrepreneurial family background and had never flown until he bought his first ticket.
- The trigger was Gary Vaynerchuk's "Crushing It", whose last chapter pitched podcasting in 2017 as a way to connect with great people, have great conversations and learn something along the way.
- He recorded the first episode of "Rise of the Young" with Apple earbuds in his bedroom, with no plan for what to say. He presses this point: "a lot of people overthink just getting started."
- After 5 years and 400+ interviews, he says the main return is relationships, not downloads. He describes it as a natural path: DM someone on Instagram, build a relationship, host them on the show, and eventually have them as an investor in the company.
- He says "99%" of the people he knows today came through social media and the podcast.

chunks.heading: Creating luck: how the Larry King interview happened
chunks.text:
Casey uses this as a case study in engineering opportunity. He interviewed Larry King at 19, at the end of 2019, when King was 87.

1. A close friend and business partner worked with Tilman Fertitta. Casey interviewed Fertitta on his show for Fertitta's book.
2. Fertitta hosted a dinner of 20-25 people who had helped promote the book. There Casey met Chance King, Larry King's son, and they became close friends.
3. Two to three weeks later, Larry King rolled past Casey in a Century City mall. Casey chose to walk up, introduce himself, mention that he'd just met Chance, and take a selfie, which he sent to Chance.
4. He told Chance he'd love to host his father someday. King was recovering from a stroke, so it looked unlikely.
5. Around Thanksgiving 2019, Chance replied that his father wanted to do it. About two weeks later Casey was in King's studio.

His lessons:
- Put yourself around great people, at dinners, networking events or through a podcast, and unexpected opportunities show up if you keep doing it.
- Taking action matters as much as the opportunity. Many people have chances land in front of them and never act.
- Mall moment: "you really have to decide in that moment" whether to say hello.

chunks.heading: Interview prep: from heavy research to pure curiosity
chunks.text:
- Early on he researched heavily and wrote out all his questions, which gave him confidence.
- He noticed he spent too much time thinking about the next question and too little listening. He cites Larry King's line, "I never learned anything while I was talking."
- After roughly his 20th-30th interview he stopped writing questions entirely.
- His current method:
  - Watch other interviews with the guest to understand their story and background.
  - Walk in curious, with no preset end goal, and treat it like lunch with a friend.
  - Keep a loose plan tied to the show's theme (business and entrepreneurship through a young person's lens), but avoid a formal Q&A.
- He says this takes pressure off and makes him more present, and that it took many reps before he felt comfortable sitting with anyone.

chunks.heading: Media Kits: origin, validation and fundraising
chunks.text:
**The problem he saw**
- Casey and co-founder Kieran (who then ran a marketing agency) helped a friend, a YouTube car creator with about half a million subscribers, build a media kit in Canva or Photoshop when a brand asked for one.
- Two weeks later Ferrari asked for his media kit. Every number was stale after a few viral videos, so they edited the numbers by hand again.
- That prompted two questions:
  - Why can't creators have a media kit that never goes stale?
  - Why can't brands see verified data instead of creators simply claiming an engagement rate or demographic?

**Timeline**
- They shelved the idea because Casey was still in high school and neither had experience launching a tech company.
- In 2020 they moved to Arizona. With TikTok exploding and creators being discovered overnight, they revisited it.
- Mid to late 2020 was spent ideating, prototyping and designing.
- They went full-time in early 2021 and raised $1.25 million in 4-6 months.
- They launched on August 11, 2021.
- A large share of investors came directly from relationships built through the podcast.

**The product and where it goes**
