- Media Kits is a tool for creators, musicians, podcasters and athletes to build a media kit with live, verified analytics. The site is mediakits.com and takes under 60 seconds to set up.
- He cites 25,000+ creators using it.
- The goal is to become the most trusted cross-platform data source, because no single place shows a creator's full social presence with verified, continuously updated numbers.
- The media kit is the "Trojan horse" into a broader ecosystem of secondary tools. He says the kit is the one thing every creator needs.
- He frames the market as roughly 50 million full-time creators and growing every year.
- He says building and shipping the software, and hiring the team, was the most educational process of his last five years, even though he is not an engineer or developer.

chunks.heading: Using social media as a producer, not a consumer
chunks.text:
- His rule: spend time on social media producing, not consuming. Producing includes:
  - Posting content and building a brand.
  - Replying to comments in your community.
  - Messaging friends and answering DMs.
- When he watches Instagram stories, he turns consumption into output. If he views 50 stories in a day, he sends a real message to a friend or someone who inspires him, reacting to their content or asking how he can help.
- He enters the apps with an intention, to respond, help someone or post something that might inspire others, so the apps don't consume him.
- His analogy: a hammer can build a project or break a window, so how you use the tool and where you put your energy is what counts.

chunks.heading: Operating principles: daily improvement and optimizing dead time
chunks.text:
- Core principle: "If I'm not getting better every day, what am I doing?" He rejects complacency at any level of success and aims to improve about 1% a day in the gym, relationships, products and work.
- He ties this to David Meltzer's idea of "the relentless pursuit of your potential." After 400 interviews he sees great people as constantly evolving, and he feels like a different person every 6-12 months.
- Favorite quote: "Get comfortable being in uncomfortable situations." He says real growth happens in uncomfortable moments such as approaching Larry King, giving a keynote, or pitching investors.
- His push to act is "If not now, when?" Opportunities come and go, so don't bet on a second chance.
- He doesn't own a car, a choice he's held for 4-5 years (a car is shared with his girlfriend). He uses rideshare so traffic time becomes time for calls, email, DMs and audiobooks. He says 30 minutes each way, four days a week, adds up to about four hours a week over 52 weeks.
- He stacks tasks. He listens to podcasts while folding laundry, and takes calls or answers messages on a 10-minute walk to the gym. He credits Ty Lopez on optimizing what you do and Dan Fleyshman, who has never owned a car.
- Long-term, he plans to keep building Media Kits, keep doing the podcast indefinitely (a goal of 10,000+ interviews by age 50), and eventually move into real estate with his brother.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Casey Adams and fiancée Jacqlyn Burnett discuss happiness, gratitude, vetting relationships and mentorship. Casey shares how he got to interview Larry King through organic relationship-building, plus the importance of listening and commitment in business and love. Light on tactical growth content.

chunks.heading: Media Kids: building and selling a creator economy company
chunks.text:
- Casey co-founded Media Kids (mediakids.com) with his co-founder Kieran. It is creator economy software that lets creators, podcasters and musicians aggregate all of their social media data in one place.
- The company raised money in 2020 and was acquired in September 2023.
- His fiancée Jacqlyn was COO and an integral part of the company's growth.
- His new company is Listener FM, named after his "Listener" Instagram handle.
- Casey was 23 at the time of this recording. He started his podcast at 17 and has done it for 6 years.

chunks.heading: Interviewing Larry King: how a relationship, not an ask, landed the interview
chunks.text:
Casey tells this as his most impactful interview story. The steps:

1. In 2019 a friend, Michael Grew, was helping Tilman Fertitta promote his book "Shut Up and Listen". Tilman was the first billionaire Casey interviewed, over Zoom.
2. A couple of weeks later Tilman's team invited about 25 people who helped promote the book to Mastro's in Beverly Hills.
3. Kieran ended up sitting next to Chance King, Larry King's son. Tilman said at the table that Larry had been an inspiration to him all his life.
4. Casey and Chance hit it off and became friends. Casey invited him to an event he was hosting in Los Angeles the following weekend.
5. Casey never asked for his dad on the show. He says he is "not one that would ever ask, hey, can I have your dad on my show". The timing and the organic relationship did the work.
6. On Thanksgiving 2019 he texted Chance. Chance said Larry had recently had a stroke but would love to be on the show when he felt better.
7. The following week Casey and Jacqlyn ran into Larry King in his wheelchair at the Century City mall. He sent Chance a photo.
8. Two weeks later Casey was interviewing Larry in his studio. Casey was 19 and Larry was 87, with about 60,000 interviews and the last 10 presidents behind him. This was 6 to 8 months before Larry passed.

Casey has done nearly 500 interviews. He says this one left the deepest imprint on his interview approach.

chunks.heading: Listening as a business and relationship skill
chunks.text:
- Larry King told him on the show: "You'll never learn anything when you're talking." Casey took this on as a core principle and built his brand identity around it (the Listener handle, Listener FM).
- He argues that anyone who wants to be great in business or in relationships needs a heavy emphasis on listening.
- The failure mode he describes is a dinner where you share your perspective the whole time and never ask the other person about their day.
- In his relationship, he says listening to the other person's perspective during fights and differences matters most after commitment, because that is how you grow with someone.

chunks.heading: Vetting people and networking
chunks.text:
- Don't judge someone you don't know. A clip on social media or one rude moment in a hallway should not define them. He notes the persona someone has online is not always the person.
- Time is how you get to know someone, so spend quality time with people before deciding whether they belong in your life.
- Having interviewed people from Larry King to Rick Ross to Elon Musk's mom and sister, he says everyone is human, dealing with their own problems and trying to get better.
- In a transactional world, his first question on meeting someone is "how can I bring value to this person's life". That might be a quick introduction or being thoughtful about something he has dealt with himself.

chunks.heading: Commitment and focus
chunks.text:
- He compares dating abundance (apps, Instagram DMs) to business: in a world of many options you need to commit to something. "You can't be the person just trying to do everything because you're going to go nowhere."
- He draws a contrast with business. If a company goes bankrupt you can move on to the next one, but a relationship has to be nurtured and "you can't just let it sink".
- He ties his happiness to a performance mindset from sports (hockey, lacrosse, football). He is most happy when he is getting better and progressing toward a goal, in sports or in business.

chunks.heading: Mentors and learning
chunks.text:
- At 15 a football injury left him in a neck brace for 6 months and almost paralyzed. He was depressed and unsure what to do with his life. That is when he first picked up personal development books such as "Think and Grow Rich" and "How to Win Friends and Influence People". Those authors were his first mentors.
- His view of mentorship has shifted from "how do I ask someone to be my mentor" to learning from people around him.
- Aristotle Loumis was monumental to Media Kids' success and acts like a big brother on business advice. He will spend 30 minutes rewriting an email in a way Casey would never have thought to write.
- He finds mentors for specific areas. Guests taught him running technique and fueling before his first marathon last year.
- On the podcast he tries to take one lesson from every conversation and apply it right away.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Casey Adams recounts how a neck injury ended his football path and pushed him into entrepreneurship, then shares how he started his podcast to build relationships and why he now prioritizes quality and just starting. He also touches on handling hate with understanding, surrounding yourself with good people, and NFTs as proof of ownership for artists.

chunks.heading: Starting from a setback in high school
chunks.text:
Casey Adams grew up in Richmond, Virginia, in a modest household. His mother was a special ed teacher (earlier a babysitter earning about $18K a year) and his father worked at Philip Morris for roughly 25 years. He played hockey, lacrosse and football and expected to play college lacrosse.

- At 15, a football drill left him with an interspinous ligament injury (his helmet came off and he slammed his head). He was told he would need a neck brace for six months and probably could never play football again.
- He describes losing his identity, spending one to three months angry and depressed, then filling the free time with YouTube and social media.
- There he found entrepreneurs such as Tai Lopez, Gary Vaynerchuk and Tony Robbins, and "something just clicked."
- He latched onto business, fundraising, marketing and Facebook ads, and "became obsessed."
- He had always been a hustler (shoveling driveways when it snowed, mowing lawns with a mower he bought), with the mindset "nothing's gonna come to me, I have to go get it myself."

His takeaway: the pivot came from a forced loss of identity, and he says he has no regrets about how it played out.

chunks.heading: Staying grounded and keeping family on board
chunks.text:
Casey earned more than his parents in a year while still in high school (age 17-18), living at home, running his first company and missing about 60 days of school to travel to LA and New York for interviews.

- His mom's advice: "stay true to your roots" and don't let outside circumstances change you for the worse.
- He kept a 4.0 GPA and took AP classes, because his parents' rule was that he could travel only if his grades held.
- Persuading his parents to let him travel alone at 16-17 was one of the hardest things he did. Their buy-in came through consistency and visible results, not arguments.
- His parents grew to love it. His mom watched Rob Dyrdek's Fantasy Factory, so when he interviewed Drama of Young and Reckless he FaceTimed her.
- He says his older brother got into real estate after attending a Seattle event Casey ran (a snowboard Mastermind).
- A regret: he never built a company with his brothers, and he cites Super Coffee (three brothers) as inspiration.

chunks.heading: Starting a podcast fast and scrappy
chunks.text:
Casey started his podcast, Rise of the Young, at the end of 2017 after reading the last chapter of Gary Vaynerchuk's "Crushing It," which covered podcasting as a way to build relationships and create deal flow.

- He had no long-term plan and no mic. The first episode was five minutes recorded with Apple earbuds.
- His first guests came from his close circle: Caleb Maddox, Kieran, and a friend named Jeff.
- He set a target of 60 interviews in 90 days and moved fast: Zoom interviews and scrappy Facebook Lives, optimized for volume, not quality.
- His motive was to build his network and meet people he wanted to learn from. Every conversation left him "smarter" and excited.
- He frames a podcast as a way to get access to busy people who won't do coffee meetings, and as meaningful long-form content in contrast to quick-scroll platforms.
- Later guests included Larry King and Robert Greene.

chunks.heading: Advice for people starting a podcast
chunks.text:
- Start now: "don't overthink it." Have a show idea, a great title and concept, then figure it out as you go. This is the most common question in his DMs (how to start, how to book guests).
- Quantity helps early, but he says quality matters more now because the space has grown (he says the industry has been doubling or tripling year over year) and there is a lot of noise.
- Differentiate. Many guests have been interviewed hundreds of times, so he thinks about what makes his show different (being young, asking different questions).
- Avoid making it a must-do, which would stress him out. Some weeks he does zero interviews and other weeks five (Monday through Friday during the NFT craze).
- Accept uneven results: some episodes get a few listens, and one YouTube interview got about 200,000.
- He names the real work as the back-end creation and uploading, plus wanting episodes to do well when they don't.

chunks.heading: Handling hate and criticism
chunks.text:
Casey says he gets little hate, but he has had messages saying guests only come on his show to leverage his audience.

- His approach is to reply personally, often with a thorough video or voice message, addressing what they said without being aggressive and explaining his intentions.
- He says about 90% of people flip and sometimes apologize.
- If someone seems to be coming from anger, he sometimes sends an interview he recorded on the issue they may be going through, and says he tries to provide resources and feedback.
- He tries to keep his own feed positive (quotes, books, purpose- and education-driven interviews), while respecting people who are vulnerable about hardships.

chunks.heading: Advice for young entrepreneurs
chunks.text:
- "Surround yourself with great people" and be careful about whose advice you take.
- Social media has real upside. He pushed back in a 10th/11th grade class that preached only its negatives, telling his own story, and says the teacher agreed.
- Avoid unhealthy comparison. Emulating others is fine, but he admits he sometimes catches himself comparing and wondering what others know that he doesn't.
- He says he has tried many things over a few years and sees them as lessons, but sometimes wonders whether he was focused enough.
- Everyone is "figuring it out" (a lesson he says he took from his interviews), and his identity changes as he grows.
- He doesn't aim to be the biggest influencer. His social presence supports the podcast, his brand and his network.

chunks.heading: NFTs and what he is building
chunks.text:
Casey views NFTs as "just the infancy" and believes in crypto as an asset and NFTs as proof of ownership, while saying he is no expert.

- He explains non-fungible: a dollar bill is interchangeable, while an NFT is unique, rare or exclusive.
- Example use case: a limited run of 1,000 event tickets minted as NFTs, kept in your wallet as proof of attendance.
- He did an NFT drop with WorldStar (CEO Danny, a friend), whose media brand is focused on music NFTs such as albums, singles and exclusive content.
- Artist example: his friend Justin (a photographer) spent three years photographing 100 sets of twins, struggled to sell the framed set through galleries, then dropped 100 one-of-one NFTs. He told his story on his blog and social and sold out in seven days, mostly to real collectors who believed in the story.
- A key benefit he cites: the original artist can attach a roughly 5-10% commission on resales, putting power back in the artist's hands.

His current company is Media Kits (medikits.com), built with his best friend Kieran, who sat on the idea for two years before they started building the tech about eight months earlier. It is a real-time data analytics product for musicians, bloggers, influencers and podcasters to create a Media Kit with live data that never goes out of date.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Casey Adams explains how six-plus years of hosting a podcast produced relationships that later became investors, advisors and clients. He covers a simple cold-DM blueprint for landing big guests, why podcasts should be monetized through brand and vertically integrated deals rather than CPMs alone, and why long-term commitment beats short-term hacks.

chunks.heading: Origin story: injury, social media, and the podcast as a foundation
chunks.text:
- Casey grew up in a small town in Virginia as an athlete, with two older brothers. A football injury in sophomore year of high school ended his playing career and left him in a neck brace for six months.
- During recovery he found Tony Robbins and Gary Vaynerchuk on social media and went "all in" on making money online, building a brand, and meeting people he could learn from.
- He launched the Casey Adams Show in 2017, when he was 16 or 17, and has hosted it for about six and a half years. It has produced 400+ interviews, including Larry King, Rick Ross, and founders of Twitch and Netflix.
- He calls the podcast "the best foundation for a career" for a teenager. It connected him with people he could learn from, kept relationships alive, and generated business opportunities.
- He skipped college, graduated high school, and moved across the country at 18.
- The show was originally called "Rise of the Young." He renamed it the Casey Adams Show because it felt more long-term and personal-brand focused.

chunks.heading: Relationship building: listening, value-first, no "stay in touch" agenda
chunks.text:
- A lesson from Larry King shapes how Casey approaches relationships. King's line: "I've never learned anything while I was listening." Casey tries to be a listener first.
- He interviews the person, not just the business: who they are, what they do, and the hardships they deal with.
- He argues podcasting "expedites relationships." Sitting down for 45 to 60 minutes (ideally in person) goes much deeper than a typical first meeting.
- He never treats staying in touch as a goal. He asks how he can be valuable to the guest, for example by trying their product, beta testing, giving feedback, or buying what they sell.
- Example: he had David Sacks on when Sacks ran Kin.com (a social podcasting app), then hosted 30 to 40 live shows on the platform.
- Dale Carnegie's "How to Win Friends and Influence People" shaped his approach from age 17.
- His principle: "no matter what business you're in, you're in the people business."

chunks.heading: Turning podcast relationships into a funded company
chunks.text:
- His last company, MediaKits.com, was a software tool for creators to aggregate cross-platform social data in one place. It was acquired by ViralNation in 2022.
- MediaKits raised a round from 37 angel investors, and about 80 to 90% of them were past guests on his podcast.
- He says this wasn't the plan. Years of interviewing investors, creator economy operators, and media builders meant he had trusted people to ask for feedback and validation.
- Because he had never asked them for anything, he could say "I'm starting this new business, would love a couple minutes of your time" and get real feedback.
- He had talked to guests' teams and assistants, so intros and conversations came naturally.
- It doesn't have to be a podcast. He earlier hosted events for a media company, which similarly made him a connector people knew, liked, and trusted.
- People he has a rapport with are more likely to take his call than a cold email, though he says cold outreach is great too.

chunks.heading: Getting guests: cold DMs, the Rick Ross blueprint, and reps
chunks.text:
- In 2017-2018 he had no network and a non-entrepreneurial family, so everything was cold DMs. Most guests still come from cold DMs on Instagram, Twitter/X, or LinkedIn.
- His blueprint is to make it the easiest possible yes:
  - Reference someone the guest likes (Rick Ross admired Robert Greene, whom Casey had just interviewed).
  - Tie it to something they care about now (Ross's upcoming book).
  - Ask for a short, specific window ("all we need is 20 to 25 minutes").
- Ross later told him on air, in effect: you presented yourself like a boss, you didn't come with your hand out, you came with a specific time frame, and my time is valuable.
- He reached out to Rick Ross about 15 times, resending the message, before getting a yes. His line: "You miss 100% of the shots you don't take."
- He frames it as asking what's in it for the guest and how he can serve them, a question that also applies to customers, audience, and partners.
- Advice for beginners: focus on reps, not big names. He says he was "terrible" around interview 13, and that getting better as a host matters more early than landing marquee guests.
- He also advises taking yourself seriously. As a young creator he did not feel he went unrespected, because he treated his own work seriously, and he says that translates.

chunks.heading: Listener.com: a vertically integrated podcast network
chunks.text:
- Casey launched Listener.com about six months before this interview, after the MediaKits acquisition. He bought the listen.com domain because it represented the brand he wanted.
- It has three components:
  1. **Services:** getting CEOs and corporate leaders booked on top business podcasts. This is the bread and butter, driven mostly by inbound and referrals.
  2. **Software:** Listener FM, an AI post-production tool where podcasters upload audio or video and get SEO-optimized titles, descriptions, show notes, and blog posts. It is used internally and has a customer base.
  3. **Media/network:** the Casey Adams Show, a second show called Questions (hosted with DJ Swivel and Brandon Jenner), and a podcasting newsletter launched about five to six weeks earlier.
- The media thesis: to be for podcasting what Barstool was for sports media. The newsletter bridges the business of podcasting (acquisitions, investments) with culture (Cristiano Ronaldo on the Whoop podcast, LeBron's Uninterrupted).
- He sees a gap in dedicated podcast media and names Sounds Profitable as a brand he respects.
- It is bootstrapped, with no outside capital raised, and run step by step. The service side is the current focus, and social-first content around the newsletter is underway on Instagram.
- He describes the pieces as synergistic: guests become clients, then newsletter participants, then users of the software.

chunks.heading: Podcast industry view and monetization
chunks.text:
- He says podcasting has matured. The 2020-2021 wave of investment (Spotify acquisitions and exclusives) has played out, and ad revenue keeps growing.
- Six years ago a poor-audio episode with no marketing could reach the top 200. Now quality is the baseline: strong audio, video for social clips, and polished production.
- His first 50 episodes were not even on video. He now says people should focus strongly on quality.
- He argues the medium is a better channel for some conversations than articles (Colin and Samir interviewing the YouTube CEO).
- Podcasting is a slow, consistency-driven medium unlike social. "You could have the biggest celebrities on for 10 episodes, but if you don't put out an 11th, it's not going to matter." Most shows stop at about 10 episodes.
- On brand deals, he did a Slack campaign in 2022 that went beyond ad reads. He hosted a LinkedIn Live panel on Slack's page for Small Business Saturday with four small business owners. His point is that hosts can package their skills creatively.
- PR firms and agencies are a hidden gem for both sides:
  - PR firms send him batches of strong guests.
  - Agencies working with brands (the Slack deal came through one) can open several brand opportunities from one conversation.
- Chris Williamson is his example of partnering well with aligned brands.

chunks.heading: Positioning a niche show beyond CPM
chunks.text:
- When asked how a niche show sells against download counts and CPM, his answer is brand over data: "Why do people pay $7 for a Starbucks coffee and $3 for another?"
- At MediaKits he saw three creators with identical data command dramatically different rates, depending on who they are and what they mean to their community.
- Treat the podcast as a vertical of a personal brand. Sell integrated deals (podcast, social campaigns, stories, reels, live events) rather than only per-download ads.
- Stand out among millions of podcasts by being a specific human with a specific audience, and aim for long-term partnerships and client work rather than one-off ads.
- He expects human hosts to stay valuable even as brands launch AI-voiced podcasts.
- He notes that podcasting influences business results: a guest, the CEO of Momentous, discussed how a partnership with Huberman Lab impacted that company.

chunks.heading: Distribution, long-term commitment, and personal operating principles
chunks.text:
- Instagram is his main lever. His approach is a long-form show plus 3 to 8 short-form pieces per episode, posted to Instagram, TikTok, and Reels, with more focus on LinkedIn this year.
- His simple view: "no one's going to listen to your show unless you put it out there," and trailers must be engaging. He cites Steven Bartlett's team (a tightly cut first minute of each episode) as the playbook to study, including split testing and team structure, and admits his own approach is still being refined.
- On a 10-year view, he says people overestimate what they can do in a year and underestimate what they can do in ten. He expects to still host his show and run Listener unless it is acquired.
- He says he commits long-term: the podcast since 16-17, a six-year plan to run all six major marathons (New York in November 2024, then Boston, Chicago, Tokyo, Berlin, London) by age 30.
- Success factors he names: adaptability to new technology, focus and commitment, openness to feedback, and learning something every day.
- He credits mentors and partners: Aristotle Loumis (met through Steven Galanis of Cameo) as his key mentor on dealmaking and raising capital, and his fiancée Jaclyn Brunett for pushing him to improve how he shows up.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Casey Adams recounts going from a casino family and mediocre student to lawyer, operator and investor who helped scale a fulfillment business to a Maersk sale. Key themes: treat investing as risk/reward math, copy experts and improve slightly, fix weaknesses by going straight to the activity, and win customers through transparency and acquisitions worth more to you than to the seller.

chunks.heading: Early life, risk, and why Casey treats investing as math
chunks.text:
- Casey grew up in a casino family (Vegas until age 11, then New Jersey). His dad worked in gaming, and as a teen Casey asked his uncle which casino game was best to win at.
- The answer he took on board: "they have those big buildings because you can't win at the games." Casino games are "games of math and the math says you lose," and apparent wins just keep you playing longer.
- Casey treats gambling as paid entertainment and nothing more. People who think they have a system to tilt the math their way are fooling themselves.
- He says this shapes how he invests. He sees investing as "very calculated math," a question of risk against reward, with the difference that investing can actually be won.
- The goal is to weigh the reward against the risk and mitigate the risk in ways you believe you can, without falling in love with the deal.
- Watching his dad drop from a casino VP earning $150-160K to an assistant manager at Wendy's within about 12 months (late 1980s to early 90s) taught Casey that a highly specialized skill set may not transfer. He wanted a baseline toolkit that would make money regardless of industry.

chunks.heading: Learning law school the hard way: find the best and copy them
chunks.text:
- Casey graduated with an economics degree and a mediocre GPA (about a 2.7 at BYU). He decided to try law school after watching his wife practice, applied to only one school, the University of Utah, and got in.
- After a first semester where he was sure he was top 10 and landed in the bottom half, he refused to accept that "those kids are smarter than me."
- He went to every professor who would take a meeting and asked how to think about getting good grades. He identified the best students, asked what they did, compared it to his own approach, and built his own process.
- He graduated in the top 10% of his class.
- He calls interviewing the best in a field and copying them one of the highest-return habits there is, and says most people skip it.
- Step one of the pattern is being honest about a weakness: "I should be good at this and I'm not." Then list the experts, talk to them, and expand out through their network.

chunks.heading: Copy 99%, improve one thing
chunks.text:
- Casey says he doesn't have business ideas to invent. He tries to take "99% copy and do one little thing a little bit better" (more charming, cheaper, nicer).
- His example is the iPhone vs. BlackBerry. The BlackBerry already had email, internet, phone, contacts and a clock, so the iPhone was "a good version of a BlackBerry."
- He knew Apple had something when his nearly one-year-old son slid the unlock block on a display iPhone and opened an app, while BlackBerry required a training course and a book at his law firm.
- He believes in not reinventing the wheel, since most things have been thought of before.

chunks.heading: Building strengths by necessity, not interest
chunks.text:
- Casey describes himself as a well-rounded executive, but says it came from need: "I needed to not suck." At the company then called Visible (later Radial's parent), operations were weak, so he studied Six Sigma, lean and kaizen.
- He says he didn't choose finance or operations out of interest. Someone had to figure it out, and he did.
- On weakness vs. strength, he reframes weaknesses as undeveloped areas: "anything's a weakness until you develop it" (a person with great lung capacity is just that until it's developed for a use case).
- His dominant strength, as he puts it, is a willingness to dig into any topic, translate it into something familiar, and build capability.
- The key to kaizen, in his view, is going directly to the activity: be present, watch it, participate in it, and get smart. He says people skip this by circling the activity instead.

chunks.heading: Leaving law practice and how he split roles with Jared
chunks.text:
- Casey left a top-100 law firm for a regional firm, then moved in-house at his friend Jared Starling's company (Visible), then roughly $10M in revenue with a couple hundred thousand dollars of earnings.
- Two things pushed him out: litigation was making him combative, and billing in 0.1-hour increments made his whole life a stopwatch. He recalls a moment at a movie thinking about the notepad with "0.3" next to his computer.
- He took a substantial pay cut and valued being proactive: getting in front of problems before they turned ugly.
- Early proof of value: a client wasn't paying Jared's company, and Casey spotted that the contract had no waiver of consequential damages. He told the other side's lawyer they'd owe for the damage to Jared's business too, and the money arrived by the Wednesday deadline.
- Their working split: Jared is the entrepreneur and engine who pushes the cadence and takes risk; Casey is "driving," mitigating risk and saying what he needs to be comfortable. Casey says "I'm not an entrepreneur, Jared is."

chunks.heading: Customer experience and the parcel insight that built the business
chunks.text:
- Early on, their biggest clients kept firing them for operational failures, unclear invoicing, or thinking they could do it themselves. Casey took over client management so "we're not going to get fired again."
- Fulfillment was an awful category experience, and he tried to see what everyone did and copy it. The fixes:
  - Let customers come into the warehouse whenever they wanted, without 48 hours' notice, so they felt it was theirs.
  - Replace one-line summary invoices ("hard cost, 12% markup, no breakdown") with activity-level breakdowns: orders shipped, units, destinations, shipping cost.
  - Recognize that the bookkeeper paying the bill was the biggest detractor, so give them transparency ("know their business better than they know their business").
- Itemizing exposed activities they weren't invoicing for, so they likely ended up charging more. His line: "people will pay for value always."
- The superpower turned out to be parcel expertise. Jared saw a mis-routed order and noticed shipping via USPS would be about $2 cheaper per order than the carrier the customer chose, but the software couldn't calculate it.
- Most competitors treated shipments as numbers (distance, weight, cost); Jared treated them as boxes with dimensions, which matter to cost.
- Casey says it made them a big USPS reseller: about $1.5M a year of spend with the Postal Service early on, and about $1.2B when he sold to Maersk 11 years later. The company's real advantage became this parcel edge.

chunks.heading: Acquisitions: buying what's worth more to you than to the seller
chunks.text:
- Roughly half of the company's growth by the Maersk sale was organic and half inorganic. Casey says the acquisitions worked because they were great operators first.
- Their test: is this business more valuable to us than to its current owner? They would look for targets broken in an area they were good at, then price what it would be worth with their contracts and cost advantage plugged in.
- Examples he gives:
  - A fulfillment company bought for around $27M that they believed would be worth $50-60M under their contracts.
  - A business with a $14M market value (private equity had looked at it) where the seller wanted $27-28M. Casey says they paid the seller's price because they believed it was worth $54M, and he thinks it was closer to $70M to them the next year. The business did about $2M of EBITDA with roughly $10M of revenue.
  - Another target the market valued as a SaaS business that they saw as a shipping business, plus others in freight and warehousing where they thought they could run it better.
- He says they were conservative in the math, so they could make big bets. One purchase took a full year of earnings, and another was half their own size.
- On exits: "if they offer a dollar more than I think it's worth I'll sell it to them." He says entrepreneurs fall in love with the business, while he doesn't, and he views a sale as selling something that is more valuable to the buyer than to him.
- He credits some of the outcome to luck: selling at a great point in the market.

chunks.heading: Faith, optimism, and playing long games
chunks.text:
- Casey defines luck as doing the right things and good things happen (or the reverse for bad luck). He says his success includes big runs of luck and that outcomes outstrip his inputs.
- He views learning something and then doing it as an act of faith. He ties his business success to a deep belief in a positive outcome from the work.
- He says this makes him willing to play long games in business: "things will always work out, I'll just buy more time."
- In volleyball, people say "I always feel like I'm about to win," even when down by eight at game point.
- He says belief plus action is a good definition of faith, and that his religious background encouraged it.
- He describes his two-year mission as hard and not enjoyable but valuable, and credits his mission companion for helping him get his head right.
- On trust and teammates, volleyball with Jared taught honest, high-trust communication: they could cover each other's weaknesses without judgment, which carried into business.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Casey Adams reflects on eight years and 400+ episodes of hosting, and how his podcast became the foundation for his companies, his angel round, and his network. He covers where podcasting is going, how he preps interviews, why curiosity and showing up beat strategy, and the thinking behind his new company Listener.com.

chunks.heading: Why Casey's podcast runs as a vehicle for business, not just content
chunks.text:
- Casey started his podcast at 17, after a neck injury in high school that nearly paralyzed him. His stated purpose has held steady for eight years: "to meet great people, learn from them, and hopefully create some type of business opportunity."
- He treats the show as a business engine. Roughly 90% of the 37 angel investors in his first tech startup's funding round were past podcast guests.
- He points to Harry Stebbings as the model for the same idea. Stebbings used 20VC to build up to a $400 million fund by age 28, after starting the show around 2015.
- His takeaway: "podcasting is a vehicle for so much more." He admires hosts who use the medium beyond the show itself, such as Stebbings with an investment fund and Steven Bartlett with a media company.
- His whole career, from his companies to the funds he has raised, "has sort of been built on the foundation of podcasting."

chunks.heading: How Casey's content focus follows his current business priorities
chunks.text:
- Casey lets the show mirror where he is in life and business: "I tend to live my life through the lens of my podcast."
- Early on he interviewed young entrepreneurs, because he wanted to meet other young people doing things.
- When he started his first software company in 2020 and raised capital, he interviewed venture capitalists and startup founders.
- Over the last three years he has run a marathon every year, and he began interviewing ultra marathoners and athletes.
- While engaged, he had guests whose conversations drifted into marriage, kids and family.
- He argues that in an era of information abundance and AI, human conversation and learning from lived experience have become more valuable to him, not less.

chunks.heading: Casey's view of where the podcast industry is going
chunks.text:
- He says podcasting has matured into a "media powerhouse": mainstream appeal, influence on elections, celebrity shows, Netflix moving in, and nine-figure deals (he cites Alex Cooper and Rogan).
- Even so, he calls it "still so incredibly early." More competition exists than ever, but there is still room to find a unique voice.
- Successful shows have large unseen operations: 30, 50 or 60 production and media team members, plus A/B testing.
- The definition of "podcast" is blurring. He notes YouTube's top podcast list included shows with no RSS feed that are not on Apple or Spotify.
- He cites Steven Bartlett's show crossing 10 million subscribers, and a Forbes report that it brings in $20-25 million a year.
- He frames his own listener-side work around this shift. YouTube is the biggest podcasting platform, so "what is a listener, where are they listening" has changed.

chunks.heading: Listener.com: a listener analytics and monetization layer
chunks.text:
- Casey is building listener.com as a listener analytics tool for modern podcasts and podcast teams.
- The first go-to-market product is a listener dashboard that shows a show's value beyond downloads and plays.
- The pitch is that top shows sell merchandise, live events and brand deals, so they need a holistic view of on- and off-platform data.
- Customers use it to pitch brands, guests and partnerships.
- It came out of an acquisition of an existing podcast tech product, which was integrated into the tech stack.
- The longer-term vision: a sales enablement tool and monetization engine for what he calls "podcast 3.0," serving everyone from independent podcasters to large networks as an infrastructure layer.
- The company's name comes from a Larry King quote on his show: "I've never learned anything while I was talking, therefore be a great listener."

chunks.heading: How Casey prepares for and runs interviews
chunks.text:
- He avoids a rigid question blueprint. He keeps topics and notes things he is curious about from his research.
- He deliberately keeps prep light so it never feels daunting. That is part of why he still has excitement and longevity after hundreds of interviews.
- His research checklist: understand the person's story and context, then ask what he does not know about them and what he would want to know.
- His format runs 45 to 60 minutes. He tries to "meet them where they are today" rather than spending 30 minutes on background and 10 on the present.
- He sometimes does less research on a guest so he doesn't "clutter my mind" and can keep curiosity open. He models this on Larry King, who asked direct questions and was curious about each person.
- He is considering testing 2 to 4 hour episodes, citing Chris Williamson, because he worries about defaulting to the same format.

chunks.heading: How Casey turns interviews into a personal operating system
chunks.text:
- He says the value is often in stories and rules that surface later, not in an immediate takeaway from a given episode.
- Example: Tilman Fertitta's "955 rule," tied to picking up trash in his restaurants, meaning focus on the 5% of things people don't see.
- He applies the idea in daily life, such as picking up small trash on the ground, and says attaching meaning, rules and stories to habits is "super empowering."
- He now rereads old transcripts and revisits old episodes, and says he picks up different things as his experience grows.

chunks.heading: Casey's approach to opportunity, relationships and ambition
chunks.text:
- He says there is no strategy behind spotting people who later became big: "it's just a curiosity." Past guests he cites include Jay Shetty and Jake Paul (interviewed in 2018 before his first boxing fight).
- Core belief: "the people that are right around you today are the movers and shakers of tomorrow." He chooses carefully who he spends time with and builds with.
- He says yes to opportunities without knowing where they lead. He is taking a last-minute London trip because he expects it to be valuable.
- His rule of thumb: the events he attends and coffees he takes are never regretted; the ones he skips stay with him.
- He believes entrepreneurship and growth are a "double-edged sword" in that it is "hard to be satisfied," and he tries to step back and recognize how far he has come.
- His biggest lesson from guests: "just keep going and never quit," with a built-in "element of delusion."
- On priorities, his advice to his future self is to know what matters most (family, wife, future kids) and not let lesser things crowd it out, and to stay present.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Casey Adams explains how a near-paralyzing football injury at 16 reshaped his identity and drive, and how he started a podcast at 17 with no plan, just momentum. He argues for focusing on the next single step, building relationships through content, and letting adversity become part of your story.

chunks.heading: Casey's drive comes from a neck injury and a "things could be worse" mindset
chunks.text:
- At 16, Casey was a sophomore athlete (hockey, lacrosse, football, about five foot six, a running back). On the first day of hitting practice he landed on his neck during a "B drill." The doctor said it was like a guillotine to his spine.
- He wore a neck brace for six months and was told he could probably never play football again. His identity, daily routine and commitments disappeared, and he spent a stretch depressed and anxious.
- He frames this as the pivot of his life. The free time led him to social media and business content, and he says he could easily have become resentful instead.
- He grew up in a small Virginia town. He did not fly until age 16, and his parents were far from entrepreneurial (his father spent 30 years at Philip Morris, his mother is a special ed teacher). His original plan was college and a job.
- His standing reminder: "things could always be so much worse." He says that perspective, along with Robert Greene's ideas about death, sits at the top of his mind daily. His response is to make something of the day, the week and the year.

chunks.heading: How Casey turns negative events into identity instead of victimhood
chunks.text:
- He argues that significant events, good or bad, become part of identity. People can attach purpose to a bad event or let it define their limits.
- He asks what question you ask yourself afterward: "Who am I now that this event has occurred in my life?" Questions tied to growth and change lead somewhere different than self-pity.
- He says to also mark positive milestones deliberately: the first customer, the day you started the company, the first client. Attaching meaning to those cements identity and gives something to build on.
- Momentum cuts both ways. A 5k, then a 10k, then a half marathon makes a marathon plausible, while circumstances you let define you stop you.
- He keeps the neck brace from that period turned into a trophy, with a plaque reading "Keep going, never quit."

chunks.heading: Starting the podcast with no plan and building on momentum
chunks.text:
- Casey started his show at 17 in 2017, first called "Rise of the Young." He was inspired by the last chapter (on podcasting) of Gary Vaynerchuk's book *Crushing It*.
- His mentality was "let me just try it." He had no mic, only wired Apple headphones, no launch strategy and no perfect title. The first episode was a roughly three-minute audio recording made while walking around his bedroom.
- He had already run a Facebook advertising agency and done social media marketing for local businesses.
- He booked a 5 to 10 minute meeting with Gary Vee by DMing him on Instagram about four months out. He then set a goal of 60 interviews in 90 days so he would have something to talk about with Gary.
- He started with friends (his former business partner Kieran, Jeff from Jr Garage) and did Facebook Live interviews, releasing one to three a week.
- He caveats that in 2023 you do need to find a way to stand out, but that should not stop you from starting and building momentum.
- Preparation was the point: the interviews put him in position so that when he sat across from Gary, he knew what he was doing.

chunks.heading: What the podcast produced: relationships, learning and business opportunities
chunks.text:
- He says the show gave him three things: meeting like-minded people (he cites Dale Carnegie's *How to Win Friends and Influence People*), lifelong learning from people who have done it (he skipped college and moved to Arizona about a month after graduating), and business opportunities that followed.
- He has done over 400 episodes. Guests include Larry King, Rick Ross, Elon Musk's mom and sister, and the founders of Netflix and Twitch.
- In 2021 he raised $1.5 million before launching Media Kits, a real-time data and analytics product for creators. He says about 80 to 90 percent of the money came from past podcast guests, and he had roughly 250 guests by then.
- He says he did not interview people to pitch them. He had worked with large creators and agencies that build media kits, and the relationships were already there when he had an idea to share.
- He sees podcast depth as the opposite of what short-form rewards: "the ability to connect on a much deeper level."
- His current company is Listener FM; he previously built and sold Media Kits.

chunks.heading: What holds people back from creating content, and the "next step" fix
chunks.text:
- Main blocker: comparison. Feeds show others' success, and people either try to be someone else or measure themselves against where they think they should be.
- He is fine with learning from others ("a good artist copies, great artists steal"), but the issue is comparing yourself instead of looking at the cards you are dealt.
- A common trap is "if only I had started earlier," which he calls a heavy thought that holds you back more than you realize. He asks instead what one thing you can do today.
- Minimum step examples: share a thought on a tweet, make a 15-second TikTok, talk to one customer, reach out to one person.
- He recommends using social media to get inspired and connect rather than to compare, and being aware of how your feed makes you feel.
- Scale the ask down: building an Amazon is incomprehensible, but selling one book today is doable.

chunks.heading: The "will this next step kill me?" lesson from Iron Cowboy James Lawrence
chunks.text:
- Casey interviewed James Lawrence, who did 50 Ironman triathlons in 50 days in 50 states and later 101 Ironmans in 101 days, much of it on a fractured leg.
- Casey asked him for advice for when Casey would be deep in his first marathon (December), listening around miles 20 to 21.
- James called it "The Hurt Locker" and told him to focus on the next step and ask whether it will kill him. If not, keep moving.
- Casey applies this to 75 Hard, where day 29 feels different from day 1, but stacked small wins give proof of effort. He concludes: "today is all you have," so focus on winning the day.

chunks.heading: 75 Hard as a mental reset
chunks.text:
- Casey has completed Andy Frisella's 75 Hard twice, the second time finishing in May 2023, and was invited onto Andy's show *Real AF* in St. Louis afterward.
- Rules: a gallon of water a day, two 45-minute workouts (one outdoors), read 10 pages, follow a diet with no alcohol and no cheat meals, and take a daily progress photo.
- He sees it as a mental toughness program rather than a fitness one, and says the small daily wins build discipline.
- He plans to do it once a year for the rest of his life as "a mental reset" because business days are fast-paced, and the outdoor time forces him to be intentional.

chunks.heading: Larry King: "Greatness is driven"
chunks.text:
- Casey interviewed Larry King in 2019, when Larry was 87 and Casey was 19. Larry had done about 60,000 interviews and interviewed every living president of his era.
- Asked what makes people great, Larry answered that greatness is driven, and that those with drive who simply don't quit are the ones who succeed.
- Casey's takeaway: those who keep going through adversity, including a failed business that they move on from without letting it define them, are the ones you hear about, and the others are not.
- He says the weight of the lesson comes from who said it and his intentionality, and he applies it to the gym, relationships, business and perseverance in general.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Casey Adams recounts how a sports injury pushed him into entrepreneurship, personal branding and podcasting, and how that network led to MediaKits. He shares principles on building credibility by showing up, documenting stories, pivoting deliberately, and spotting product ideas from repeated client requests.

chunks.heading: How Casey built credibility as a teenager
chunks.text:
- Casey's core principle for credibility: "build credibility by associating with credible people," and to do it genuinely.
- His vehicle was a podcast, started December 2017 by interviewing friends his own age, including his business partner Kieran and Caleb Maddox. It grew from there to guests like Larry King, Rick Ross and Gary Vaynerchuk.
- He set a goal of 60 interviews in 90 days. He did two to three interviews a day after high school, being "obsessive in the DMs."
- He started small and stayed consistent: he spent all of 2016 putting out content before the podcast launched.
- He says the podcast became a huge part of his identity and "opened up 99 doors," including MediaKits.

chunks.heading: Showing up in person: the Grant Cardone and Miami story
chunks.text:
- From 2017 to 2019, while still in high school, Casey flew to LA almost once a month and spent every dollar he made on trips to events. Mentor Dan Fleischman invited him to his "elevator nights."
- He calls the hardest sale of his life asking his parents to let him travel to California alone at 17.
- Tactic from Grant Cardone's book *Sell or Be Sold*: he DM'd Cardone for a podcast spot, got routed to Cardone's assistant, and emailed her that he would "be in Miami next week from Wednesday to Friday."
- He had no plans to be in Miami and had never been there. She booked him for Thursday at 3, so he booked flights with friends and missed two or three days of school.
- He used the same move to land an interview with the mayor of Miami.
- His takeaway: it isn't the most scalable strategy, but "just get in the room with people." He says to commit first and figure out logistics after.

chunks.heading: Showing up digitally and documenting the journey
chunks.text:
- Casey says to show up in the DMs, in content and in physical rooms. Some investors in MediaKits' pre-seed round came from a cold DM.
- He says to document your experiences and tell the stories: "you learn through stories."
- He tells people to tell their story authentically, and stack credibility over time.
- His personal brand began as book reviews and a record of his learning on Snapchat while he was in a neck brace for six months after an injury ended his football career.
- During that period he followed Tai Lopez, Gary Vaynerchuk and Tony Robbins, and journaled a personal brand game plan.
- He says the content then stacked into a brand that has shifted a lot over almost five years.

chunks.heading: Pivoting and how he handles it
chunks.text:
- Casey's pivots: affiliate marketing on Snapchat, then a book, then a podcast, then Build Your Empire (a media company running events in Scottsdale, about two years), then MediaKits.
- He moved across the country after high school to join Build Your Empire. The dozens of events there helped him meet early guests such as Drama, Rob Jurdeck and Robert Green.
- He also renamed his show from "Rise of the Young" to "The Casey Adams Show" when he felt he'd outgrown it.
- Before MediaKits he was working on a podcasting startup called PodSwipe. It never launched and raised no money.
- Rule he uses: "find where pivots make sense and go all in on it." Build it, see whether it works, stick to it if it does, and pivot again if it doesn't.
- He admits pivots are scary in your head, and says the moment you do it "it feels so good."
- He has journaled "be comfortable getting uncomfortable" since age 16. When he gets comfortable, he adds a challenge. He stepped up from 2 to 3 mile runs to 5 miles, then began training for a marathon, because physical challenges transfer to business.

chunks.heading: The MediaKits origin story
chunks.text:
- A media kit is a document creators use to pitch themselves to brands, showing bio, past work and analytics.
- Around 2018, friend and automotive YouTuber J.R. Garage got a Pennzoil brand-deal inquiry and asked Casey and Kieran to build him a media kit.
- They built it by hand in Canva or Photoshop with screenshots of his analytics. It took a couple of hours, and he got the deal.
- About two months later Ferrari reached out and wanted to fly him to Daytona Beach for a brand deal. His stats had changed, so they had to update everything manually, "changing twos to threes and fives to sixes."
- That was the light-bulb moment: why isn't there a way for creators to build a media kit that never goes out of date and can be shared through a link?
- They shelved the idea because they lived in Virginia and lacked time and resources.

chunks.heading: Timing the launch and building MediaKits
chunks.text:
- In 2020, Casey and Kieran were roommates during the pandemic. TikTok was exploding and creators like Charli D'Amelio and Addison Rae became celebrities overnight, so they judged the creator economy to be growing year over year.
- Casey had relationships from the podcast to help raise money. Kieran told him the timing was right, and Casey dropped PodSwipe to build MediaKits.
- They hired a developer and a designer, then held a launch party in LA with around 600 creators (the Callee performance mentioned).
- Launch: the first two months were "a disaster," with bugs and international developers to fix. After about a month and a half of fixes they relaunched in mid-October.
- Afterwards they kept shipping integrations, most recently Twitch. He says hundreds of streamers are using it and hundreds of creators message them saying it helped them land a brand deal.
- Their stated vision: let creators of every type (musicians, podcasters, athletes, streamers) organize cross-platform data in one place.
- Casey says being a creator himself and getting pitched with media kits all the time gives him conviction about the product.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Casey Adams explains how he raised $1.5M pre-seed for Media Kits largely from podcast-guest relationships, and how he built a network from a small Virginia town. He shares how to land high-profile podcast guests, prepare for interviews, build lasting relationships, and why to just get started.

chunks.heading: How Casey raised his first round from his podcast network
chunks.text:
- Casey's first fundraise was a pre-seed "family and friends" round for Media Kits, just over $1.5 million, closed in mid-2021. It was his first time raising capital for a startup.
- He says the round came almost entirely from relationships he already had. His line: "your network is your net worth."
- The majority of the money came from previous guests of his podcast, which he has hosted since he was 17.
- He did not pitch broadly. He picked a handful of people in his network who could add value, understand the product, and give quality feedback.
- He set up "dozens and dozens" of meetings in a short period.
- He leaned on a mentor, Aristotle Loomis, who coached him through the process and "picks up the phone whenever you call." Casey says a mentor who stays with you through the hard times and teaches you the process matters more than just "find mentors."

chunks.heading: Casey's three pieces of advice for first-time fundraisers
chunks.text:
1. **Nail your story.** Every product and company is a story: why you, why now, and why this market. Know why you're the best operator for the role, especially when building the deck.
2. **Pitch people who give real feedback and want you to win.** Cold email pitches are fine, but get your first 10, 15 or 25 pitch meetings with people you already know. Their feedback sharpens the story and builds the confidence to pitch well.
3. **Be consistent.** His raise took about six months of "pure consistency": hearing no, getting rejections, and staying consistent with outreach, pitching and follow-ups.

He adds that there is never a perfect time to raise, and that fundraising conditions were drying up in places. His advice is to use confidence in the story and get feedback as early as possible.

chunks.heading: Building a network from nothing
chunks.text:
- Casey grew up in a small town in Virginia (Chesterfield) and knew nobody in business, marketing or startups.
- At 16 he went to his first networking event, a real estate conference in downtown Richmond. He was the youngest person in the room among roughly 500 people.
- At the start of 2017 he was invited to speak at an event in San Diego through a friend, Caleb Maddox. It was his first trip to California, and his parents did not want him to go.
- That led to more events in LA, New York and Miami. He says he skipped about 60 days of school in junior and senior year to attend.
- He then recorded podcasts with many of the people he met. He describes the payoff as compounding over four to five years, showing up in his ability to raise capital and get into certain rooms.
- His core point: "finding a vehicle to connect you with people in a deeper way is highly underrated."

chunks.heading: Why an interview podcast is a growth hack
chunks.text:
- Casey calls starting an interview show "such a growth hack to building a network."
- He lists three benefits:
  1. You learn from the people you interview.
  2. You build a network.
  3. You build content and a personal brand you can use your own way.
- He sees podcasting continuing to get better as more people recognize this.

chunks.heading: How he attracted high-quality guests
chunks.text:
- It didn't start with big names. He started in his bedroom with Apple headphones and a quick two-minute intro, posted right away to build momentum.
- He set a goal of 60 interviews in 90 days, which forced him to learn his interview style and sharpen his skills.
- Step one: his first 20 to 30 guests were people he had already met at events or had talked to briefly in Instagram DMs. Saying yes was easier for them.
- Step two: use that base of interviews to reach out to others: "I have a show, I've done XYZ type of interviews, would love to have you on."
- Most of his guests came from social DMs, mainly Instagram and Twitter, sometimes LinkedIn.
- He advises never being afraid to reach out and follow up, and asking in a polite, unique way. He talks about finding "that unique third door" that gets a person to say yes.
- He believes genuine passion and curiosity naturally pull bigger guests over time.
- His 400+ interviews include the founder of Twitch (Justin Kan), the founder of Netflix (Marc Randolph), Elon Musk's mom and sister, and Larry King.

chunks.heading: His interview preparation process
chunks.text:
- He now goes in without written questions and focuses on listening and curiosity. He researches the guest and watches past interviews, then jots down ideas.
- He wants it to feel like "a coffee shop with someone getting to know them for the first time": background, current work, struggles, challenges, what excites them.
- He tells new podcasters to test both extremes, an interview with 50 questions written down and one with none, and then pick whatever feels most comfortable.
- He credits Larry King's quote: "I've never learned anything while I was talking."

chunks.heading: Building lasting relationships with guests and influencers
chunks.text:
- Relationships are built, which takes continual effort: showing up to events they invite you to, answering texts and calls, and small gestures like sending a green juice to someone who posted they were sick.
- His view: "the little things in any relationship are the big things."
- Example: he met mentor Aristotle after interviewing the CEO of Cameo (Steven Galanis). He had Aristotle on the podcast, and they have rarely gone more than a few days without talking since 2020.
- He says relationships also depend on timing. People who aren't close now may be closer in a couple of years.
- His summary: put in the effort and time, and show up when people present an opportunity.

chunks.heading: Advice for people in their 20s
chunks.text:
- Casey's main advice is "just get started." He started at 16 with no background in business and no relationships, relying on work ethic and drive.
- He says not to let opportunities pass without taking action, and to learn by trial and error what to say yes and no to.
- He sees ages 18 to 25 as a special window to learn, meet people and have experiences with youthful energy.
- He writes "keep going" in his journal every day, because reaching a milestone just reveals the next one, and he says the value is in the journey, not the destination.

chunks.heading: Media Kits context
chunks.text:
- Media Kits is a platform for creators to build a media kit with real-time data and analytics. It launched at the tail end of 2021.
- It was acquired by Viral Nation, announced about four weeks before this interview. Casey continues to build the product inside Viral Nation.
- He mentions Viral Nation exclusively represents 500+ talent. His stated plan is to hit KPI goals and launch new features within that ecosystem.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Casey Adams explains how starting a podcast with no plan at 17 compounded into 450+ interviews, a funded startup and an exit. He covers shipping fast, consistency, intentional relationships, building products from real pain points, and listening as a learning edge.

chunks.heading: Casey's path into podcasting and how he got started
chunks.text:
- At 15, a football neck injury (spine unstable, neck brace for six months, no more football) pushed him toward business content. He followed Gary Vaynerchuk and Tony Robbins and came out "fueled up" for business and marketing.
- He had no entrepreneurial family background. His mom was a teacher and babysitter; his dad worked at Philip Morris for about 30 years.
- The podcast idea came from the last chapter of Gary Vee's "Crushing It" in 2017, when Casey was 17. He started with no strategy or plan, recording on a phone with wired Apple headphones. The first episode ran about three and a half minutes and was live within a day or two.
- His advice: many people spend six months to a year conceptualizing a podcast. In most cases, "just getting started is the best thing to do."
- The original goal was to interview successful founders, learn from them, and create business opportunities through networking.

chunks.heading: Getting guests: the 60 interviews in 90 days push
chunks.text:
- Casey cold-DMed Gary Vee on Instagram asking what it would take to get five minutes of his time. Gary replied and Casey skipped three days of school to meet him in New York.
- Ahead of that meeting he set a goal of 60 interviews in 90 days.
- He began with friends of similar age, then "shot his shot" with bigger names. Early guests included Andy Frisella, Ed Mylett and Grant Cardone.
- By the time he met Gary he was doing 40 to 50 interviews, and Gary encouraged him to keep going because opportunity compounds from "micro occurrences."
- Six years in (December 2023) he had done about 450 interviews, with guests ranging from Larry King and Rick Ross to Elon Musk's mom and sister and the founders of Twitch and Netflix.

chunks.heading: Why long-form podcasting pays off
chunks.text:
- He cites three benefits: meeting people and building depth in relationships faster, learning from others' stories, and the opportunities that follow.
- Hour-long conversations "expedite relationship building," which creates trust, respect and openness to working together later.
- Long form builds more trust with an audience than short clips, because listeners get to know you through depth.
- He acknowledges the downside: podcasting is hard to master and slow to reward compared with short-form video where someone "can just put out 10 TikToks."
- The podcast is "the backbone of everything," not his only income. It feeds conversations and opportunities across his businesses.
- Concrete payoff: his last company raised about $1.5M from 37 angel investors, and roughly 90% of those investors were former podcast guests.
- He stayed consistent through gaps (sometimes a month to a month and a half without an episode) by asking why he does it, and by thinking about compounding over 20 years.

chunks.heading: Building companies from problems he lived
chunks.text:
- MediaKits.com launched in 2020. It let creators aggregate cross-platform data in one place to share with brands, updating in real time. It was acquired in September 2022, and he worked at the acquirer, Viral Nation, for six months.
- The idea came from a friend, a YouTuber with about a million subscribers, who was assembling screenshots of Instagram, TikTok and YouTube for a brand's media kit request. Casey and his co-founder started with the first step, a Media Kit built in Canva, to learn the pain points.
- His approach: "What are problems that creators deal with," then take the first step.
- Listener.fm launched about four months before the recording. It is a post-production tool for podcasters: upload an audio or video file and get SEO-optimized titles, descriptions, show notes, blog posts and newsletters.
- He built it because he deals with the problem himself and uses it every time he records. His stated direction is a "vertically integrated podcast network" with owned IP and unique shows, plus services for podcasters.
- He is also launching a new show with two co-hosts about a month after the recording, and says he now thinks harder about go-to-market and content strategy than he did six years ago because there are far more podcasts.

chunks.heading: Learning and questions as an operating principle
chunks.text:
- He did not go to college. He moved to Arizona a month after high school to run a media company.
- He frames lifelong learning as being willing "to learn anything from anybody," and says he learns most from stories and others' experiences, which cuts his learning curve.
- He named Listener.fm for this idea. He cites Larry King: "I've never learned anything while I was talking."
- Practical habits: put yourself around people who have done it before. For his first marathon he interviewed ultra-marathoners and James Lawrence, who did 101 Ironmans.
- He warns that with abundant content, "a superpower" is choosing who to learn from, since there is "no one size fits all" in advice.
- Quality questions make for better listening. He tells the story of acquiring the Instagram handle @questions, which led to a podcast called "Questions" with Jordan Young (DJ Swivel) and Brandon Jenner.

chunks.heading: Recommended resources and habits
chunks.text:
- Book: "How to Win Friends and Influence People," which he rereads about once a year.
- Podcast: All-In, and more broadly, find one to three podcasts to listen to consistently.
- Practice: find something that makes you feel inspired, such as journaling, sunrises or sunsets.
- Networking early on: he attended events (e.g. ones run by Dan Fleshman) as a teenager when he had little to offer beyond "a youthful spirit and a hardworking ambitious mindset," and mostly listened.

chunks.heading: Life priorities he builds around
chunks.text:
- He describes four pillars: business, foundational relationships, health, and quality relationships.
- Health: he was training for a marathon about 25 days out in Palm Beach, Florida, after running his first in Hawaii the prior year, when his longest run before training had been three miles.
- He plans year-defining moments (a book, a company, an exit, a trip) and had just bought the "big ass calendar" from Jesse Itzler's team to map them.
- He values longevity in everything, quoting Warren Buffett that reputation "takes 20 years to build but two seconds to ruin."
- He treats mortality as a reminder to treat people better and check in on them.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Casey Adams (Listener) argues that podcast value now lives beyond the monthly download. Publishers should represent their whole ecosystem (long form, clips, newsletters) to sponsors, and small shows should win creative long-term deals with brands already in their orbit.

chunks.heading: How Casey's podcast and clip strategy evolved: from scrappy interviews to a business development vehicle
chunks.text:
- Casey started his show in 2017 at 17, in high school, as a way to connect with founders. He has since had 500+ founders on, from Netflix founders to Elon Musk's mom and sisters.
- The first ~50 episodes were Facebook Live streams on a roughly $100 Blue Yeti mic; he downloaded the audio and uploaded it as the podcast.
- He set a goal of 60 interviews in 100 days to get reps in before a meeting with Gary Vee in his junior year. Early guests became friends and later his co-founder at his last startup.
- He says episode 151 felt like his first real episode: by then he knew what not to do, what his curiosity and format were. He didn't care about listeners or opportunity, and the reps opened doors.
- Two years in, at 19, he interviewed Larry King (then 87). King's reason for starting a new show: asking questions and having conversations is "what I'm built for."
- He frames the show as a business development vehicle, not a bid to build the biggest show. His last company had 37 angel investors, and nearly all were past guests.

chunks.heading: Casey on brand deals: host-read plus partnerships that extend beyond the mic
chunks.text:
- He says he rarely did core programmatic advertising. He did host-read ads, but more often branded partnerships that went beyond the mic.
- Example: Adobe and Slack, years ago, three- or six-month campaigns with four to eight host-read ads, each with about three clips per episode.
- His creative pitch to Slack: because his show interviews founders and Slack wants to talk to founders, he would interview small business owners live around Small Business Saturday.
- The live stream ran on Slack's LinkedIn channel (about a million to a million and a half executives following, with paid promotion behind it) and reached about 200,000 live concurrent viewers over a roughly two-hour interview series.
- His view: the podcaster is the talent and must bring the creative ideas. Good brands will take a bet, as TBPN's did with logos at the bottom of the screen and large payments.
- Most deals beyond that came from founders he had already interviewed whose companies were testing podcast advertising. They were already in his ecosystem, so he didn't need to cold pitch.

chunks.heading: Advice for emerging shows: find brands you believe in that believe in you
chunks.text:
- Casey's advice to small shows: don't cold pitch 100 brands that are allocating budget across the biggest shows in the world.
- Instead ask what brands you already use, what relationships you have, and (for interview shows) who you can interview and how to pull your existing ecosystem in.
- Look for brands that align closely with you, then give them the creative ideas, because at this stage of the market that is the host's job.
- Aim for long-term partnerships with brands you believe in and that believe in you.

chunks.heading: The Formula 1 model behind TBPN's sponsorships
chunks.text:
- Casey's read: TBPN's Jordy said it was "not a podcast." You could list it on podcast apps, but they built a cutting-edge media company, the "ESPN of tech."
- Their sponsorship model was not CPM-based. It was effectively "get in or get out": brands who wanted to associate with them paid big budgets for long-term presence in all the clips and content.
- Casey says the talent mattered. The hosts had built and sold companies and worked in venture, so people came for them and not only for their guests. He also pointed out their unfair advantage of top CEOs appearing frequently.
- He adds that they were also tech influencers, active on X all day, in replies and posting funny things.
- His takeaway for interview shows: ask whether people care about the host or only the guest, and build the host into the draw.

chunks.heading: Beyond the download: measuring an episode as a cluster
chunks.text:
- Casey's view on measurement: an episode is more than downloads. It is a cluster of the long-form YouTube, X and Apple/Spotify versions plus newsletter, short form and live event activations.
- A download is just a device fetching an episode. He notes you could download 12 episodes in a month and listen to none.
- His example of the gap: a show might have 1,000 downloads a month yet get 1 million to 8 million impressions on social. If an advertiser only sponsored the long form, they missed those impressions, and showing that missed opportunity is a sales tool.
- Practical consequence he describes: publishers should control how they pitch the show as an ecosystem, using retention data (for instance YouTube) and omni-channel campaign reporting, instead of handing advertisers a spreadsheet of numbers.
- He argues comparing 5,000 streams on one show with 10,000 downloads on another is not a fair equation, because the depth of trust and type of listener differ.

chunks.heading: How advertisers should diligence a podcast
chunks.text:
- Casey's advice to advertisers: before looking at downloads, check whether an emerging listener base exists. Can you find a culture in social comments and shares?
- Using shows like All-In or My First Million as examples, he says you can tell from word of mouth and audience interaction whether people care, whether the show has 100 or 100,000 listeners.
- He says there are many ways to manipulate downloads, so advertisers can be left holding the bag.
- He suggests advertisers do their own diligence on a brand's presence across platforms in addition to reading the download report.

chunks.heading: Quality versus volume, and less-is-more as something you earn
chunks.text:
- Casey's view: there is polarity in the space. Some creators put out hundreds of pieces a week, while shows like Acquired release a handful of long episodes a year and are still huge.
- He argues less-is-more has to be earned. His quote from Charlie Munger: "take a simple idea and take it serious," which he applies to David Senra's show, whose guests (Dana White, Evan Spiegel) make every episode a top-tier listen.
- His example on the short-form side is James from School of Hard Knocks: on the main account, which has about 8.5 million followers, he posts roughly 10 clips a month rather than more, and in over two and a half years there is no clip under a million views.
- His point is that once you find something that works, you can say "how are we the best in the world at what we do" and make less but higher quality.
- He says there is no one-size-fits-all format and you have to figure out which approach applies in your world.
- He also references Hormozi putting out about 100 clips a week from live conference Q&A after noticing a comment with 1,000 likes saying the new format was great, as an example of volume surfacing what resonates.
- He notes a signal of format mix: people say "love your podcast" when they mean they watch clips on Instagram, and that works, as with a Caleb Pressley show built for 1-3 minute clip-oriented brand deals.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Casey Adams explains how a podcast started at 17 became the foundation of his career, funded his last startup from past guests, and led to Listener. He covers data fragmentation beyond downloads, AI features for podcast networks, how brands should use podcasting, and his delusional-optimist view of AI.

chunks.heading: How Casey got into podcasting and why it became his career foundation
chunks.text:
- Casey launched the Casey Adams Show in late 2017, at 17, from his bedroom in a small Virginia town. He had been an athlete (hockey for roughly 10-15 years, then lacrosse, then football), and a football injury put him in a neck brace for nearly 6 months.
- He picked podcasting after reading the last chapter of Gary Vee's *Crushing It*, which was about podcasting.
- His goal was clear from day one: "meet great entrepreneurs, learn from them, create business opportunity."
- The first six months were about 50-60 interviews, built by cold pitching anyone he could reach on social media. A few unexpected yeses gave him the confidence to keep showing up.
- Within two years he was interviewing Larry King. Over eight years he has interviewed 500+ founders and leaders and still releases roughly an episode a week.
- He credits that clarity of purpose for the show's longevity.

chunks.heading: Podcasting as a relationship engine: raising over $1M from past guests
chunks.text:
- Casey moved from Virginia to Arizona right out of high school, skipped college, and started Media Kits in 2020 with a co-founder. The product let creators aggregate cross-platform social data and present it to brands.
- They raised just over $1 million from 37 angel investors, and pretty much all of them were past podcast guests.
- He says his intention was never to interview people in order to raise money from them. Years of building high-quality relationships meant that when he had a company to raise for, he already knew some of the smartest people in his network.
