- His approach was to share what he was building, ask for thoughts and advice, and then offer the chance to invest.
- Takeaway he draws: podcasting "really is what you make it," and the less traditional ways to build, grow and monetize a show are often where the value is.
- Media Kits was acquired in 2022 by Viral Nation, a Toronto company.

chunks.heading: Why Casey built Listener: data fragmentation "beyond the download"
chunks.text:
- After the Media Kits exit he wanted to build in podcasting. He had watched podcast tech for years (Riverside, Anchor, Spreaker) as well as the roll-ups and acquisitions.
- His pitch for Listener is an AI-powered listener analytics platform for the modern podcast and podcast network, tying together audio, content and commerce integrations for sales enablement and episode reporting.
- Core insight: podcast data is more fragmented than creator data was. People care about and track different metrics on different platforms.
- Hosting platforms don't track social views tied to episodes, even though Spotify and others tell podcasters to post clips on social to grow. Clips live on different platforms and mean different things, with no easy way to attribute them to an episode's growth.
- His view of the "modern podcast" is audio plus video, live events, private communities and merchandise, so a show is effectively a multimedia company.
- The market gap: the money that came in around 2020 for roll-ups has played out, and he sees an opening for a tool built for "podcast 2.0 or 3.0."
- Listener launched in May 2025 and, as he put it, "the lack of analytics to track and manage everything in the space is real."

chunks.heading: Selling sponsors on multi-platform campaigns
chunks.text:
- His largest brand deals (Slack, Adobe) were vertically integrated, not just host-read ads. They included social clips, segments built to become clips, and newsletter blasts for specific episodes.
- He says those multi-platform campaigns led to the larger deals and to more successful campaigns for both sides.
- His conclusion: podcasting should be treated as "social first, video first," and measured that way.
- He did a six-month campaign with Slack that was tightly associated with his brand.

chunks.heading: How Listener uses AI: episode clusters and "conversation with your data"
chunks.text:
- **Episode cluster reports:** when an episode is published via RSS, Listener scans the connected social integrations. It pulls the long-form YouTube video and the associated Shorts, Reels, Facebook reels and TikTok clips, and attributes them to the episode.
- The data refreshes every 24 hours, so a report shows growth for the episode's downloads plus its cross-platform clips.
- Episode Clusters 2.0 automates what used to be manual clip-to-episode linking. The AI suggests, for example, 15-20 clips using transcription data and sentiment analysis, and the user approves or denies.
- He frames the workflow as "inbox zero for your podcast" and accepts it won't be 100% accurate, which is why thumbs up/down review exists.
- **Listener AI (insights):** a ChatGPT-style interface scoped to the network's own data. Example questions: top-performing social platform, which platform is growing most over 3 months, views and downloads in April vs May.
- Core customer today: podcast networks managing 5 to 50 shows.
- His view of where AI fits: pulling insights and speeding up workflow, not replacing hosts.

chunks.heading: How a network workflow breaks down and where the small-team advantage is
chunks.text:
- He describes a network or production company's work in four steps: produce, edit, publish, then track and manage content. Listener sits at the fourth step, reporting.
- Listener's team is five people, and his thesis is that AI coding platforms let a team of five feel like a team of 15.
- On speed: "if you spend 6 months building something, the reality is in 6 months things will be a lot better, be a lot different." He argues that being lean and shipping quickly to get product feedback on AI features is the main advantage against larger companies with podcast-tech acquisitions.
- On risk: the biggest risk isn't how you implement AI but "being unaware of the true capability and the impact of what is happening right now." He calls himself a "delusional optimist" who leans into the upside without being naive about the downside.
- He names a line for podcasting: he would not want to interview an AI version of a guest, and wouldn't want a world where more people listen to AI-narrated podcasts than to real people. He mentions Wondercraft (AI-generated host-read ads) and Delphi AI as examples of tools worth understanding.

chunks.heading: How brands should use podcasting
chunks.text:
Casey splits brand involvement into three plays:

1. **Start a show.** Own your narrative. Variants include a simple one-person show, or hiring influencer talent to host and bring in guests.
2. **Advertise on shows.** Build long-term relationships, as BetterHelp and AG1 have done, not just one-off episode sponsorships.
3. **Get executives and founders booked as guests** on other shows to go direct to consumer and borrow their audiences. He cites the way major executives and politicians use appearances like Rogan's. He says he tries to bring value to executives by helping them get on other shows.

His hot take: brands should build internal podcast networks, not just produce their own shows. Example: a project management app could convince outside marketing or productivity podcasters to join its network, as HubSpot (HubSpot Podcast Network) and Morning Brew have done. He predicts that over the next 5 to 10 years many tech companies, large and small, will want such networks.

chunks.heading: Why the company is named Listener
chunks.text:
- He's proud of the one-word domain, listener.com, and says the name reflects the thesis that everything in the industry "comes back down to the listener": advertisers want to reach listeners, and shows create content for them.
- The name came from his Larry King interview, where King said: "I've never learned anything while I was talking. Therefore, be a great listener."
- Product implication: the platform is meant to meet listeners where they are, across social, live events and private communities such as Patreon, and he sees the next era as reframing what a podcast is, with long-form in audio or video.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Casey Adams, who leads global business solutions at Degreed, explains how a market-defined category can trap an innovator, why he says no to distracting customer demands, and how hiring and hard-problem handling shape culture. He closes with a view that breaking an employee's vulnerability-based trust is the worst leadership betrayal.

chunks.heading: Casey's view of how leaders build culture and trust
chunks.text:
- Casey argues culture "is not about perks," it is about how a company handles and solves hard problems. He cites Ben Horowitz's *The Hard Thing About Hard Things* as the source of the idea.
- Degreed has roughly 10 operating values covering how people think, operate, treat each other, and balance work and relationships. He says those values earn their keep when applied to hard cases:
  - customer demands that would pull the company off its product roadmap
  - good or bad financial news
  - a market downturn and a possible reduction in force
- Treating people with dignity and respect in those moments shapes culture more than anything else.
- Every person added to or removed from a team shifts the culture. Hiring "the best people wrapped around a core set of values" matters more than adding controls.
- He prefers finding the right fit over forcing someone into an existing model.
- Degreed is virtual-first and hires the best people regardless of location. It was recently named one of the top 100 most flexible companies to work for in the US.

chunks.heading: The biggest betrayal a leader can commit
chunks.text:
- Casey says the worst betrayal is breaking trust and confidence, not someone leaving or a role changing. He sees departures as normal business: "I don't take it personally. If I were to leave, I wouldn't want them to."
- A team member may admit "I'm actually not very good at these two things" out of vulnerability. A leader can use that to build a development plan and give mentoring and experience.
- Betrayal is repeating that confidence to others, or using it in a performance review to downgrade the person in comp. Casey says: "the biggest betrayal you can do is to create that environment and then take that trust and then put it somewhere else."
- An environment of trust creates a highly productive team. A leader's job is to build on people's vulnerabilities and lift them up.
- He endorses the principle from Jocko Willink and Leif Babin's *Extreme Ownership*: "there's no bad teams, only bad leaders." If people aren't lifted up, "it's on you."
- He wants to be "someone that people want to work for and work with" and sees his role as serving his people and making their jobs easier.

chunks.heading: Hiring: missionaries first, then specialists
chunks.text:
- Early hiring at Degreed was around mission-driven people who believed in the mission to "jailbreak the degree" and make skills matter, giving people the path to own their careers.
- Later hiring shifted to filling specific roles and skills, while trying to keep the passion.
- Casey names these sources of hires:
  - customers, who bring industry and vertical knowledge and a customer perspective (he stresses "we're not poaching")
  - people from commoditized learning management system vendors who love the space but want something more innovative
- He notes there are over 400 learning management system providers that are "basically a commodity." Degreed gives those people a chance to work on something that isn't.

chunks.heading: Market categories: take the revenue, don't let the box define you
chunks.text:
- The market labeled Degreed a "learning experience platform," a category it created but, Casey says, "never wanted to be."
- He sees real benefits in accepting the label:
  - You can make money.
  - The market understands what you do.
  - You stop fighting educational battles on many fronts.
- The risk is complacency. "To do that in an innovative tech space is a surefire way to become irrelevant."
- He credits leadership with not losing sight of the original goal and finding "the courage and sort of the right moment" to break out of the category. The category credibility now lets them push the market into new places.
- He admits Degreed "probably could have held on to who we wanted to be a little better."

chunks.heading: Educating the market, then re-educating it
chunks.text:
- Around 2016-2017, Degreed had to teach the market that skills, not degrees, titles and prerequisites, are what make up a person. Companies thought in ladders; he describes the reality as lattice moves, where a skill set like marketing and demand work might make someone a great product designer or engineering leader.
- Once "everyone in the space just talks about skills," the word became "almost meaningless." Early on no one wanted to listen; today no one does because everyone claims it.
- The second round of education shifts to execution: how to compile and normalize skills data and use it for business impact (internal mobility, retention, faster time to market).
- He frames this as a head start. Degreed has been doing the hard data work for a long time.

chunks.heading: Selling learning to business leaders
chunks.text:
- Learning has often been an afterthought or compliance, and it is hard to measure. It is the first thing dropped when budgets or tech get consolidated.
- Casey's approach is to stop selling only into the learning team. Sell to the business line leaders and executives who own the goals.
- The pitch runs like this:
  - a company has a goal, such as "a 2027 goal of being here"
  - the goal cascades into gaps in talent and capacity (his example is AI, a space the company has never built teams for)
  - if those reskilling and upskilling gaps aren't closed, "the greatest objectives for the business can never be attained"
- The value proposition is closing business gaps, not better content or leadership programs.
- Go-to-market is a standard enterprise mix: events, marketing, outbound sales, and original research on how the workforce learns.
- He reminds himself that the playbook is often "more of the same, then better," not a shiny new thing.

chunks.heading: Managing distractions and priorities as a product company
chunks.text:
- Casey says customers will offer to "write you a check to do other things that will distract you." Degreed refused to build its own LMS despite customers asking, because it isn't the company's DNA and why be "401" among 400 providers.
- Some distractions can be positive. AI was a "helpful distraction" or "detour" that can shorten the time to the north star, through curated content, less time for instructional designers, and adaptive coaches.
- Which obstacles to say no to and which to say yes to is the core decision. Each yes creates new obstacles, so plan for them.
- Regulated customers like financial institutions can be averse to AI, which brings back the education problem.
- His example of build-versus-buy: voice agents progressed so fast that it makes little sense to build your own when you can use APIs from businesses that did.
- His "magic wand" wish is for a tech stack with interoperability, so tech debt stops competing with innovation for resources. That makes the company more responsive to customers and new ideas.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Casey explains how he used a podcast and in-person networking to build a personal brand that opened doors to investors, mentors and his startup, Media Kits. He covers focusing on one platform, earning confidence through track record, and treating time quality as more important than hours.

chunks.heading: Personal branding as authentic perception and authority
chunks.text:
- Casey defines personal branding as "building the most authentic perception of yourself online." Everyone already has an in-person first impression; the digital footprint is the same thing maintained online.
- He started in 2016 at age 16 after reading Gary Vaynerchuk's Crush It and Crushing It. He never tried to be someone he wasn't: he reviewed the self-development books he was reading, which led to daily Snapchat book reviews and Snapchat affiliate marketing.
- His view now: a personal brand is built on accomplishments. "You can put out the most content in the world but what gives you credibility?"
- His early credibility came from association. At 17-18 he interviewed successful entrepreneurs on a podcast while starting a digital marketing agency, then promoted the interviews across social media. The collaboration lent him authority.
- He quotes Jay-Z: "I'm not a businessman, I'm a business, man."
- He says personal brand does not guarantee success, since many successful people stay low-key and behind the scenes. But it speeds up what used to require knocking on doors, and gives instant authority in a niche.
- Your brand changes as you change; the work is maintaining it over time.

chunks.heading: How a personal brand attracts investors and equity partners
chunks.text:
- Casey says business partners bet on him because of his relationships from the podcast and what he has shown on social. He has taken equity in multiple companies as a result.
- He describes a specific case: a man he was pitching for Media Kits wanted to invest after seeing him on Instagram as a young hustler, without knowing his background. Casey credits four years of consistent personal branding.
- Raising money for Media Kits was easier and faster (a roughly $1M round over about 30-60 days) because of the relationships and podcast built over the prior four to five years.
- His podcast and brand are "a vehicle" for the business. His current focus is deal structures, fundraising rounds, acquisition, and starting an angel investment fund, and he uses interviews with venture capitalists to feed that interest.

chunks.heading: Platform strategy: pick one and start small
chunks.text:
- His early mistake was trying to do everything at once: Snapchat, Instagram, a Facebook page, viral videos, and thinking about numbers rather than content.
- His advice: go in on one thing. He argues TikTok is the best platform for new creators right now.
- Reasons he gives: you get more fulfillment when you have traction; starting a YouTube channel and reaching even 100 subscribers is hard without a viral video; Instagram is still very curated.
- Tactic: make 15 to 30 second TikTok clips, put out 25 or more in a month, and see what sticks.
- He admits he has under-used TikTok and YouTube himself, partly through procrastination. Now his social time is spent meeting people, pitching investors, and fueling his company.

chunks.heading: The podcast as deal flow, networking and relationships
chunks.text:
- He started the podcast at the end of 2017, now about 300 episodes, initially interviewing friends and people he wanted to talk to. Notable guests include Larry King, Jordan Belfort, Grant Cardone, Robert Greene, Rick Ross and Chris Voss.
- He calls the podcast "deal flow, networking opportunities." Having it positions you as a person of value while you also learn from every guest.
- Example: he interviewed Aristotle Loomis (founder of Ellison Eyewear, later a cannabis tech startup that raised over $60M). After the interview Casey told him what he was working on, they set up a follow-up call, then texted daily. Within about six months Loomis became a mentor, investor and board member for Media Kits and helped with fundraising.
- Lesson: when someone is willing to give you time, keep them close. "If someone's giving you their time they could be spending their time anywhere else."
- Casey stresses that not every guest turns into a relationship; you find the few you really hit it off with.

chunks.heading: Showing up in person and where confidence comes from
chunks.text:
- His biggest investment in himself over five years: travel to events, to meet people, and "to shake someone's hand in person." He cites hosting and attending events.
- In-person meetings make you easier to remember and build a deeper connection than Instagram DMs or Zoom.
- Story: in 2018 he messaged Grant Cardone, got a reply from his assistant, and when offered an in-person interview in Miami the following Thursday, he booked a flight despite never having been to Miami and having to miss school. He has since spoken with Cardone at events and talked with him often.
- His confidence comes from track record: Cardone was roughly his 30th-40th interview, so he could point to guests Cardone knew. His first 10 interviews were scripted and scattered. A sports upbringing with two older brothers also shaped his mentality.

chunks.heading: Media Kits: origin, problem and positioning
chunks.text:
- Media Kits (mediakits.com) is a real-time data and analytics tool that lets influencers, creators, podcasters, musicians and bloggers build an online media kit, a "digital resume," with live data.
- Origin: about three years earlier, YouTuber friend Jeff (JR Garage) asked for a media kit when a company reached out, then asked for an update after Ferrari wanted to fly him to Daytona. His PDF was already outdated after growing by 100,000 subscribers. That sparked the idea of a media kit that never goes out of date.
- Timeline: the idea sat for about two years; when COVID gave them time, Casey and co-founder Kieran bootstrapped for five months, then built a team of about eight full-time. As of the interview it was in beta with a 5,000-person waitlist and a planned launch party.
- Casey sees the problem as a user too: guests pitch him with media kits, and when he pitches guests they ask for his podcast's media kit. He sees potential in influencers, musicians, podcasters, athletes and eventually gamers pitching brand deals and sponsorships.
- He believes every creator who wants to work with brands efficiently will need one, "like having a website or having an Instagram account."

chunks.heading: Routines, creativity and efficiency
chunks.text:
- Sleep: he does not believe in staying up for days. He aims to sleep by 10 to 10:30 and wake at 5 to 7 depending on the day, and says it differs per person. An ideal pattern is asleep at 10, up at 5 or 5:30.
- He says it is about quality of time, not quantity: "Are you actually moving the needle?" He sets tangible daily, weekly and monthly goals, such as the million dollar raise, and notes missed goals slow the ship.
- Creativity comes from a run, the gym with a podcast, or reading. As co-CEO juggling team, investors, partnerships, design and developers, he says the work can "fog your mind"; 20-30 minutes of one of those activities puts him back on center.
- He likes biographies and company stories (he was reading Super Pumped on Uber) because seeing others' problems puts his own in perspective and gives him an idea he can apply to operations, team building, scaling or raising capital.

chunks.heading: NFTs as a learning experiment
chunks.text:
- He first heard of NFTs in February 2021. With digital artist friend Television he dropped his own one-of-one piece depicting him at a table with Larry King, Elon Musk and Rick Ross.
- His goal was not the sale price but learning the process: minting, building hype, marketing, and promoting.
- He points to Gary Vaynerchuk's project raising $30-50M in two to three weeks and attaching NFTs to in-person events, and expects similar links to concerts and album releases.
- He considers himself not an expert but sees blockchain ownership, tickets and IDs as a change over the next decade, dependent on adoption.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Casey Adams, founder of Listener.com, argues that podcasting has outgrown RSS and download counts. Shows are now ecosystems spanning long-form video, short clips and newsletters, and publishers should treat them as media companies. He covers per-platform measurement, brand trust over CPMs, and why execution matters more than ideas in the AI era.

chunks.heading: Podcasting is now a format, not an RSS feed
chunks.text:
- Casey argues "podcast" has evolved from a technical delivery mechanism (RSS) into a format: an episodic, conversational show.
- He uses a book analogy: books began on paper, but Kindle and audiobooks are still books. The format survived the change of container.
- Netflix and Tubi signing podcast-style shows are, in his view, contracting for a talk show comparable to the big podcasts.
- He says YouTube, Spotify and social platforms raised the medium's value, business opportunity and cultural influence. Much of the RSS loyalty comes from people who remember the first 10 to 20 years, when it was neither visual nor social.
- He rejects the idea that audiences are wrong to call a Netflix or YouTube video show a "podcast". "Who am I to say the audience is wrong in how they perceive it?"
- His taxi/Uber analogy: both move you from A to B, and fighting the new delivery method means you lose out. He cites the car versus the horse in the same spirit.
- He ties this to a generational shift: people who grew up on social media met podcasts on YouTube and clips and have no context for RSS.

chunks.heading: Why Casey thinks the industry loses sight of the listener
chunks.text:
- He says people in the industry get absorbed in internal debates and forget who they serve: the listener (or viewer), where they are, and how they consume today.
- That belief is behind the company name. He quotes Larry King: "I never learned anything while I was talking, so be a good listener."
- Brands sponsor and advertise on podcasts because they want to reach listeners, so the audience's behavior should drive the measurement.
- He accepts that RSS is a valid origin story worth honoring, but says the industry has matured well past downloads.
- His stance on whether he is still a podcaster: yes, 100%. The term describes the format, not only the pipe.
- He keeps a direct-to-audience channel in mind: RSS gave a direct line to listeners and trust. In a short-form, algorithmic world that is harder, so build direct links via email or a newsletter and be present on the platforms your audience already uses.

chunks.heading: Listener.com: aggregating a show's whole footprint
chunks.text:
- Listener.com launched in May 2025 as an AI-based analytics and intelligence platform for modern podcast publishers, from the biggest publishers to large independents.
- Thesis: combine audio data, long-form video data and short-form content data (plus newsletters) in one place.
- Casey's framing is "Episode Clusters": one episode becomes a cluster of audio downloads, a long-form YouTube/Facebook/X video, and dozens of short clips on YouTube Shorts, Instagram, X, Facebook and TikTok.
- His example: an episode with about 16k audio downloads reported as roughly 1.3 million total reach once YouTube, audio and social are combined.
- Platforms are not equal. An X viewer, an Instagram viewer, a long-form YouTube viewer and an Apple/Spotify listener are different consumers, so each platform gets its own treatment and is not collapsed into a single impression number.
- Integrations (15+) fall into three groups:
  - **Audio:** Apple, Spotify, and hosts such as Megaphone and Simplecast.
  - **Content:** YouTube, Instagram, Facebook, TikTok, X.
  - **Third-party:** newsletters (Beehiiv now, Substack in progress), added from customer requests in the last six months.
- Matching clips to episodes: if a guest or episode name appears in the title on Apple/Spotify and in the caption of social clips, the system suggests clusters automatically. He says it's imperfect, and building clusters manually takes minutes once the workflow is understood.
- He launched a Listener MCP so teams can query their data from Claude or ChatGPT, or via "Listener AI" in the product. Example questions: "What's our best content?" "How is our show growing across everything?"
- His line on AI: "We're not building an AI podcast." They use AI to understand data better and deliver more effective insights, not to produce shows.

chunks.heading: Reporting to advertisers and brands
chunks.text:
- Casey says Listener now tracks tens of millions of dollars in ad campaigns for roughly 50 to 70 brands.
- Publishers send brands a Listener campaign report. His example: a brand spent $1M across five shows and 50 episodes, and sees performance across YouTube, audio and social, including host-read ads and social integrations.
- Brand feedback he cites: "This is exactly what we were looking for. How did this not exist before?"
- Advertisers sometimes learn they appeared in far more places than expected, such as 37 pieces of content with their logo or caption, when they thought they bought a single host-read ad.
- Data stays in the publisher's hands. Publishers share Listener links or dashboards with brands, and the platform supports verification through the underlying integrations.
- On measurement standards (Spotify's 30-second count, IAB's 60-second standard, YouTube's opaque view definition): Casey says Listener isn't leading those standards conversations. His position is to pull each platform's data as that platform counts it, and he expects eventual convergence.
- He advises against waiting for an ideal industry standard: "You shouldn't rely on the perfect scenario happening, because most of the time it never will."
- He wants Listener to define an industry-style format for reporting host-read ads across platforms, not a programmatic ad format.
- For small shows: a young podcaster may have modest downloads but a big social community and newsletter list. Showing the combined footprint stops advertisers from undervaluing them based on a downloads estimate alone.

chunks.heading: Who Listener sells to
chunks.text:
- Go-to-market started with networks and large multi-show publishers, for three reasons: they have the most data to work with, they care most because the stakes are high, and they are the ones monetizing with big budgets and big brands.
- Customer example: Jomboy Media, a New York baseball media company (he compares it to Barstool Sports for baseball) with about 40 to 50 podcasts. He says MLB took a minority stake in it.
- Over the last 60 to 90 days, Listener started onboarding independent publishers using a self-serve model with a free trial. His view is that the big-publisher endorsement had to come first, and independents followed.
- Network customers get a guided onboarding because the product integrates into their workflow. He also offers demos via the site.

chunks.heading: What the new media winners do: TBPN as the case study
chunks.text:
- Casey calls TBPN a model for modern media. Founders who are experienced operators with deep tech-ecosystem relationships built a live daily show with top guests.
- His account of their results: revenue went from $5M to $30M a year because they treated the show like a Formula 1 team, with many sponsor slots and exclusive year-long deals per sector.
- His takeaways:
  - Treat the show and network as an ecosystem: long-form, short-form and newsletter are all ways of reaching people.
  - Treat it as a media company. Greatness shows up in the studio investment, the daily suits, the 5-days-a-week, 3-hours-a-day commitment.
  - Be clear about whom you serve and what you want out of it, then build a business around it.
- On why TBPN was valued by OpenAI: brand trust and credibility with a community, plus influence on perception. He says the hosts advise OpenAI's comms team after each show.
- Control of narrative is why companies launch their own podcasts. He cites a16z's new media arm and Substack's founders' show as examples of controlling narrative with long-form, high-production content. He contrasts that with a short TV hit where you risk being misunderstood.
- Brand and trust matter because they sustain a show: a luxury brand and a plain product can be nearly identical but valued very differently.
- He rejects reading TBPN's deal as "a podcast that got a deal". In his framing it was a strategic deal, different from Joe Rogan's or Alex Cooper's.

chunks.heading: Execution, AI, and why the creator still decides
chunks.text:
- On using AI for content strategy: tools like ChatGPT or Claude can give ideas and direction, but "execution is all that matters".
- His examples: AI can give you a rocket recipe or YouTube ideas, but who actually follows through and commits to being the best at it? He says no original idea exists and the cliche is true for a reason.
- Why tech fans didn't get OpenAI-sized deals: they didn't execute the format or put their own taste in front of an audience.
- His advice: "Your show today shouldn't look like your show a year from now." Keep adjusting week by week, as MrBeast's early videos compared to today show.
- Use AI as a thinking partner: connect your data to understand what is growing and what works, then add your creative touch.
- Casey's own motive for his show: not to be the biggest show, but to learn from great founders, build relationships and create opportunity. He says some of his best opportunities, investments and capital raised for companies came from conversations that began on the show.

chunks.heading: Honesty with the audience in sponsorship
chunks.text:
- Casey describes early podcast advertising: hosts got products to try before reading ads. His example is Casper mattresses: hosts were sent beds for a week, and some reported a back problem on air.
- That honesty built trust in podcast advertising and gave brands useful feedback over the long term, even if it hurt in the short term.
- He applies the same standard today: audiences can read between the lines, "People can tell when they're being misled," and creators must stay honest and transparent with sponsors and acquirers.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Casey Adams traces his path from a high school sports injury to podcasting, a book, and co-founding MediaKits, a creator analytics tool. He stresses stacking small wins, going all in on a venture, spotting problems firsthand, and building confidence through uncomfortable repetition.

chunks.heading: From injury to business: how Casey Adams got started
chunks.text:
- At 16, a football neck injury (neck brace for six months, no more football) left him with free time and led him to YouTube and business content.
- He followed Tony Robbins, Gary Vaynerchuk and Tai Lopez. He and a friend each put in $30 for Tai Lopez's 67-day course.
- He bought more books than ever (Think and Grow Rich, How to Win Friends and Influence People, Crushing It) and describes the stretch as creating "this new identity."
- By sophomore year he cut his course load to the bare minimum, committed to business, and skipped the college path.
- He moved to Arizona a month after graduating high school, with a media company and a podcast already running for two to three years.
- He calls curiosity his biggest innate advantage, and says it is "very easy to shut off an opportunity."

chunks.heading: Stacking early wins to build momentum
chunks.text:
- Casey says small early wins let him keep going, and that they matter for earning trust from parents as much as for himself.
- At 16-17 his first company ran Facebook ads and Instagram for local businesses (dentist, chiropractor, sports shop) on monthly retainers.
- Earning a couple thousand dollars a month at 16 won his parents' belief and gave him freedom to travel to LA, New York and DC for events.
- Around his 30th-35th podcast interview he booked Chris "Drama" Pfaff, which his mom had watched on TV with him as a kid. He calls it reinforcement of his commitment, not a money win.
- His advice: actually publish episodes instead of thinking about starting a podcast. "Micro wins do build momentum," and momentum helps you stick with something longer.

chunks.heading: The 90-day podcast sprint
chunks.text:
- He read the podcasting chapter of Gary Vee's Crushing It and it "instantly spoke" to him.
- He started listening to many shows, followed favorites, then launched his own.
- A simple Instagram DM set up a meeting with Gary Vee. Within 90 days he had done 60 interviews and was a full-time podcaster.
- He says he did not realize in the moment that reading the chapter would become his whole identity and brand.
- He sees every career chapter starting the same way: something captures attention, consumes your mind, and you read and watch everything about it.

chunks.heading: The origin of MediaKits and why timing mattered
chunks.text:
- In 2018, friend Jeff (JR Garage, an automotive YouTuber then at roughly 500-600K subscribers) was asked for a media kit by Pennzoil.
- Casey and co-founder Kieran O'Brien built it by hand in Canva or Photoshop (headshot, bio, analytics screenshots) in a couple of hours, and Jeff got the deal.
- Weeks later Ferrari asked for one. The kit was outdated, so they manually updated numbers and re-exported a PDF.
- That manual work sparked the idea of a link-based media kit with real-time data that never goes stale.
- They shelved it because they lacked the experience and network to launch a tech company in 2018.
- In 2020 (COVID, TikTok creators like Charli D'Amelio and Josh Richards exploding) they restarted it as a side project: 20-30% of their time, bootstrapped, using contractors.
- In early 2021 they raised a family-and-friends round, closing about $1.25M in four to five months, and launched in August 2021.
- His takeaway: "the time will never just be right," and an idea can still be worth pursuing years later.

chunks.heading: What MediaKits is and how it was built
chunks.text:
- It is software that lets creators connect social platforms in about 30 seconds and share a real-time-data media kit with brands.
- Integrations at launch: Facebook, Instagram, Twitter, YouTube. Later TikTok and Twitch. Spotify for podcasters and musicians is next.
- Casey is a non-technical founder; the team relies on an engineer who built the product.
- He turns the non-technical status into an advantage by making team-building the core focus.
- He says "there's no part-time founder": once you commit, a company becomes your life.
- He frames the fundamentals as being excited about the idea and excited about the people you build with.
- As of the interview there were just over 20,000 creators on the platform, and the team regularly surveys them.

chunks.heading: Knowing when to move to the next chapter
chunks.text:
- Casey says transitions happen gradually and you often do not notice them while you are in one.
- He journals daily or at least weekly to document what he is doing, what matters to him and his goals.
- His career steps: Facebook ads, podcasting, media company, live events in Arizona, a book at 17, viral TikTok marketing help, then MediaKits.
- He argues "saying yes to something is saying no to another thing," so follow what is pulling you.

chunks.heading: Building confidence
chunks.text:
- Put yourself in uncomfortable rooms. At 16-17, around 30-50 year old speakers and founders, his confidence deflated, and the fix was to keep introducing himself.
- Story: he met Larry King's son Chance, then saw Larry King in a wheelchair at the Century City mall. He took about 6-10 seconds, said hello, got a photo and sent it to Chance. A month later Larry was on his podcast (late 2019).
- Watch how you talk about yourself. He says he used to say "I'm not a runner" before training for a marathon (17 miles was his max when he hurt his knees).
- Use repetition through things like cold emailing, cold calling and sales. He sold fundraising cards for his football team in high school.
- He pairs confidence with gratitude: being grateful for past lessons makes you confident in the next move.

chunks.heading: Web3 and the creator economy
chunks.text:
- MediaKits is Web2 today, built on social integrations, but Casey says the team has plans for some Web3 integrations (no details given).
- He has been deep in NFTs for about a year and made an NFT drop with Television (as referenced in the conversation).
- He says most creators know the word "NFT" but not the impact on their business over the next 5-10 years.
- His view is that launching an NFT project is not the right first step. Community and real utility come first.
- He cites Gary Vee's VeeFriends as the model: real-life utility, an annual event, podcast access, real IP, and a "10, 20, 50 year play."
- He mentions a travel influencer whose NFT project fit his brand and community goals.
- His advice for creators is to take even 1-10% of what Gary Vee does and learn from the community he built, whether or not you hold the NFTs.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Casey hosts Chase Chewning and mostly asks questions; his own contributions are brief. He frames podcasting as a brand and networking tool, shares that he launched imperfectly on AirPods and a $100 mic, and notes that frequent episodes and Spotify tagging drove download spikes.

chunks.heading: Starting a podcast: Casey's three-step blueprint (via Chase's questions)
chunks.text: Casey's host-side material here is thin, since Chase (the guest) does most of the talking. The source is Chase Chewning's interview on Casey's show, and the substance (health coaching, military, monetization, daily routine) belongs to Chase, not Casey. The only content attributable to Casey is a few remarks about his own podcast setup and tactics.

chunks.heading: Start imperfect and upgrade quality later
chunks.text:
- Casey began his podcast on a roughly $100 Blue Yeti microphone, and the first episode was recorded on AirPods, which he calls "terrible because of bluetooth."
- He says he "didn't care about the quality" at the start and was "so obsessed with putting it out there getting something going and going with that momentum."
- His principle: quality can always get better, but you can't wait for it to be perfect. Take imperfect action.
- He has since upgraded his full podcast setup (Shure microphones, new equipment sourced from Chase).

chunks.heading: Share to Spotify via Instagram Stories to drive downloads
chunks.text:
- Tactic: tag the guest in an Instagram Story that carries the Spotify podcast link. If the guest reshares the story, they automatically reshare the Spotify link too, with no copy-paste or swipe-up needed.
- Casey says Rick Ross did this when he was a guest (11 million Instagram followers) and his downloads "went through the roof."
- Casey calls this the reason he'd recommend sharing via Spotify's native story share, because it removes friction for the guest.

chunks.heading: Use Zoom interviews to increase output and downloads
chunks.text:
- During the pandemic Casey did 60 to 90 Zoom interviews, something he wouldn't have done otherwise.
- The high frequency of episodes, made easy by remote interviews, produced a large spike in downloads.
- In 2019 he had been trying to do mostly in-person interviews because he wanted to meet guests; remote recording made frequent publishing much easier.

chunks.heading: Why Casey does a podcast
chunks.text:
- He tells people that starting a podcast is very beneficial to your brand and networking, and that is the main reason he does it.
- He says the payoff "comes back tenfold."
- His distinction: that brand and networking value is separate from directly monetizing the show.

chunks.heading: Casey's podcast listening habits
chunks.text:
- He leans toward business, financial and news shows rather than interview shows, and names Robinhood Snacks as one of his favorites.
- He uses Spotify and notes that he often tags guests in his own Spotify shares.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Casey Adams recounts starting his podcast at 16-17 after a football injury, how it led to fundraising from past guests and building listener.com, and his tactics for landing big guests. He stresses starting now, staying flexible, offering value to guests, and doing hard things.

chunks.heading: How he got into podcasting and what it did for him
chunks.text:
- Casey started his show in December 2017 at 16-17, in Richmond, Virginia. His mom is a special ed teacher and his dad worked in a tobacco factory for 30 years, and he had no business mentors.
- A football injury put him in a neck brace for almost 6 months and stripped away his athlete identity. He fell down social media rabbit holes (Gary Vaynerchuk, Tony Robbins, Jay Shetty), started a Facebook-ads agency for local businesses, then read the podcasting chapter of Gary Vee's *Crushing It*.
- He started a podcast "to meet entrepreneurs, learn from them and maybe create some level of business opportunity." He says there was "a naive aspect of not overthinking."
- He calls podcasting "the foundation of my career": it helped him launch companies, fundraise, and meet founders he later invested in.
- His first 15 episodes charted on the top business charts alongside Tim Ferriss and Gary V.
- He thought he was late back then, and cites "the best time to plant a tree was 20 years ago. The second best time is today."
- He did not go to college; he moved from Virginia to Scottsdale, Arizona a month after graduating high school. He calls his ~500 episodes his business school.

chunks.heading: Podcasts as a fundraising and relationship engine
chunks.text:
- His startup MediaKits (2020) helps creators, podcasters and Twitch streamers aggregate their data and present it to brands.
- It raised just over $1.5M from 37 angel investors, against a $1M goal. He says "pretty much all of the investors were past guests on my podcast," and he had no prior fundraising experience.
- His view: an in-depth interview is "an expedited way to build trust and relationships." A 45-60 minute sit-down builds more depth than months of social interaction.
- He uses guests as free advisors for whatever he is doing. He interviewed endurance athletes before his first marathon in 2022. He interviewed CEOs about keeping a marriage strong while scaling a business when he was getting married.
- From interviewing nearly 500 founders, he took away that the key question is "what's your unique advantage," meaning founder-market fit.
- He says a big sample of data points beats one data point. Founders give contradictory advice, so you have to sort it for yourself rather than take it as is.

chunks.heading: Getting big guests: his outreach playbook
chunks.text:
- Early on he set a goal of 60 interviews in 90 days, and describes the early intensity as what set him on his path.
- He used his youth as an advantage: "lean into your advantages." Guests like Andy Frisella were doing him a solid because he was 17 and DMing them 15 times a month. His rule is to be consistent and hard to ignore.
- The core rule is to make the pitch about what's in it for the guest, not about you or your show. Find what matters to them now (a new book, a sold company, a story they're telling on other shows) and build the pitch around it.
- Do the research. He notes AI can now dig through 20 years of someone's social content so you can reference things they don't usually hear.
- Name-drop past guests the person follows. Check their Instagram following for people you have had on, and reference them; it "expedites that level of trust" and lowers the guard.
- Example: he cold-DMed Rick Ross about 50 times, unsending and resending. The one that worked said he had just had Robert Greene (Rick's favorite author) on the show, offered to promote his new book, and promised only about 20 minutes. Rick later said he came on because Casey "presented yourself like a boss," not with a hand out, and respected his time.
- Be everywhere: cold email, cold DM, show up at events. The biggest guests came from consistency, follow-up and serendipity, like going to an event in LA where the person or their team would be.
- A short personal video DM still works. Send a quick Instagram video to someone you follow or have interacted with, because "you're going to watch the video." It is how he met one of his best friends, who was a groomsman at his wedding.

chunks.heading: Personal brand, niche and evolving the show
chunks.text:
- Rise of the Young (2017) became The Casey Adams Show around 2020, when he was turning 20 and no longer identified with "young people" as the mission. A personal name brand is something you can "forever stand on."
- He has rebranded the cover and style many times and says each rebrand feels like a new season. People stall out because they stop identifying with the show and don't change it.
- He points to Justin Kan, who went through roughly six rebrands before Twitch (originally justin.tv, a GoPro on his forehead).
- Don't pigeonhole yourself early. His show's topics evolved with his interests: fundraising, marathon training, marriage.
- He argues we're moving from a social media economy to an interest economy, where a new account can get millions of views. Owned channels like podcasts and newsletters matter more because they give you direct access to your audience.
- If the name, format or set doesn't excite you and make you proud to promote it, reinvent it. Options include adding a co-host or changing the format.
- He admits he posts too little and has "left a lot of growth on socials on the table," because he lives much more offline now.

chunks.heading: The podcast industry and where it's going
chunks.text:
- The industry is more commercial than in 2017: bigger budgets, video production, and more focus on how you gain awareness. He still thinks it's the best time to start because it's "really just getting started."
- Most podcasts quit early (the average podcast puts out about 10 episodes and stops). He calls the medium the antithesis of quick short-form content, which is why depth and trust with an audience are worth more.
- He sees podcasters of the future building a "modern media business" rather than just a show: podcast, newsletter, live events and tours, merchandise, brand deals, and their own products and services.
- He sees live tours and cinematic sets (Chris Williamson, Sweetgreen's location for a founder interview) as a differentiator. He cites a partnership with Eventbrite as evidence that live podcasting is rising.
- Past guests don't carry you forever: "you can't just stand on the shoulder of your past episodes, the past guests. You have to continue to reinvent it."
- Copy the blueprint of the top shows, then "crumble it up" and make it your own. Examples he gives are Caleb Pressley and Mel Robbins, who started podcasting at 52.
- He built Listener (listener.com) out of this experience. It is AI-powered analytics for podcast publishers running 10-50 shows (think The Athletic, The Ringer, Barstool). It aggregates audio, long-form video and social data for sales enablement and episode reporting, and is moving toward campaign management between brands and publishers.
- He could only see the need because of 8.5 years as a host across platforms (Spotify, Megaphone, Spreaker). Publishers were "living in spreadsheets."

chunks.heading: Doing hard things, seasons and consistency
chunks.text:
- Andy Frisella's influence taught him to do hard things. He has done 75 Hard three times, and sees its value in following through on what you say you'll do, not in the program being optimal.
- He has run four marathons and plans to do all the world majors over about six years (New York, Boston, Chicago, Berlin, London, Tokyo, Sydney). Long runs are phone-free time with himself.
- He works in seasons: when not training, he lifts to build muscle; when marathon training, he spends about 3 months dialed in on zone 2 and says no to more things.
- He cites Jesse Itzler's "Misogi" idea: pick one year-defining hard thing, such as a physical pursuit, a business, a book or a podcast.
- He believes you can't be perfect across the board in every season of life, and recommends choosing where to give 100%.
- Quitting is also valid: if you truly believe it's a waste of time and the signs are there, pause or pivot. He notes YouTube began as a dating platform.
- He gave Matt Rife as a persistence example: roughly 15 years of grinding before an overnight breakout, which Dane Cook described to him.
- Closing advice: get started today, and "don't get in your own way," because people are mostly worried about themselves.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Casey Adams explains how he started a podcast at 17 to meet great people, learn, and create business opportunity, and how that network later funded Media Kits and led to Listener. He shares his cold-outreach framework for landing big guests and why founder-led media is a distribution channel.

chunks.heading: Starting at 17: injury, pivot, and the podcast as a business engine
chunks.text:
- At 16 a football neck injury (inner spinous ligament damage) ended his sports identity; he spent about 6 months in a neck brace, which he calls the "white space" that forced him to find a new path.
- He went from social media rabbit holes (Tony Robbins, Gary Vaynerchuk) to running a Facebook ad agency at 16, serving his dentist, chiropractor and local sports shop, then retainer clients.
- He had no entrepreneurial family background (mom a special ed teacher, dad at Philip Morris), though his dad ran a side-hustle asphalt business.
- He started his podcast December 22, 2017, at 17, with a three-point checklist: "meet great people, learn from them, and create business opportunities."
- Before the podcast his content was book reviews on Instagram and Snapchat stories: he didn't pretend to be an expert, he brought people along as he learned.
- Senior year he was making about $15K/month on average, including a $15K/month client who became a partner, and he dropped out of the college path (he had planned lacrosse at UVA) after taking only three classes.
- His advice to young people on skeptical family: "it's the actions and results" that make the conversation easier.

chunks.heading: Why the podcast is never judged on direct revenue
chunks.text:
- He says the show was never required to make money; if it meets the three checklist items, he'll keep doing it "forever" because it is "foundational to my career."
- The payoff came indirectly: his media kits company raised $1.5 million in 2021 when he was 20, from 37 angel investors, and about 90% of them were past podcast guests.
- He built a live events company in Scottsdale (about October 2018) as an extension of the show, inviting past guests like Drama (Chris Pfaff) to speak with no budget.
- That led to two co-hosted LA events with Drama's Young and Reckless brand in 2019, where he met Robert Greene, who later led to Rick Ross.
- Takeaway he draws: one relationship (guest, then speaker, then partner) compounds into the next opportunity over years.

chunks.heading: Booking big guests: the cold outreach framework
chunks.text:
- Fearlessness came from being the youngest of three brothers, playing with kids six years older: he wasn't afraid of rejection or a "no."
- Gary Vaynerchuk's book *Crushing It* (last chapter on podcasting, cold DMs) prompted the approach.
- First big guest was Drama (Rob Dyrdek's cousin from Rob & Big): he DM'd after Drama posted a book, saying he'd just started his podcast and done 20 interviews; Drama replied in about 10 minutes.
- Gary Vee: he sent a DM with a photo shoot of himself wearing Gary's K-Swiss sneaker; that led to a 15-minute in-person meeting in New York months later, and he used the wait to do as many interviews as possible so he had something to show.
- Rick Ross, two years after Drama: his message was short, referenced a mutual friend, respected time, and tied to something Ross cared about: "I recently had your friend Robert Green on my podcast. It would be such an honor to have you on my show for 15 minutes to talk about your new book."
- The framework: short message, social proof via someone they know, a specific small time ask (15-30 minutes), and a hook tied to what they're promoting right now (book, movie, charity).
- Most pitches get nothing: "I've probably had more nos or messages that didn't respond than I've ever had received," with hundreds of non-responses behind the guests people know.
- Timing matters: big names are on press tours for something specific, so know "why now."
- His assistant now sends outreach proactively to people he'd like to talk to; he believes the more personal the message, the better.

chunks.heading: Listening as a principle
chunks.text:
- He credits Larry King (his 2019 interview was reportedly King's last long-form interview) with the line: "I've never learned anything while I was talking. Therefore, be a great listener."
- This shaped his show style (no scripted questions, lean on curiosity) and the company name Listener.
- He applies it to outreach too: learn what someone cares about before asking.

chunks.heading: Listener.com: product thesis and positioning
chunks.text:
- Positioning: "AI listener analytics for modern podcasts and podcast networks," a single hub aggregating Apple, Spotify, social analytics and newsletter data.
- Core feature: a shareable public profile page (listener.com/casey) that works like DocSend: viewers enter name, email and company, and the host manually approves access, so the host controls who sees their data.
- Aim: let hosts pitch sponsors with confidence and "tell a story with your data"; two shows with 100,000 monthly downloads can differentiate on audience and impact.
- Extra use case he's noticed: public-figure guests' teams ask for listener counts and cross-platform reach before agreeing to appear.
- Origin: a separate AI podcast product, listener.fm, was a 2024 "testing year" (alongside a podcast network and services); an acqui-hire of a small podcast tech tool and a shift in Q3/Q4 2024 turned into listener.com.
- He bought the .com after the .fm product validated the idea; the starting price was over $250,000 and he got it well below that after about 10 months stuck at the $100-150K range. He didn't wait for the .com to launch.
- Funding: no formal round; a handful of strategic investors, including big podcasters and his former co-founder/board member.
- He sold media kits in 2022 to a Toronto company, then did brand partnerships and consulting before returning to tech.

chunks.heading: Revenue mix and services around the show
chunks.text:
- Services he has run: executive guest booking (getting C-level people on top business podcasts, a concierge booking agency), founder guest booking, and podcast strategy for brands launching shows (he's de-emphasizing these).
- Brand partnerships: each year he works with a few anchor brands, e.g. a big Slack podcast campaign in 2022-2023, plus social content partnerships.
- He declined to share last year's revenue.

chunks.heading: Founder-led media as the new distribution channel
chunks.text:
- The host frames podcasts as the new SEO as AI answers and tracking changes reshape traditional channels, and Casey agrees: "founder brands are not only the future but we're living in it."
- He cites Mr. Beast and Feastables, Logan Paul and Prime, and Alex Hormozi's personal brand as a lead generator for companies he acquires stakes in.
- His contact for podcast questions or guest pitches: casey@listener.com; he's on Instagram and X as "Casey" / "Casey Adams."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Casey Adams explains how a high-school podcast became a business development engine: guest outreach by DM, a network that funded his startup, and bundled sponsor deals. He also covers how Media Kits got its first 10k users organically and the long-game mindset behind it.

chunks.heading: How Casey got started: injury, Gary Vaynerchuk's book and a podcast at 16
chunks.text:
- Casey grew up in a small town in Virginia with no business-minded friends or family. A football injury in sophomore year left him in a neck brace for over six months (inter-spinous ligament damage). He calls it "a blessing in disguise."
- During recovery he moved into personal development and entrepreneurship content (Gary Vaynerchuk, Tony Robbins). The last chapter of Gary's book *Crushing It* is about podcasting. Casey saw it as a low-effort, low-output format for learning from people he wanted to interview.
- The podcast launched in December 2017, when he was still in high school, with three motives:
  - Meet people and build a network, since nobody around him was going to help him level up.
  - Learn from them.
  - The business opportunity and long-term value of a strong network.
- Early episodes were solo talks about his neck injury and building a personal brand, then interviews with friends met on social media, including his later business partner Kieran O'Brien.
- Five and a half years in he had done over 400 interviews, from Larry King to Elon Musk's mom and sister to the founders of Twitch and Netflix. He says you can't predict which guest leads to which door, but one guest leading to the next creates a network effect.

chunks.heading: Booking guests: outputs, reference points and who they admire
chunks.text:
- His first "wow" guest was Chris "Drama" Pfaff (Young and Reckless, Rob & Big). It took one DM about a book Drama had posted. Casey says you're often "one message away," though sometimes it takes 10 follow-ups.
- Early goal: 60 interviews in the first 90 days. That came from a 5-10 minute meeting he had lined up with Gary Vaynerchuk in New York in early 2018. Casey got it by DMing Gary after K-Swiss sent him early-access Gary Vee shoes. He skipped school for the day to go. He credits that sprint with building his interviewing momentum.
- His outreach rules, using the Rick Ross booking (2020, about 10 interactions over roughly a year) as the example:
  - Give a reference point. He told Ross he had just interviewed Robert Greene, one of Ross's favorite authors.
  - State the time frame up front ("20-25 minutes, short and sweet").
  - Ask for nothing else. Ross later said Casey "approached me like a boss."
- Be curious about the guest's sphere of influence. Before Ross he interviewed the CEO of Sovereign Brands, which runs Bel Air champagne. To reach Wiz Khalifa he interviewed Ludy, then Will Dzombak, CEO of Taylor Gang records.
- That chain led to Will investing in Media Kits and Wiz performing at the Media Kits launch party in 2021.

chunks.heading: The podcast as a long-term business asset, not just ad inventory
chunks.text:
- Casey says the real value is not one-off sponsorships. About 90% of the investors in his $1.5M Media Kits round came through the podcast.
- He compares typical podcast ad rates, roughly $25 CPM, with how he structures deals: a "vertically integrated deal stack" across the whole personal brand.
- Slack example (three months, last year): podcast ads, Instagram Reels, TikTok and Twitter content, plus hosting a live workshop of about an hour and a half for small business owners on Slack's LinkedIn page. The page has millions of followers, and the workshop ran during small business appreciation month.
- He pursues equity over cash where possible. He is an advisor to Callin (the social podcasting app run by David Sacks) after doing a deal there.
- He uses guests as research. Before launching a SaaS company he interviewed about 50 SaaS founders. Before one day launching a venture fund he plans to interview about 50 fund GPs.
- His definition of luck: "planting seeds with the expectation of watering them," for example sending a sick contact green juice.

chunks.heading: Media Kits: origin, fundraise and launch
chunks.text:
- The idea came in 2018. YouTuber Jeff Jarrett (Pennzoil, then Ferrari) kept asking Casey and Kieran to update his Canva media kit as his subscribers grew. They asked why creators couldn't have a media kit that never goes stale, shareable by link with real-time data, and why brands couldn't see verified data.
- They shelved it in 2018 because Casey was in high school and had no tech or SaaS experience. They revived it in mid-2020 as TikTok-driven creator economy growth took off, spending six months bootstrapping, ideating and collecting creator feedback.
- Fundraise (2021):
  - Raised about $1.5M pre-seed from 37 angel investors over roughly six months (January to June/July 2021, a rolling close).
  - Check sizes ranged from $15K to $25-50K, with a few $100-150K.
  - It took about 150-200 meetings to get the 37 yeses. Casey says the hardest check to get is the first one, and momentum is everything.
  - He notes it consumed a lot of founder time while they were still building and hiring.
- At launch (August 2021) the team was seven full-time: three engineers, two co-CEOs, a COO and marketing help.
- Mentor: Aristotle Loomis. He describes a true mentor as someone who will "get their hands dirty," such as helping craft an email or script a call.

chunks.heading: Launch party that backfired, and the organic growth that fixed it
chunks.text:
- Launch was August 11, 2021: a party-plus-networking event at Dan Fleischman's Elevator Studio in downtown LA. Speakers included Tanner Fox and David Meltzer, with 700 creators attending and Wiz Khalifa performing.
- It put the brand on the map, but they scrambled to finish the site against the clock. The product shipped with bugs and crashes, signups from the event were roughly 1,000, and growth flatlined for two months (August and September).
- What got them to the first 10,000 users with no paid media (September to year-end):
  - Organic TikTok content showing creators' and investors' media kits (Josh Richards, Wiz Khalifa).
  - A Twitch integration, followed by going deep in the Twitch community on Twitter and running giveaways such as gifted subscriptions.
- That reached 25,000+ users by early 2022, then a B2B model for talent agencies and managers (WME Sports, Taylor Gang, Landing Records). It let them build 10-50 media kits for a talent roster in one place.
- Casey says lessons from the launch party include that things are usually more expensive and take longer when you match a product timeline to a fixed event.

chunks.heading: Acquisition and what he's building next
chunks.text:
- In 2022, while deep in a seed raise with an elite lead investor lined up, the CEO of Viral Nation (a 400-person influencer marketing company that raised roughly $200M in private equity, per Casey) reached out on LinkedIn. After meeting the team in Toronto, they were acquired in September 2022, just over 12 months after the August 2021 product launch.
- He says the product fit Viral Nation because they manage thousands of creators exclusively and could drop the talent roster product straight in.
- Next: Listener.fm, a podcast post-production tool built with an engineer. You drop in an audio file and it outputs titles, descriptions, show notes and other assets using AI. He built it because he has the problem himself and uses it for every episode.
- He applies the venture "founder-market fit" idea: build where you have industry experience and access. He is also interested in angel investing and eventually raising a fund.

chunks.heading: Keep going, never quit, and doing hard things
chunks.text:
- His core motto is "keep going, never quit." He says the biggest common thread among 400+ guests is that they kept going through adversity and didn't quit when a logical person would have. He adds that top performers know when to pivot, not just when to persist.
- "The day I think about quitting is the day you die." He argues for committing to the long game (relationships, business, process) over short-term games, and notes everyone gets the same amount of time. He cites the "time billionaire" idea and regular reflection on mortality (from Robert Greene) as a motivator.
- Hard physical challenges as a business practice:
  - 75 Hard (Andy Frisella); he was on day 63 when recorded and had done it once before in 2020.
  - Daily cold plunge. He says it never gets easier, you just get better.
  - Running a marathon a year for 20 years.
- He cites James Lawrence ("Iron Cowboy"): 50 Ironmans in 50 states in 50 days, then 101 in a row. Lawrence's lesson, per Casey: it starts with one step, so focus on the next step. He applies that "one foot in front of the other" framing to business.
- He says people can't obsess over outcomes. Obsess over the journey, because no one had it figured out until they did.

chunks.heading: Lessons from specific guests
chunks.text:
- **Larry King:** "I've never learned anything while I was talking." Casey now treats intentional listening as his default. King's answer to what makes people great was that "those who are great are always the most driven." Casey met King's son Chance at a Tilman Fertitta dinner, then by coincidence ran into King at a mall a week later, and interviewed him in December 2019. Casey says it was one of King's last in-studio interviews, and he describes King as completely present for the 45 minutes.
- **Maye Musk (Elon's mom):** His takeaway is how tightly knit the Musk family unit was and how strongly it stayed aligned. He argues you should find your "family" (friends, masterminds) because it's too hard to go alone.
- **Robert Greene:** Casey calls him a friend. Greene handwrites every page, builds 150 note cards of research per chapter, works 12-18 hours a day for years per book, and wasn't successful until his late 30s or early 40s. Casey says 48 Laws is meant to equip you to recognize manipulation, and tells people that "no matter what business you're in, you're in the people business."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Casey Adams explains how podcasting from age 17 became the foundation for his network, his first raise ($1.5M from 37 angels, mostly past guests) and his MediaKits exit to Viral Nation. He then shares lessons from that exit and how he keeps his second company, Listener, lean while preserving optionality.

chunks.heading: Starting a podcast young: the neck-brace origin and the "why"
chunks.text:
- At 15-16, Casey was almost paralyzed playing football and spent six months in a neck brace. He lost his identity (he had planned to play lacrosse at UVA) and calls the first three months the most depressing period of his life.
- He rebuilt his identity by reading about founders and entrepreneurs, which planted the seed for his career.
- He started his podcast in December 2017 at age 17, recording in his bedroom on wired Apple headphones. Video wasn't an option then.
- His reason for starting: he realized he knew nothing about business, so interviewing business owners was a way to learn from them.
- He skipped college and moved to Scottsdale a month after high school.
- Advice to aspiring podcasters: "know why you're doing it." Long-form is hard and attention is hard to get, but with a clear why, "it should never feel like that heavy lift."
- His own why was threefold: meet great entrepreneurs, learn from them, and create business opportunity.
- He has now done the show for about 9 years and credits it as the foundation of his career.

chunks.heading: How he landed Larry King at 19: volume, asking, and showing up
chunks.text:
- He set a goal of 60 interviews in 90 days, partly to have something to talk about when he got a meeting with Gary Vaynerchuk in New York. He interviewed anyone and everyone in business, including young founder friends aged 16-17.
- Larry King was on his dream guest list from the start because of his blunt, authentic interviewing style.
- Path to King: he interviewed Tilman Fertitta (owner of the Houston Rockets) around his book *Shut Up and Listen* (2019). Fertitta invited him and other creators who helped with the book promotion to a dinner at Mastro's in Beverly Hills.
- He sat next to Chance King (Larry's son) without knowing who he was, talked about his podcast, and left with a soft ask: if there was ever an opportunity to have his father on the show, it would be a privilege. He asked without expecting anything.
- A week later he spotted Larry King in a wheelchair at Century City Mall and worked up the courage to say hello, mentioned meeting Chance, and took a selfie. Chance then asked his dad, who agreed. The interview happened around December 10, 2019, when Casey was 19 and King was 87.
- Lessons he draws:
  - Know when to ask.
  - The 60-100 interviews beforehand are what prepared him for the opportunity.
  - Someone like King took the time for a 19-year-old's podcast, so "we're never too busy" for meetings or calls you're tempted to skip.

chunks.heading: Early hustle: Facebook ad agency and podcast as a business-development engine
chunks.text:
- Before MediaKits, from ages 16 to 19, he ran a local Facebook advertising and social media management agency for his local dentist and chiropractor, on monthly retainers.
- That income paid for his own plane tickets. In junior and senior year of high school he missed roughly 80 days of school, persuading his parents to let him travel to LA to interview people like Jay Shetty and Jake Paul (both on one day in 2018, at age 17).
- The podcast served as his network and fundraising pipeline later: about 37 angel investors in his first company were past podcast guests, including a manager for Wiz Khalifa. He calls this "business development on steroids."

chunks.heading: MediaKits: idea, raise, launch, and exit
chunks.text:
- Origin of the idea (2020): a friend, the automotive YouTuber JR Garage, asked Casey and his co-founder to make a media kit one-pager in Canva or Photoshop for a brand sponsorship. It took a couple of hours and he got the deal.
- Months later the friend had grown by 100,000 subscribers, had different engagement rates, and was bigger on Instagram and Facebook. He asked them to update the numbers.
- The insight: there was no easy way for social creators to aggregate their cross-platform data and represent it to brands.
- He moved to LA at about 19-20 to start the company. He and his co-founder were non-technical (this was before AI coding tools), so they needed to hire engineers and raised money.
- Raise: about $1.5 million from 37 angel investors, which took roughly eight months, done on SAFE notes with no product yet. His investor and board member Aristotle Loumis, whom he met through Steven Galanis (CEO of Cameo), guided them through how SAFEs and fundraising work.
- Launch: a launch party in 2021 with Wiz Khalifa performing and about 700 creators.
- Exit: about 18 months after the launch, MediaKits was acquired by Viral Nation, a Canadian talent agency. Viral Nation's CEO DM'd him on LinkedIn. He stayed under a year.
- Positioning: they were "an inch wide and a mile deep," a single-focus product named MediaKits.com ("the easiest way to build a media kit"), in a creator-tool market where he says many tools "did a lot of things good, but not one thing great."

chunks.heading: When to sell: taking the early win
chunks.text:
- When the acquisition came, they were about to do a proper seed round after a harsh fundraising process and had finally got a term sheet. The acquisition was a chance to "just get a win on the board."
- He explains the reasoning: it was very uncertain, they had not figured everything out (cap table and other founder issues), and the exit could be used in future ventures.
- His framework:
  - A big part of business is proving to yourself that you can take something from idea to launch, growth, scale, and exit; completing that full lifecycle taught him a lot.
  - Weigh the time-and-effort-to-outcome ratio when the future is uncertain and partners may want different things.
  - There are exceptions (founders who turned down billion-dollar offers), but the early win is a lesson to build from.
- His observation about buyers: the endgame is often unclear to young founders and the right buyer is rarely the obvious one.
- Preparing for an exit: keep your books clean, keep a clean cap table, stay capital efficient, and plant seeds with potential strategic acquirers early.
- His former co-founder later sold a second company (Shop Genie, an auto-repair-shop CRM) two years in to a private-equity-backed company in Texas; Casey was a small partner. He says once you've done an exit, you understand the process.

chunks.heading: Listener.com: positioning and go-to-market
chunks.text:
- Listener launched in April 2025 as an AI-powered analytics and intelligence system for modern podcast publishers.
- It aggregates audio, video, and social data (podcast hosting downloads, YouTube long-form data, and social clips) so the top 1% of publishers can represent their shows and campaigns to advertisers more effectively.
- Target customer: teams running networks of 20 to 50 shows. He went after the biggest shows first because they have the most analytics, monetize best, and have the biggest data-fragmentation problem across platforms.
- Thesis: social clips are part of the show, not just a promotional vehicle. Modern podcasts are sold and measured in a way that includes clips, so advertisers want to be part of that clip culture.
- Example he cites: Caleb Pressley (an investor and a podcaster/comedian), who has no Apple or Spotify feed but sells ads through clips, with each clip getting about a million views.
- His view of the market: the old-school podcast industry (audio natives) is disconnected from the creator ecosystem building the biggest shows, though both are moving to the same point.
- He used strategic investors with aligned interests (Caleb, Ben Kaplan, founder of Jerry Media and What Do You Meme).

chunks.heading: Fundraising approach for Listener: stay lean, keep optionality
chunks.text:
- First company: raised $1.5M as first-time founders before having a product. For Listener he has not done a proper round; he took strategic capital from a former co-founder, a former board member, and people like Ben and Caleb.
- Team: three people, kept extremely lean, building for a need in the market.
- Why lean: in the AI era, customers ask "could we just build this?" so he wanted relief to shift product direction in the first six months. He's glad he didn't have a conviction he wasn't willing to move on, and notes that what Listener is has shifted a lot since last year.
- His biggest lesson as a founder: give yourself optionality.
  - He has the option to raise a proper round (he could commit to that path) or to keep growing sustainably with customers.
  - He doesn't want to over-raise before he's figured it out and then be forced to sell or return capital.
- He notes that his advice should be taken "with a grain of salt" since it comes from his own experience, and that he drew on about 500 conversations with founders.

chunks.heading: Long-term outlook and operating principles
chunks.text:
- Family is a priority; he got married last year. He cites Mark Randolph (Netflix co-founder), who kept a hard stop every Friday.
- He wants to back founders at the ground floor as an angel (he has done an SPV and some angel investments), inspired by Harry Stebbings building a media-led fund; he has an appetite for something like that, not "a fund to raise a fund."
- He believes "what worked in the past isn't going to work in the future," and says to shed experience and stay curious about the world as it is today, rather than hold strong beliefs that block seeing what's ahead. He cites the shift toward AI, robotics, and space, and reads *Life at the Speed of Play* by the Zynga founder.
- He sees himself as an entrepreneur at his core who will always be starting things, and plans to take his podcast to the next level as a long-game commitment.
- Habit: he has run a marathon every year for the last four years (the Sydney Marathon was upcoming); the 2-3 hour runs give him a bird's-eye view and a chance to think.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Casey Adams (then 18, CEO of Build Your Empire) explains how a neck injury, a DM to Ty Lopez and relentless outreach led him to interview 80+ entrepreneurs. He lays out a simple personal-branding playbook: commit fully, define three pillars, collaborate constantly, and climb the interview ladder through associates.

chunks.heading: Branding is commitment, not credentials
chunks.text:
- Casey argues personal branding "comes down to laying out your story over time" in an authentic way. Everyone has a story, whether just starting or having sold a company for $100 million.
- Titles, companies and past achievements are not the point. What counts is how your content makes people feel and what value you give them.
- His advice to beginners: "tell people that be authentic as possible because that's what people want, that's what they respect."
- He says people dislike big labels like "e-commerce expert" or "stock trader". They want real stories and useful information in your own voice.
- He warns against copying Gary Vee, Grant Cardone or Ty Lopez. Study what they do (content creation, publishing, connecting with people), then pick and choose, because a brand "is geared towards you".
- He frames a personal brand as the asset that survives company failure: "if a company fails... you still have your personal brand".

chunks.heading: Three brand pillars and a clear bio
chunks.text:
- Casey's first tip is committing fully. At 50% commitment, thinking about the brand two days a week and scrolling and consuming the rest, "you're going to lose".
- His second tip is defining three brand pillars: why you want to brand yourself, how you want to brand yourself, and what that looks like.
- His own pillars, visible in his Instagram bio: (1) interviewing world-class entrepreneurs via his podcast, (2) CEO of Build Your Empire, (3) traveling and networking.
