- The first line of the Instagram, YouTube or other bio should make clear exactly what you want people to know.
- Consistency of collaborations and willingness to be rejected separate him from other 18-year-olds. He has DM'd hundreds of people, and some said yes, some no, some never replied. The yeses (Grant Cardone, Ed Mylett, Andy Frisella) helped shape his brand.
- He treats it as a numbers game: more outreach gives more interviews, more calls give more business, and you create opportunities by being in rooms like networking events and Facebook groups.

chunks.heading: Document the journey, don't fake it
chunks.text:
- Casey says there are no shortcuts to building a brand. Consistency and collaborations are the keys.
- Advice for 18-25 year olds: "document the journey, talk about what you're doing day to day, talk about the struggles, talk about things that are not sexy."
- He notes that Gary Vee has 32 people on his brand and Grant Cardone has 50 people making calls and a studio worth about $200,000. Beginners should not feel everything must be perfect.
- He started his podcast with plain Apple headphones: "it's not about being fancy, it's about making things happen."
- He sees faking clout or credentials as a losing move. He says people don't know your character, they know your reputation, and a reputation built through content, collaborations and consistency lasts.

chunks.heading: How he landed big-name podcast guests
chunks.text:
- He did not start with big names. He began by calling friends and people in his network, such as Kieran O'Brien, Jaden Gross and Jeremy Haynes, to build his craft.
- His rule: go from zero to one, one to two, two to three, building stepping stones rather than jumping from zero interviews to Gary Vee.
- Once he had 5-10 interviews, he could pitch bigger guests by naming the people he had already interviewed.
- He leads with value, not a request. For Grant Cardone, he said the books had changed his life (he had read five) before mentioning the podcast.
- He interviewed associates and right-hand men first, because "you don't want to know Drake personally, you want to know Drake's right-hand man."
- Practical pitch tip: reference a mutual connection. A DM like "I interviewed [mutual person], he said great things about you" gives you "10 times more likelihood" of a yes.
- He says to still DM the big names directly, even 10 times, but not to rely on that route.
- His interview style changed. His first 15-20 interviews were fully scripted, and now he goes in with no questions: a conversation driven by curiosity, open-mindedness and a willingness to listen. Andy Frisella called him one of his best podcast interviews.

chunks.heading: The DM and event that changed his trajectory
chunks.text:
- At 15 he suffered a neck injury (ligament damage) playing football, spent 25 weeks in a neck brace, and was told he could never play again. He turned to self-development: Ty Lopez's 67-step program (split about $33 each with a friend), Gary Vee's "Crush It", and "Think and Grow Rich".
- Early money came from affiliate marketing. He sold "Online Sales Pro", an email automation tool at $37/month with $20/month residual, and sold about 50 memberships through a Snapchat group of about 500 people that he built by posting in forums and doing book reviews.
- He sent 50 reporters a day to get press, and a local news station interviewed him. He shouted out Caleb Maddox, who then invited him to speak at an event in San Diego on January 13, 2017, with about 100 people in the room.
- He bought a plane ticket impulsively, with his dad accompanying him as a condition, and it was his first flight. He met Caleb Maddox, Dan Fleyshman, Jeremy Haynes and Gerard Adams there.
- Afterward he sent Ty Lopez a gratitude DM of roughly 5-7 sentences, after earlier unseen attempts. Ty replied within about 20 minutes and flew him to LA.
- At Ty's house he met Jaden Gross, who flew him out the next month. He took this as proof of a core belief: "you're only a DM away, a conversation away, a call away from that next pivot point."
- In 2017 he flew to LA about once a month, funded by a social media marketing agency running ads for personal branding clients. His advice: spend money on experiences and relationships rather than things.

chunks.heading: Build Your Empire and what he was building (late 2018)
chunks.text:
- Casey and two partners acquired the Build Your Empire brand about eight months before the interview. It came with 1.5 million Instagram followers, the email list and the name rights.
- He said they were restructuring the brand to be more than a motivational page, with new colors, scene structures, videos and content that has "real value and real core information".
- The plan was an entrepreneur incubator (the Build Empire house) with quarterly events, the first on January 19-20, 2019, and niche events such as real estate, e-commerce, social media and music.
- It also included an interactive learning platform, described as "the Netflix for entrepreneurship content", with a membership site and a Lightspeed VT backend, plus a personal branding agency and consulting for personal brands.
- He was also CMO of a peer-to-peer consulting app that handles on-screen invoicing and conversation records, and said they were raising money for it within three months.
- His podcast, "Rise of the Young", had interviewed over 80 entrepreneurs, with a book of the same name. He said it ranked as a top 25 business podcast.

chunks.heading: Mindset notes
chunks.text:
- He says "things don't happen to you unless you make them happen", and that most beginners set goals and then nothing happens within a week or a month because they don't commit.
- He quotes Gary Vee that "you're only as good as your last at bat" and says to fall in love with the journey rather than treating a milestone as "I made it".
- On clarity, he says today's abundance of information (e-commerce, Forex, Amazon, SMMA, stocks) makes it essential to pick one thing and commit.
- His default question for planning is: where are you now, where do you want to be, and what's next.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Casey Adams explains how he landed Grant Cardone, Larry King and Rick Ross interviews by getting creative, showing up, and valuing people's time. He covers relationship building through presence and context, staying consistent with a long-term project, and the origin of his creator-economy startup Media Kits.

chunks.heading: Getting interviews with big names by getting creative and showing up
chunks.text:
- Casey has run his podcast for almost five years, with 400+ interviews including Larry King, Rick Ross, Grant Cardone and Elon Musk's mom and sister. He started at 17, in his bedroom in Virginia, on a pair of Apple headphones, with no connections.
- Grant Cardone story: Casey DMed Grant on Instagram, was told to email his assistant, and emailed saying he'd "be in Miami next Wednesday and Thursday" and would love to do it in person (or on Zoom if easier). He had never been to Miami and had no plans to go. The assistant confirmed a time and studio address, so he flew out from Virginia with friends, including his business partner Kieran, and did the interview.
- His lesson: "putting yourself in positions to win and to create opportunity starts by getting creative with how you think about things." He threw the ask out first and figured out the logistics once they said yes.
- In high school he took about 80 days off school across junior and senior year, flying to LA on a Friday and back on a Monday, to make this kind of thing happen.

chunks.heading: How the Larry King interview happened (show up, act on small opportunities)
chunks.text:
- A friend invited Casey to a dinner for Tilman Fertitta's book promotion (about 20-30 creators). His business partner ended up seated next to Larry King's son Chance. Casey introduced himself to Chance afterward, invited him to an event he was hosting in LA the following weekend, and Chance came.
- The next weekend, Casey spotted Larry King himself at Century City Mall. After 10-15 seconds of hesitation he walked up alone, said he'd just met Chance, admired his work, and had hosted his own podcast for about three years. He got a selfie and sent it to Chance.
- About six to eight weeks later, around Thanksgiving 2019, Chance replied to a holiday text that his dad would be interested. The interview was recorded December 10, 2019, under two weeks after that text. Casey was 19. Larry was recovering from a stroke earlier, so an earlier ask had been bad timing.
- Larry passed away later; Casey was among the last people to interview him, and BBC World News DMed him that day to go on air.
- His lesson: "never have an expectation of opportunities coming up, just get out there and put yourself in a position to win." Accept the dinner, the event, the coffee invite, because you don't know which one turns into something. A lot of opportunities cross your plate and people don't act on them.

chunks.heading: Pitching a hard-to-get guest (the Rick Ross approach)
chunks.text:
- Rick Ross told Casey on air that he "presented yourself like a boss." Casey's message had these elements:
  - Referenced someone Ross respects: Casey had just interviewed Robert Greene, whom Ross constantly cites (48 Laws of Power).
  - Tied the ask to Ross's own goal: a book he had coming out that the interview would promote.
  - Asked for very little time: only 10-15 minutes.
- It took repeated DMs over time. Ross saw them, didn't respond, then eventually said to email or text it, and it got done.
- Principle: busy, successful people value their time. Understand what matters to them and how you can help.
- Casey advises thinking about who influences the person you're approaching: "who does this person follow, who do they care about," and use that in the pitch. It applies beyond podcasting.
- Before approaching someone at an event, he checks Instagram for mutual follows or connections and context, so the conversation starts past surface level. In DMs, context is how you break through "just another DM."
- He keeps re-applying advice from his own past wins, since "if you're not practicing the same things that got you to where you are then you're not going to grow as fast."

chunks.heading: Building and nurturing relationships
chunks.text:
- Casey calls relationships his superpower and says it comes down to "caring about someone": paying attention, caring about what they care about, finding ways to help (for example offering guests his Vegas studio).
- Presence matters. He cites Gary Vaynerchuk: even a 30-second interaction was fully dialed in, not distracted.
- Staying top of mind: instead of watching 50 Instagram stories, reply to a few with a quality message about their day (a tactic from Nick Dio, who works with Gary). He says this restarts good conversations, even with people he hasn't talked to in a long time.
- About 80% of his time on Instagram is in DMs: 10-20 short messages a day, asking questions and reaching out to guests. Over a year those touch points add up, even when individual ones lead nowhere.
- He uses social as a producer, not a consumer. When scrolling, he goes deeper (looks up a place, learns something) instead of just liking.
- In person, going the extra mile builds deep bonds; a friend of five-plus years flew to Michigan for his birthday.
- Good energy: how you make people feel matters (coffee line, Uber driver, podcast). He describes himself as a "delusional optimist" and says positive energy comes back "tenfold."

chunks.heading: Staying consistent with a long-term project
chunks.text:
- Casey publishes at least one episode a week. The show began as "Rise of the Young" with 2-3 minute solo episodes, moved to Zoom interviews, then in-person interviews, then Zoom again during COVID.
- Around a year and a half ago he questioned why he was doing it. He concluded he loves interviewing and listening ("99% of your time listening"), and treats the show as a lifelong consistency play: he wants to be 49 having done "5,314 interviews since I was 17," regardless of view counts or revenue.
- He rebranded the show from "Rise of the Young" to "The Casey Adams Show" because he'd outgrown the name, and says "your name is forever going to be with you." That one change "reinvigorated so much of my passion."
- A second reinvigorating change: via mentor David Meltzer he got into Blue Wire's Las Vegas studio (a podcast network, mostly sports, with a business slice). Since last October he flies out about once a month or every other month and records four to six interviews in a day.
- His advice: figure out small things that rekindle the fire (new name, new recording place, a new laptop for editing). "Sometimes it's a small change that will make a big difference."

chunks.heading: Resilience and gratitude
chunks.text:
- At 15-16, as a sophomore, he was injured playing football, spent six months in a neck brace, almost paralyzed, and could never play sports again after a decade as an athlete. He got depressed, then found personal development (Think and Grow Rich and other books) through social media, which reset his mindset.
- Gratitude is his tool for bad days. His tactics:
  - Journal future-based messages, such as "your future self thanks you for going through this because it's made you a better man."
  - Call his mom, dad or brothers, people disconnected from his business.
  - Reflect on why he's having a bad day instead of ignoring it.
- He took the leap young: moved from Virginia to Arizona at 18 with a few suitcases to run a media company with friends, and said it's a challenging jump a lot of people never make.
- He says the age you feel is quantified by your experience (business, travel, relationships), and that his maturity came from the mentors and people he spends time with.

chunks.heading: Media Kits: the startup Casey co-founded
chunks.text:
- Media Kits lets creators connect social accounts (Instagram, Facebook, TikTok, Twitch, Twitter, YouTube) via first-party APIs and build a media kit with real-time data in about 30 seconds. A media kit is a "digital resume" for creators; brands also get a trusted way to see creator data at scale.
- Origin: in 2017-2018, Casey and co-founder Kieran made a media kit by hand in Canva/Photoshop for friend Jr Garage, a big automotive YouTuber, after Pennzoil asked for one. Three weeks later Ferrari asked, the numbers were already outdated, and they were "changing ones to twos and threes to fours." That prompted the idea of a media kit that never goes stale.
- They shelved it (Casey was in high school, Kieran had a marketing agency), then in 2020, with TikTok and the creator economy booming, they hired a designer and went all in.
- Raised a $1.25 million friends and family round (David Meltzer was the first investor). Launched in August 2021 with a launch party in LA featuring Wiz Khalifa; Wiz's manager is an investor.
- Now over 25,000 creators use it monthly, with a team of eight, mostly remote. It's a "set it and forget it" tool, with more planned beyond the media kit.
- Casey says tech and raising capital were new to him, and the last year taught him more than the previous four. He notes that in the current downturn (layoffs, few raises, crypto correcting), you have to think harder about how to put yourself in a position to win.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Casey Adams explains how, after a football injury at 15, he went all-in on social media and podcasting, interviewing Gary Vaynerchuk, Grant Cardone, Jordan Belfort and Larry King. He covers value-first outreach via Instagram DMs, association marketing, personal branding pillars, building skills, and communication as the core skill.

chunks.heading: Starting from a negative: the injury that created the brand
chunks.text:
- At 15, Casey was diagnosed with an injury (he describes it as inner spine ligament damage from football) and wore a neck brace for about six months.
- He had planned to play football or lacrosse in college. The injury ended that and he says he lost his identity.
- He used the setback to rebuild: personal development, social media marketing, and networking.
- He went all in at 15 with no plan B and no plan for college. A month after graduating high school he moved across the country to live with friends he met on social media.
- He is from Richmond, Virginia, from a non-entrepreneurial family, and did not fly in a plane until he could pay for it himself.
- At 19 he says he has interviewed Larry King, Jordan Belfort, Gary Vaynerchuk and hundreds of other successful people, while providing services to their teams.
- His framing: daily and monthly wins compound, and "the journey is long".

chunks.heading: How he got world-class guests on his podcast
chunks.text:
- Casey started the podcast in late 2017 with no long-term vision, only to network with people he had already talked to on social media.
- He did about 40 interviews in four to five months while preparing for his Gary Vaynerchuk interview.
- His core premise: a podcast is a platform you give to someone to talk about themselves, their product or their business. That is the value you bring.
- He worked to get the show into the top 200 business podcasts and invested in the marketing behind it, so the platform had real value.
- Tactic: nearly every guest came from a simple Instagram DM. He asked directly ("loved the podcast, are you free next week?").
- Brand, content and consistency are what make the DM get a reply. Example: a sports broadcaster he had pinged repeatedly said he was free that same day at 3:00.
- Keep outreach short and simple, and be consistent.
- Creative effort: Grant Cardone said yes to an in-person interview next Thursday at 3:00. Casey had never been to Miami and booked a flight that Thursday, then showed up at Cardone's office. He says he learned that tactic from Cardone's book.
- Strategic value: for Jordan Belfort, Casey leveraged an in at TikTok (he had worked with their corporate team for about eight months) to help get Belfort verified on the platform, which led to the podcast.
- Compounding: after 5 to 10 quality guests, he could reach out to their friends and collaborators ("hey Grant, I've had X on the show"). He calls this "association marketing": building a brand on top of qualified people instead of saying "look at me".

chunks.heading: Building a personal brand in 2020
chunks.text:
- Definition: "building the most authentic perception of you online". The foundations stay stable while the tactics keep changing.
- Follow trends: in 2020 he says TikTok (valued around $75 billion at the time) was the place to build an audience quickly. Create an account and go all in on content.
- Drive followers to Instagram, which he still calls the main place to build community and network. Keep a quality presence there.
- Start simple. Pick three brand pillars. His were podcasting, networking and traveling.
- Ask yourself what you want to be known for and whether you have credibility in it. If not, build it and document the process publicly so the audience grows with you.
- Collaboration is his "number one secret of branding". Reach out to people in your industry (chef, trainer, entrepreneur, athlete) and build through them.
- Podcasting is a good vehicle. He says there were under 2 million podcasts, about half inactive, and recommends starting on Anchor FM (acquired by Spotify about a year earlier), where he moved his show's network.
- His two 2020 foundations: start a podcast and learn to talk, plus consistent content and networking.
- He keeps one authentic Instagram account, the same one he started at 14, rather than separating a "brand" account from a personal one.

chunks.heading: Handling fear, imposter syndrome and judgment
chunks.text:
- Casey's own start: he posted Snapchat and Instagram story videos about books from his room, and his brothers and parents questioned it.
- He says he was not good on camera or at public speaking and still redoes podcast intros. If you are not good on camera, do a video every day.
- Questions to ask: what am I putting out content for, and who am I trying to reach?
- He cites "fear is false evidence appearing real".
- Focus on the action and the outcome you want, not on the fear. People stall because they worry what friends will think.
- Get clear on intention first: write down what you are grateful for, your goals, and why you want them.
- Intention and passion make imposter syndrome fade.

chunks.heading: Manifestation, preparation and give-to-receive
chunks.text:
- He writes down who he wants to interview weekly. His journal had a 2017 note: interview Larry King.
- He calls himself a realist and a "delusional optimist": "execution creates the reality". Manifestation needs the steps, like an airplane trip needs the airport, TSA, check-in and boarding.
- Sculptor versus lottery approach: chip away at the rock daily instead of staring at it. Even a lottery winner had to buy the ticket.
- Larry King told him "preparation creates luck".
- Case study: friend Charlie Rocket posted a fan-made Nike commercial. Casey reached out and spent about $200 on Facebook Ads. It reached 1.2 million views in a week, a Nike executive saw it, and Nike signed him as a sponsored athlete.
- He believes in give and receive: whatever you want, give it first. In one quarantine week he reached out to about 20 people and recorded about five podcasts in a day.
- Do not attach to your current version of yourself. Define who you need to become for the goals to become real.

chunks.heading: Daily habits for mindset
chunks.text:
- He has not owned a TV in four years and avoids watching the news, because its business model is negativity.
- During quarantine he advises one of three things: build a new habit, do what you were putting off, or learn a new skill (a book, a podcast, starting a podcast).
- He keeps a roughly 600-page journal and each day writes a brain-dump of gratitude, sometimes a list of about 50 items. He says repetition is key to happiness.
- He controls his environment: positive posters and affirmations, and people who do not shut down positivity. "You are a product of your environment."
- Core values he wrote down daily early on: never change, stay humble, stick to your morals.

chunks.heading: Starting a business and which skills to build
chunks.text:
- His own work: affiliate marketing, social media advertising, podcasting, personal brand consulting, brand strategy and social media management for executives and brands.
- Recently (past 6 to 8 months) he has worked on TikTok at the corporate level, helping brands and laying out franchise-style TikTok campaigns.
- Example: a brand named Popsockets-style tag product (he says "poeple") whose fourth TikTok video went to a million views in a week and later reached 70 million. He uses it as evidence of the platform's opportunity.
- He is building podcast software to connect podcasters, guests and advertisers. He expected to focus on it heavily over the next three to six months.
- Advice for starting: build a skill set first. Know what you are good at (sales, design, contracts, hiring).
- Reach out online to run ideas by people, because ideas should keep evolving (he notes Facebook in 2010 is not Facebook in 2020).
- "Don't force ideas, let ideas come to you." His podcast software idea came naturally over about six months of events and conversations.
- In a downturn, you cannot control the economy but can control your knowledge, skills and response. Pick a concrete skill such as graphic design, audio engineering, Facebook advertising or social media management, and learn from free YouTube and Google content.
- For services, ask how you can help a business on a new platform where they already have a presence.

chunks.heading: Communication as the core business skill
chunks.text:
- Casey calls communication "the most important skill set" for raising money, building a team, serving clients and building an audience.
- He recommends "How to Win Friends and Influence People" (use someone's name, provide value).
- He used to fear speaking in front of the class and says confidence came from passion and practice. A podcast improved how he asks questions and adapts to a room of two or 20,000 people.
- Communication includes body language and how your Instagram brand communicates.
- Everything is people-oriented: "every business is run by people".
- While confined at home, practice by starting a podcast with friends as guests, or by sending 10 to 15 second video or audio messages to contacts.
- His daily volume: he sends about 10 to 25 DMs a day and responds to about 50, and engages with his community.
- Vulnerability, as he defines it, is saying what you truly mean even when you hesitate. He recommends the "We're Not Really Strangers" card game for building connection.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Casey Adams explains how a cold-outreach podcast started at 17 became the foundation for relationships, a ~$1.3-1.5M raise from past guests, and the acquisition of his Media Kits startup. He also covers building a personal brand by producing consistently, pitching brands proactively, and acting despite fear of failure.

chunks.heading: Why Casey started the podcast and how it compounds
chunks.text:
- Casey started "The Casey Adams Show" at 17 (late 2017), after reading Gary Vaynerchuk's "Crushing It", whose last chapter pushed podcasting as a conversation-based medium.
- He had no podcast experience and began by walking around his room on Apple headphones.
- He gives three core reasons, all still true: meet quality entrepreneurs and build a network, learn from them, and create business opportunities.
- He believes "business is a people game". The people on the team are the critical element, even in the AI era (he cites Sam Altman at OpenAI).
- He sees the show as the foundation of his brand, career, fundraising, relationships and later business ventures.
- He says you can never predict what an intentional conversation with someone you want to learn from will do for your life.

chunks.heading: Cold outreach and the 60-in-90 interview sprint
chunks.text:
- His early approach to getting guests was mainly cold outreach on Instagram, plus having friends on the show first.
- He set a goal of 60 interviews in 90 days, because he had a 5-10 minute meeting lined up with Gary Vaynerchuk and wanted to arrive with reps and momentum.
- That momentum built "such a fire" for high-quality conversations and relationship building.
- He admits he had to "get my reps in": his early interviews look very different from his current ones.
- On pitching brands or guests, he says never expect anyone to reach out to you, even while gaining momentum.
- In the early days with no audience, guests are "literally zero" unless you do the work: pitch, follow up, then schedule once you get a response.

chunks.heading: Raising the media kits round from podcast guests
chunks.text:
- Media Kits (launched 2021) was a tech product that let creators, podcasters, musicians and athletes build a digital resume with real-time, verified analytics, shareable by link.
- It solved two problems: creators had no way to aggregate social stats in one place, and brands had no way to view trustworthy, verified creator data (numbers on static kits are easy to fake).
- Origin: in 2018 a YouTuber friend (J.R. Garage) kept asking Casey and his partner Kieran for Canva media kits for Pennzoil and Ferrari. Each took about an hour, and the numbers went stale within weeks.
- The idea was shelved in 2018 because the timing was wrong. They revisited it in 2020 in Scottsdale, Arizona, when TikTok and influencer marketing were booming.
- They validated by surveying qualified creators and people in the space, then bootstrapped with a design agency in mid-2020.
- In early 2021 they committed and raised just over $1 million (he also says "1.3, 1.5").
- The product launched in August 2021, with a Wiz Khalifa performance at a launch party attended by 700 creators.
- Roughly 90-95% of the investors (about 37 people) were previous podcast guests.
- He credits years of trust and people watching his journey. He could sit down with them and present the opportunity directly.
- Neither founder was technical and they had no founding CTO. He says they "had to think so differently about business".
- About a year later, in 2022, Media Kits was acquired by Viral Nation, an influencer marketing tech company in Toronto that he says raised a $200 million private equity round. He worked there about six months.
- Fit with the buyer mattered to him: Viral Nation represents 1,500+ creators, and its vision matched how the founders saw the product's future.

chunks.heading: How to build a personal brand
chunks.text:
- He defines personal branding on social media as "representing the most authentic version of yourself in a digital format".
- Step 1: pick your medium. Short-form clips, or long-form like a podcast that you then cut into short clips for distribution.
- Step 2: clarify your foundational story. He suggests recording yourself telling it to get clear on "the story that I tell myself" versus the story you want to put into the world.
- Step 3: choose your niche or what you want to be known for, even if you're, say, a realtor.
- Step 4: model the top 5-10 people in your space in your own way.
- Don't overthink it. Posting one Instagram story with 200 followers counts as the first step: documentation and output over input.
- Consistency is the hard part. He frames it as being a producer, not a scroller, and ties it back to discipline.
- When he started at 16 he had no businesses or successes, so he built the brand on book reviews, his personality and his story.

chunks.heading: Pitching brands when you don't have a big following
chunks.text:
- He spoke to a UCLA class of creators and marketers about this.
- Brands "appreciate and respect" creators who proactively reach out, get on a call, build a relationship with someone on the team, and express genuine enthusiasm for the product.
- He says to put about 99% of your effort into creating those opportunities, rather than waiting for a payout or expecting a brand to come to you.
- Pitching brands works like podcast guest outreach: do the work to pitch, follow up and schedule.
- Brands want to work with truly aligned creators. Big creators get paid through managers and marketing budgets, so small creators win on relationship and fit.

chunks.heading: Fear of failure, the voice in your head, and "keep going"
chunks.text:
- Casey cites a quote he may be butchering: "the fear of failure kills more dreams than failure ever will".
- He says you don't have to silence the voice of doubt (imposter syndrome, "why would anyone listen to me"), but you can't listen to it or believe it.
- He counters it with small wins and small daily actions. Stacking daily momentum is how you prove to yourself you're capable.
- His mantra is "keep going, never quit". He writes it at the end of nearly every journal entry and put it on a gold-painted neck brace trophy.
- He tells the story of the Honolulu Marathon CEO, who regretted stopping during his first marathon: "you'll never have the opportunity to run your first marathon ever again".
- He says there are moments for reflection and pivoting, but the default is to not stop.
- He adds that regret lasts a lifetime while failure is temporary.

chunks.heading: Discipline, 75 Hard and the neck brace origin
chunks.text:
- Casey's drive traces to a football injury at 16 that put him in a neck brace for six months and ended his football career.
- He spent about three months depressed, then dove into Gary Vaynerchuk, Andy Frisella and Tony Robbins content.
- That led to his first business at 16: managing Facebook ads for local businesses. He had no entrepreneurial family background.
- He did 75 Hard in 2020, did it again this year, and kept going past day 75 (about day 95 at recording).
- The daily list: two 45-minute workouts (one outdoors), a diet, a progress photo, a gallon of water, no alcohol or cheat meals, and 10 pages of a physical book.
- He values the "no deviation" rule: 10 pages seven days a week, not nine pages across six days.
- His rule for continuing was asking why he wouldn't do each task that day. He couldn't answer, so he kept going.
- He says it becomes a lifestyle and second nature, and compares discipline to a muscle.

chunks.heading: Listening, and what Casey says about advice
chunks.text:
- The best advice he has received is from Larry King: "I've never learned anything while I was talking".
- He applies it to teams, customers and investors, saying the best leaders and entrepreneurs "are all great at listening".
- He ranks the Larry King interview as his most impactful, recorded when Casey was 19 and King was 87.
- On the unknown future he echoes the Steve Jobs line that you can only connect the dots looking backwards.
- He says that if you don't know the dream, you can start with what you don't want, then mimic the lifestyle you want today.

chunks.heading: Listener.fm and where he's building now
chunks.text:
- He recently launched Listener.fm, an AI tool that automates podcasters' post-production.
- It generates topics, summaries, timestamps and suggested titles for segments.
- He says he uses it himself and believes the podcasting medium will keep changing and growing, citing the growth of ad revenue and investment since 2017.
- He also mentions a new Instagram page called "manifestation", built with his team around short video content.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Casey Adams moderates a Podcast Movement panel with brand buyers from Timeline and Caraway on moving past midroll ads into multiplatform partnerships. His own contributions are framing points: brand experts as guests, using missed-impression reporting to upsell multiplatform, and reporting that earns renewals. Most of the substantive insight comes from the panelists, not Casey.

chunks.heading: Casey's approach to testing multiplatform podcast campaigns (publisher-side view)
chunks.text:
Casey is the founder of listener.com, a multi-platform campaign reporting platform for podcast publishers. He has also hosted his own podcast for eight and a half years, mainly interviewing founders, and has had scientists on the show.

- Listener works with top publishers such as Johnboy Media. He says some of them start brands with audio only, then show the brand what it missed. His example: "you missed out on 20 million impressions of the short form," so the next campaign includes it.
- He frames the audio-to-multiplatform progression (audio, YouTube, short form, newsletter) as a testing phase brands often go through before a full multiplatform campaign.
- He notes the brand often controls campaign length, not the creator or publisher, which is why the choice between a one-year and a three-month sponsorship is hard for sellers.
- His question to the panel: how do you know when to keep testing versus "let it ride" over a longer partnership? He observes that some creators skip testing because they know results take three to six months or longer.

chunks.heading: Why brand-team interviews belong in podcast sponsorships
chunks.text:
Casey endorses having a brand's own experts appear on shows rather than relying only on host-read ads.

- He argues there is "such a value in that not only long format of, you know, brands spending money on shows." He likes when brands say "you should have our CEO on the show or a head scientist."
- He calls this a trend that "people don't talk about enough or hear about enough."
- Example from his own show: he worked with Merrick Health, a specialized blood work company with 150 biomarkers. He interviewed about three of their scientists because he was not the best person to explain the product in depth.
- His takeaway: complex products need customer education, and the brand's team supplying guests is how that education happens on the show.

chunks.heading: Reporting and attribution as a publisher's renewal tool
chunks.text:
Casey's company sits on the reporting side, so he frames the whole conversation around what publishers need in order to win renewals.

- Publishers hear what brands care about, then have to represent the campaign back to them well "for the goal of getting renewals" and "hitting those KPIs or the earned media."
- He asked the brand-side panelists what specific signals and internal tools they hold in their back pocket for judging campaign success, beyond just knowing what works.
- Signals the panelists named, which he used to frame publisher reporting needs: last touch, attribution, earned media value from social posts, post-purchase survey data, and blended code, survey and pixel attribution.
- His framing: multiplatform reporting (audio, YouTube, short form, newsletter) is what lets a publisher show the total footprint of a campaign instead of just downloads.

chunks.heading: Framing for the session
chunks.text:
- He sets the topic as going "beyond the download or beyond the midroll" in podcast advertising, and treats it as "a full scale partnership with creators."
- He positions the panel from a technology lens: working with publishers while brands speak to what multiplatform campaigns look like from their side.
- He asks both panelists for dos and don'ts and for case studies of best and worst campaigns, looking toward 2026 into 2027, aimed at both brands and publishers bringing ideas to the table.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Casey Adams recounts going from a teenage podcaster to co-founding MediaKits (raised $1.5M, acquired about a year after launch) and then Listener.fm. He stresses unscalable hands-on user contact, using a podcast as a relationship and fundraising engine, and telling the founder story relentlessly.

chunks.heading: Starting from small things that scale later
chunks.text:
- Casey started his first company at 16 running Facebook ads for local businesses (a chiropractor, a dentist, a local sports shop).
- The trigger was a neck injury on day one of sophomore-year football that ended his playing career and put him in a neck brace for six months. He went down social media rabbit holes on business, which got him into content creation and digital advertising.
- Earlier he shoveled driveways in snow and sold bracelets at the local pool for movie money, with no entrepreneurial family background.
- He started his podcast at 17 and calls himself someone who "got the bug."
- By the time he raised capital he had done 200+ podcast interviews with founders, VCs and creators, and treated the show as a way to build trusted relationships he could run ideas by.

chunks.heading: Spotting the MediaKits idea and validating it
chunks.text:
- The idea came from a friend, an automotive YouTuber with roughly 600-700K subscribers, who was asked by Pennzoil for a media kit and didn't know what one was.
- Casey and his co-founder googled it, made one in Canva/Photoshop in about an hour and a half, and he landed the deal. Three weeks later Ferrari asked for one and the data was already outdated after 100K new subscribers.
- That exposed two gaps: creators had no media kit that never goes stale and shares via a link, and brands had no verified, trustworthy creator data, since "it's so easy to say you have X engagement."
- Timing was wrong in 2018 (he was finishing high school and ramping his podcast), so they shelved it with no capital and no tech experience.
- They revisited it in late 2019/early 2020 when TikTok creators were being "minted overnight," bootstrapped with their own resources, served dozens of creators from their networks, and validated before fundraising.
- Early 2021 they went to raise, got $1.5 million in about six months, and launched in August 2021.

chunks.heading: Fundraising through the podcast network
chunks.text:
- Of 37 angel investors plus a couple of funds, Casey says roughly 90% were podcast guests or people he had nurtured relationships with.
- Fundraising meant stacking up 10 to 20 nos in a row, which he compares to getting kicked in the face.
- One breakthrough: a short, authentic DM on Twitter to Balaji Srinivasan. The reply was "send me your deck, and send me your wire instructions. If I like it, you'll see money in your account." Money arrived the next day.
- His takeaway on the highs and lows: a single influential believer can flip a bad stretch, and outside belief from people beyond your core team is strong feedback.

chunks.heading: Launch stumbles, traction and the acquisition
chunks.text:
- The launch party in LA (with 700 creators attending) happened while the website and application weren't fully working. His fix in hindsight: put hard dates on the calendar and fill the time you have.
- The first ~60 days after launch "fell flat." They were non-technical co-founders shipping a scrappy product and things kept breaking.
- Traction came 60-90 days in after shipping TikTok and Twitch integrations: from roughly 500-1,000 creators to over 10,000, then over 25,000 by early 2022.
- They were preparing a formal seed round when the CEO of Viral Nation messaged him on LinkedIn. Open conversations about partnering turned into acquisition talks, and the company was acquired in September 2022, about a year after launch.
- Casey was 20 when he started the company and 22 at the time of the interview.

chunks.heading: Do things that don't scale, and be hands on
chunks.text:
- His main lesson from MediaKits: build the product through boots-on-the-ground conversations with creators, and "do things that aren't scalable" in the earliest days (he references the Airbnb co-founder's advice).
- He warns against living in "the clouds of projections" and focusing on brand and communication before anyone has tried the product.
- Practical version: get as much feedback as possible on how the product looks and feels, prioritize DMs and direct interactions with potential users, and aim for a base of 1,000 true fans. Getting people to know, like and trust you through effective communication matters more early on than polish.

chunks.heading: Tell your story as the founder
chunks.text:
- He argues founders must be "the biggest evangelists for what you're building," whether through organic social content or telling friends and family, so people are aware of it at all.
- He cites a Gary Vaynerchuk clip where a nonprofit founder who wanted to change the world was posting one video every couple of weeks; the point was that volume of output has to match ambition.
- His reasoning: people fall in love with stories, not single moments, and brands, products and communities are built by sharing the story authentically so people can attach themselves to it.

chunks.heading: Listener.fm: building for your own problem and finding users
chunks.text:
- Listener.fm is an AI post-production tool for podcasters. It takes an audio file and generates SEO-optimized titles, show summaries, timestamps, blog posts and social content.
- He frames podcasting in three buckets: recording, post-production, and publishing/sharing. Post-production is the bucket where podcasters fail, give up, or hire a team, and it is what he built for.
- It came from his own problem, from running a show for almost six years. It launched roughly 90 days before the interview.
- Early distribution was not marketing but direct conversations: he tapped his network of podcasters and used Twitter, searching "podcast" to find shows that had just gone live and reaching out genuinely, sometimes with an audio message or a crafted message tied to their show.
- The goal was to get the first 10, 20, 50 people through the process and collect feedback to iterate on, with a roadmap toward an all-in-one podcast tool and a better listener experience.

chunks.heading: Principles on relationships and curiosity
chunks.text:
- Casey says his superpower is curiosity about people's stories, which is why he stayed consistent with podcasting even when people asked why he spent time on a show with no sponsors or brands.
- His view: "you are in the people business," from executives to customers to team, even as AI shifts things.
- He treats kindness, quality relationships and doing the right thing as the foundation, and calls being a true listener and staying curious (rather than always wanting to share an opinion) the "North Star" for how he runs his business.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: In this Slack Q&A, Casey Adams recounts starting a podcast at 16, co-founding MediaKits (acquired by Viral Nation), and what he took from 300+ interviews. He shares leadership and small-business advice on listening, adaptability, competitive pricing and customer relationships, plus how he uses Slack to run his team.

chunks.heading: Path from a high school injury to podcasting and MediaKits
chunks.text:
- At 16, Casey suffered a severe football injury that left him in a neck brace with a threat of paralysis. He says the experience sparked his passion for entrepreneurship, business, social media, technology and interviewing.
- He started his podcast, The Casey Adams Show, from his bedroom as a high school junior.
- Over five years he conducted over 300 interviews with influential and successful people.
- The podcast led him to co-found MediaKits, which uses real-time data and analytics to help creators design professional media kits.
- Timeline: raised $1.5 million in early 2021, officially launched in August 2021, and was acquired by Viral Nation in September 2022. Viral Nation is described as a leading force in the creator economy and the world's first influencer talent agency.

chunks.heading: Listening as a leadership skill (the Larry King lesson)
chunks.text:
- Casey names his interview with Larry King as the most memorable of his 300+ interviews.
- The lesson that stuck: King's belief in the power of listening, summed up in his line "I've never learned anything while I was talking."
- Casey applies this by spending more time listening to employees and team members.
- Result he reports: by actively listening he gains insights and perspectives he would not have considered otherwise, which helps him make better decisions and be a more effective leader.

chunks.heading: Weathering economic headwinds as a small business (2023 outlook)
chunks.text:
Casey's framework for a small business facing increased competition and economic headwinds has three parts:

1. **Stay agile and adaptable.** Keep up with industry trends, stay open to new ideas and technologies, and be willing to try new things and pivot to new challenges.
2. **Stay competitive.** Offer high-quality products and services at a competitive price. That may mean streamlining operations, reducing costs, and being mindful about pricing and promotions.
3. **Build strong customer relationships.** In a crowded market a loyal customer base is a major advantage. He ties this to excellent customer service, responsiveness to customer needs, and building trust and credibility through consistent, high-quality interactions.

His summary: the future of work for small businesses needs "a combination of adaptability, competitiveness and customer focus."

chunks.heading: Using Slack huddles for focused, fast collaboration
chunks.text:
- Casey calls himself a productivity expert and Slack power user.
- Huddles are the feature he singles out: quick, ad hoc small-group discussions for specific projects or tasks.
- Why it works for him:
  - Conversations stay focused and free of interruptions from the main channels.
  - A team can be gathered quickly for time-sensitive projects.
  - Discussions are synchronous and get input from everyone.

chunks.heading: Building team relationships virtually
chunks.text:
- Casey uses direct messages and huddles for personal, focused conversations with team members.
- He gets to know the team on a personal level by sharing updates about life outside work, such as pictures of his family and pets.
- He says this creates a more human connection that strengthens professional relationships and fosters a sense of community.

chunks.heading: Tool stack for a small business: Slack integrations
chunks.text:
Casey's advice is to take full advantage of Slack's features and integrations, using the tools the team already depends on inside Slack to streamline workflows and improve productivity. His favorites:

- **Google Drive:** share and collaborate on documents, spreadsheets and presentations inside Slack; saves time and improves asynchronous work across teams.
- **Zoom:** schedule and join meetings from Slack, making team collaboration and communication easier.
- **ClickUp:** project management inside Slack. Users can create and assign tasks, set reminders and due dates, receive notifications, and use Slack commands to search tasks and projects.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Casey Adams explains how owning MediaKits.com gave him conviction and trust that fueled 25,000 creator signups in 6 months, and why he pursued Listener.com for six-plus months of slow broker conversation before buying. He argues founders should secure social handles and premium domains early as brand and IP assets.

chunks.heading: Origin of the Listener name and the podcast-first career
chunks.text:
- Casey started a marketing agency at 16 after diving into business biographies, marketing and entrepreneurship during a six-month recovery from a sports injury.
- He launched The Casey Adams Show at 17, in December 2017. It is a business interview show with 450+ episodes and guests including Tyler Winklevoss, Rick Ross, Larry King, Netflix co-founder Marc Randolph and Whoop CEO Will Ahmed.
- His interview with Larry King in 2019 (Casey was 19, King was 87) shaped his core principle. King said he'd never learned anything while he was talking.
- Casey's takeaway: being a better listener is how you make "not only a great interview, but a great life and great relationships."
- That idea became the brand: "everything in the world of podcasting goes back to the listener." Every piece of content, episode and sponsoring advertiser is listener-focused, so "listener" is a powerful word in podcasting.

chunks.heading: Using a premium domain to launch MediaKits
chunks.text:
- Casey co-founded MediaKits, a startup that helps influencers design media kits from real-time social data. It was his first tech company.
- It got traction after YouTubers such as JR Garage used and recommended it.
- Owning MediaKits.com gave him "so much conviction, not only around the idea, but as the industry leading media kit tool for creators." His reasoning: with that domain, "there's no other place to go."
- He says the domain was "such an edge to first impressions, brand building awareness, and that initial growth and trust."
- Result: 25,000 creators signed up within 6 months, and he and his co-founder sold the company to social media marketing agency Viral Nation in mid-2022.

chunks.heading: How Listener is structured
chunks.text:
- Casey built Listener as a vertically integrated podcast network aimed at the pain points of podcasting, with three arms:
  - A tech platform for AI-driven podcast post-production (Listener.fm).
  - A network to elevate and distribute podcasts (Listener.com).
  - A premier podcast booking service that matches guests with hosts.
- He began working on Listener.fm right after selling MediaKits (the first domain inquiry was December 2022).
- The Casey Adams Show and other shows, including "Questions," are distributed by the Listener.com network, which is how he seeds the network with his own audience and assets.
- He launched the network about a month after acquiring Listener.com and got significant attention across social media.

chunks.heading: How he bought Listener.com (slow, low-pressure negotiation)
chunks.text:
- He searched for his ideal domain, found Listener.com for sale via a GoDaddy search, and inquired in December 2022.
- He treated it as exploration: "I wanted to learn more. I wanted to understand the cost and just go from there. It wasn't like this urgent need."
- He kept the conversation going "slowly but surely" with an Afternic broker for roughly a year before closing. He says the actual negotiation at the end was swift.
- The trigger to buy was brand growth. After building the tech product on Listener.fm, he concluded he needed the .com: "there was no other option but to go do the same thing again" as with MediaKits.com.
- It was his first time using a broker, and he valued having one for the process and for answering questions.
- His expected payoff: "long tail effect of brand building." Owning the category word means anyone in podcasting who thinks or says "listener" thinks of Listener.com.
- He places heavy emphasis on valuable domains, trust and brand value, especially for first impressions on social media and when his podcast is presented under Listener.com.

chunks.heading: Digital assets and brand names as a startup priority
chunks.text:
- Casey interviewed the founder of Plunge about buying Plunge.com for $250,000, and Acquire.com founder Andrew Gazdecki about securing Acquire.com through a broker, so he has studied domain acquisition closely.
- He holds premium social handles for his brands: @Questions, @Listener and @Casey on Instagram.
- His advice to founders before starting a business:
  - Check whether you can get the social handles on all platforms.
  - Check whether the preferred domain is available for sale.
- On intellectual property: "If you don't value the intellectual property of whatever you're building today, you're going to have to value it later if you're ever going to have to go through an acquisition or take a company public."
- He says a premium domain won't make or break the business, but you can prioritize getting it now or later, and the key is to "just start a conversation, like I did twelve months ago with Listener.com."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A 2019 local profile of Casey Adams, who built a personal brand, the Rise of The Young podcast and the Build Your Empire events company as a teenager. He shares what he learned about time, saying no, relationships and bringing people together.

chunks.heading: Origin story: injury to personal brand
chunks.text:
- At 15, Casey was diagnosed with interspinous ligament damage while playing football.
- He spent six months in a neck brace, unable to move around much. That is when he got introduced to personal development.
- After months of reading books and building a positive attitude, he learned about the power of social media and decided to build a personal brand.
- By 2019 (three years later), he says it "truly changed my life forever." He has since traveled the world speaking on stages about personal branding.
- His core takeaway: people have a lot of power in how they position themselves online.

chunks.heading: Rise of The Young podcast as a distribution engine
chunks.text:
- Casey started the podcast "Rise of The Young" at the end of 2017.
- It became a top 200 business podcast in the world, and he says his content and podcasts have reached millions of people.
- He used the show to sit down with some of the world's most successful entrepreneurs and leaders, interviewing them from age 18.
- He says interviewing impactful people that young gave him insight into "the power of listening."
- He positions himself as someone who specializes in interviewing world-class entrepreneurs, networking and connecting people, and building personal brands.
- His differentiator: in about three years, at only 18, he connected, networked, interviewed and collaborated with many influential entrepreneurs and business leaders.

chunks.heading: Build Your Empire and the events business
chunks.text:
- Build Your Empire is his company, focused on showcasing world-class entrepreneurs through content and events.
- It is known for world-class business events, and its stated aim is revolutionizing the business event industry.
- He found a passion for hosting events and has thrown dozens of business events across the world.
- He co-hosted an event with Chris "Drama" Pfaff, founder and CEO of "Young & Reckless."
- His biggest lesson from the events: "there is power in bringing people together."

chunks.heading: Partnership with MOTI Chat
chunks.text:
- Casey partnered with the app MOTI Chat for over a year as of 2019.
- He describes it as the #1 consulting app in the world: a peer-to-peer consulting app that changes how consultants and business professionals get paid for their time.
- He credits the experience of building with the MOTI team as a pleasure.

chunks.heading: Building a relationship-driven career
chunks.text:
- Over three years he says he learned a great deal about communication skills and what it takes to build real, genuine relationships.
- Listening, gained through interviewing, is the skill he highlights most.
- His network, podcast guests and event partners all stem from the same habit: connecting and collaborating with influential people early.

chunks.heading: Running a company while in high school
chunks.text:
- Time management was a major lesson. He ran a company while going to school and learned where his time was best spent.
- Example: he had his phone taken away in math class, and the teacher had no idea he was texting a client about their Facebook ad campaign.
- He learned to say NO to opportunities. As an entrepreneur you are introduced to many opportunities, and learning to say no "has truly impacted my life."
- He also learned when to distance himself from people: "You must know when to let go, and when to move on from a situation or an individual."

chunks.heading: Mindset: luck and support systems
chunks.text:
- He defines "luck" partly as being born when he was: a thriving economy where technology is accessible to anybody.
- He calls access to today's technology "such a blessing."
- He counts being born into a caring family as true luck.
- He calls having a support system of people who truly care about you "the most important asset I have."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Casey Adams argues that podcast campaign reporting undervalues what shows deliver because it centers on downloads, while modern shows span audio, YouTube and social. He positions Listener.com around omni-channel campaign reporting and outlines a four-step workflow for networks and brand partners.

chunks.heading: Podcast reporting undersells what shows deliver
chunks.text:
- Casey argues the podcast industry is underselling itself. A show today is audio, YouTube, and social content, and innovative brands are paying for all of it.
- Modern campaigns succeed when they are sold and measured across those channels, not audio alone.
- Most campaign reports still lead with downloads, which he calls "only one piece of what a show or network delivers."
- His diagnosis: reporting that stops at downloads understates the value of a show or network and weakens the case to brand partners.

chunks.heading: Positioning Listener.com around omni-channel campaign reporting
chunks.text:
- Heading into Q4, Casey's team sharpened Listener.com around one thing: omni-channel campaign reporting for the modern podcast industry.
- The product is positioned as a fix for a specific, felt problem (reporting that undersells shows) rather than as a broad platform.
- The call to action is aimed at that pain: "If your reporting is underselling your shows, let's fix that." Interested networks book a call with the team.

chunks.heading: The Listener workflow for networks and shows
chunks.text:
Casey lays out the workflow as four steps:

1. Pitch your network with one link.
2. Prove your true reach across episodes.
3. Run campaigns and watch pacing live.
4. Report results your brand partners can see for themselves.

- The sequence covers the full sales cycle: pitching, proving reach, delivering and monitoring, then reporting.
- The last step is built on transparency: brand partners see the results themselves instead of relying on a network's summary.

chunks.heading: How to sell podcast advertising more effectively
chunks.text:
- Sell the whole show: bundle audio, YouTube, and social content into the pitch, since that is what brands are already buying.
- Prove reach across episodes, not just single-episode downloads.
- Monitor campaign pacing live so delivery issues surface during the campaign instead of in the post-mortem.
- Give brand partners direct visibility into results so the report stands on its own.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A short LinkedIn promo for Listener.com's omni-channel campaign reporting, quoting Jomboy's VP of Sponsorship Sales. The pitch is that sponsor campaigns across audio, YouTube and social are reported in one place, giving sales teams what they need to sell and renew.

chunks.heading: Omni-channel campaign reporting on Listener.com
chunks.text:
- Casey promotes Listener.com's omni-channel campaign reporting for sponsor campaigns that run across audio, YouTube and social.
- The pitch: every podcast, video and clip is reported in one place, instead of stitched together from separate platforms.
- Casey frames the product's purpose as giving a sales team "everything your team needs to sell, report, and renew with confidence." Reporting is positioned as a sales and renewal tool, not just a measurement feature.

chunks.heading: Partner proof: Jomboy
chunks.text:

What we call a “podcast” today goes far beyond audio. Shows now live across YouTube, TikTok, Spotify, Apple, and social platforms, but the data behind them remains fragmented.

There’s no single place to truly understand your audience, track your growth, or clearly communicate your value. And that’s a problem if you’re trying to grow your show, attract sponsors, or make more money. So today, I’m proud to share what we’ve been working on.

@Listener is an AI-powered listener analytics platform built for modern podcasts, networks, and publishers.

We bring podcast and social data into one clean dashboard, giving podcasters, agencies, and networks a complete view of their audience, performance, and cross-platform growth.

It’s not just another analytics tool, it’s the infrastructure layer this industry has been missing. Because while podcasting is built on listeners, it’s the teams behind the content who need better tools.
